units.title: The wine world
units.summary: Where wine comes from: the wine belt, the classic countries and the names on bottles.

cards.title: Two bands around the globe
cards.body: Most of the world's vineyards sit in two bands, roughly **30° to 50° latitude** north and south of the equator. Closer to the poles, grapes struggle to ripen; closer to the equator, vines never get the winter rest they need.

cards.title: Old World and New World
cards.body:
- **Old World**: Europe and the Mediterranean, where winemaking goes back thousands of years: France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Germany, Austria, Greece.
- **New World**: places where European vines arrived later: the USA, Chile, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa.

cards.q: Between which latitudes are most vineyards found?
cards.explain: Most vineyards lie between roughly 30° and 50° latitude in both hemispheres, the wine belt, where it is warm enough to ripen grapes but cool enough to keep freshness. Altitude and cold ocean currents let some regions go beyond these limits.

cards.q: Old World or New World?
cards.explain: Old World means Europe's traditional regions, New World everywhere else. Italy has made wine for thousands of years; Chile's industry grew from Spanish missions in the 1500s, and the Americas, Australia and South Africa were planted by European settlers.

cards.q: Australia is considered an Old World wine country.
cards.explain: Australia is New World. Vines arrived with European settlers in 1788, and the style tends to be riper and fruitier, with the grape name on the label.

cards.q: Which country makes the most wine by volume in a typical year?
cards.explain: Italy and France usually trade first place by volume, with Spain third, although Spain has the largest vineyard area in the world. Spain's vines are widely spaced and yield less per hectare.

cards.title: The classic regions
cards.body:
- **Bordeaux**: red blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
- **Burgundy**: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
- **Champagne**: sparkling wine.
- **Rhône**: Syrah in the north, Grenache blends in the south.
- **Loire**: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc.
- **Alsace**: aromatic whites.

cards.q: Which French region is famous for sparkling wine?
cards.explain: Only sparkling wine from the Champagne region in north-east France may be called Champagne. The name is legally protected: elsewhere, the same method must be called Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta or similar.

cards.q: Highlighted on the map is…
cards.explain: Bordeaux lies on France's Atlantic coast, around the Gironde estuary and the Garonne and Dordogne rivers. The ocean moderates the climate, and the rivers split the region into Left Bank and Right Bank.

cards.q: Provence is famous for pale, dry rosé.
cards.explain: Provence is the world's rosé capital, along the Mediterranean coast: pale, dry, light and usually made from Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah. More than 80% of the region's wine is rosé.

cards.q: Match the French region to its grape
cards.explain: French labels name places, not grapes, so learning which grape grows where is essential. For example, red Burgundy is Pinot Noir, white Chablis is Chardonnay, and Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.title: The big names
cards.body:
- **Italy**: Chianti and Brunello (Sangiovese), Barolo (Nebbiolo), Prosecco.
- **Spain**: Rioja (Tempranillo), Cava, Sherry.
- **Germany**: Riesling.
- **USA**: Napa Valley Cabernet.
- **Argentina**: Malbec. **New Zealand**: Sauvignon Blanc. **Australia**: Shiraz.

cards.q: Match the country to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each country became famous worldwide for one star grape: Argentina for Malbec, New Zealand for Sauvignon Blanc, South Africa for Chenin Blanc and Pinotage, Australia for Shiraz. Matching them is a good way to guess a wine's origin.

cards.q: Rioja comes from which country?
cards.explain: Rioja lies in northern Spain along the Ebro river and is made mainly from Tempranillo. Its labels (Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva) tell you how long it was aged before release.

cards.q: Napa Valley is in…
cards.explain: Napa Valley is in California, north of San Francisco, and famous for Cabernet Sauvignon. Warm days and cool nights from the Pacific fog give ripe fruit and good acidity.

cards.q: Prosecco is a sparkling wine from Italy.
cards.explain: Prosecco comes from the Veneto and Friuli in north-east Italy and is made from the Glera grape. It usually gets its bubbles from a second fermentation in a tank, which keeps it fresh and fruity.

cards.title: Old World and New World
cards.body:
**Old World** means Europe's traditional wine countries: France, Italy, Spain, Germany, Portugal. Wines are usually named after the **place**.

**New World** means countries like the USA, Australia, Chile and New Zealand. Wines are often named after the **grape**, and styles tend to be riper and fruitier.

cards.title: Latitude and climate
cards.body:
Most vineyards lie between **30° and 50° latitude**. Closer to the poles, grapes struggle to ripen; closer to the equator, it is too hot for quality wine.

Altitude and cold ocean currents can cool a warm place: think of the high Andes or California's foggy coast.

cards.q: Old World wines are usually labeled by…
cards.explain: Old World wines are usually labeled by place: a Sancerre or a Chianti is named after where it comes from, not the grape. New World labels usually name the grape instead, like Chardonnay or Malbec.

cards.q: Most quality vineyards lie between 30° and 50° latitude.
cards.explain: This wine belt (about 30° to 50° latitude) gives enough warmth to ripen grapes and enough cool to keep freshness. Outside it, grapes either fail to ripen or lose their acidity.

cards.q: Match the country to a famous grape
cards.explain: Each New World country has a signature grape: Argentina for Malbec, New Zealand for Sauvignon Blanc, Chile for Carmenère, Australia for Shiraz. These grapes arrived with settlers and found a home.

cards.q: How can a region in a hot country still make fresh wines?
options: High altitude or cool ocean influence
cards.explain: Mountains and cold ocean currents lower temperatures, keeping acidity in the grapes. That is how Argentina's high Andean vineyards and Chile's Pacific-cooled valleys make fresh wines in hot countries.

cards.q: Wine regions in Europe are often called the ___ World.
cards.explain: Wine regions in Europe are called the Old World. Old World versus New World is shorthand for tradition-led versus fruit-led winemaking: Old World wines are typically more savory and structured, the New World riper and fruitier.

units.title: Food & wine
units.summary: How food changes the taste of wine, and the few rules that make pairing easy.

cards.title: Food changes wine
cards.body:
A wine that tastes perfect alone can turn harsh with the wrong food, and vice versa. Some food components make wine taste **worse**, others **better**.

- **Tougher on wine**: sweetness and umami make wine taste more bitter, more acidic, less fruity.
- **Kinder to wine**: salt and acidity make wine taste softer, fruitier and less acidic.

cards.q: A sweet dessert makes a dry wine taste…
cards.explain: Sweet food makes a dry wine taste more sour, bitter and thin. That is why a dessert needs a wine at least as sweet as the dish, such as Sauternes, Moscato d'Asti or late-harvest Riesling.

cards.q: Which food component makes wine taste softer and less bitter?
cards.explain: Salt is wine's friend: it reduces bitterness and acidity. Think salty Parmesan with Chianti, or oysters with Muscadet.

cards.q: Acidic foods make a wine taste less acidic.
cards.explain: Match acid with acid: when a dish is as acidic as the wine, such as a tomato sauce or a vinaigrette, the wine tastes rounder and fruitier. A crisp wine against a sharp dish otherwise tastes thin and sour.

cards.q: Mushrooms, cured meats and soy sauce are rich in ___.
cards.explain: Mushrooms, cured meats, aged cheese and soy sauce are rich in umami. Umami amplifies bitterness and acidity in wine, so choose fruity, low-tannin wines (Pinot Noir works well with mushrooms) or add salt, which reduces the effect.

cards.q: Match the food to its effect on wine
cards.explain: Three interactions explain most pairing successes and disasters: sweet makes wine taste drier and more sour; salt softens tannin and acidity; umami and chili amplify bitterness and heat. Thinking in terms of these effects beats memorizing pairings.

cards.title: Spice and protein
cards.body:
- **Chili heat** makes alcohol burn more and tannin taste bitter. Pick low-alcohol, off-dry, fruity whites such as Riesling or Gewürztraminer.
- **Fat and protein** soften tannin. That is why a big Cabernet loves a steak.

cards.q: Which wine best suits a spicy Thai curry?
cards.explain: A touch of sweetness and low alcohol calm the heat of a Thai curry, and an off-dry Riesling or Gewürztraminer is the classic answer. High-alcohol, tannic wines make chili burn more, because alcohol dissolves and spreads the capsaicin.

cards.q: Why does a tannic red work well with steak?
options: Protein and fat soften the tannin
cards.explain: Tannin binds to protein, so the meat softens the wine's grip, and the wine's tannin and acidity cut through the fat and refresh your mouth. This is why Cabernet Sauvignon and steak is the classic pairing.

cards.q: Chili heat makes wines taste less alcoholic.
cards.explain: The reverse: chili heightens the burning sensation of alcohol, so wines taste hotter and more alcoholic with spicy food. Choose lower-alcohol wines, and a touch of sweetness helps.

cards.q: With chili dishes, choose wines low in alcohol and ___.
cards.explain: Tannin and alcohol both clash with spicy heat, making the food taste hotter and the wine harsher. Choose wines low in alcohol and tannin, such as off-dry Riesling or a light, fruity red served chilled.

cards.title: Match weight, then flavor
cards.body:
Pair **light with light** and **rich with rich**. A delicate sole would be crushed by a Barossa Shiraz; a beef stew would make a Pinot Grigio vanish.

And remember regional pairing: **what grows together goes together**. Light seafood loves crisp, salty coastal whites such as **Albariño** from Spain's Atlantic coast or **Muscadet** from the Loire.

cards.q: Match the dish to the classic wine
cards.explain: Each is a textbook match: brine with crisp Muscadet, tangy goat cheese with high-acid Sauvignon Blanc, steak with tannic Cabernet, and rich duck with fresh, fruity Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Which wine suits a light seafood salad?
cards.explain: Light, fresh and saline, Albariño from Rías Baixas in Galicia matches delicate seafood perfectly, which is what the region's coast eats. The other wines are powerful and would overwhelm the dish: match the weight of the wine to the weight of the food.

cards.q: 'What grows together goes together' means local wines often suit local food.
cards.explain: Chianti with Tuscan steak, Sherry with tapas, Alsace Riesling with choucroute: centuries of trial and error.

cards.q: Which pairing follows the weight principle?
cards.explain: The weight principle: delicate dishes with light wines, hearty dishes with full wines. A hearty stew needs a full-bodied red with enough flavor and tannin to stand up to it, or the wine disappears.

cards.title: Sweetness and spice
cards.body:
**Sweet food** makes dry wine taste thin and sour, so pick a wine at least as sweet as the dish.

**Spicy heat** is made hotter by alcohol and tannin. Off-dry, low-alcohol whites like Riesling cool things down.

cards.title: Match the weight
cards.body:
Pair light with light and rich with rich. A delicate fish needs a light white; a braised beef stew wants a full-bodied red.

Then think of **acid**: acidic wines cut through fat and salt, and love tomato and lemon.

cards.q: What happens to a dry wine served with a sweet dessert?
cards.explain: Sweet food makes dry wine seem more acidic and bitter, and strips out its fruit. The wine should be at least as sweet as the food, which is why dessert wines exist.

cards.q: Which wine suits a spicy Thai curry best?
cards.explain: A touch of sweetness and low alcohol soothe chili heat; tannin and alcohol amplify it. Off-dry Riesling, with its high acidity and low alcohol, is a favorite with spicy Asian dishes.

cards.q: High-acid wines go well with fatty and salty foods.
cards.explain: Acidity cuts through richness and is balanced by salt, like Champagne with fries. High-acid wines such as Chablis, Champagne and Riesling refresh the palate after fatty or salty bites, so they suit fried foods and cheese.

cards.q: Match the dish to a classic wine
cards.explain: Classic pairings work through contrast or harmony: acid with acid (Sancerre and goat cheese), tannin with protein (Cabernet and steak), and sweet with salty (Port and blue cheese). Learn the logic and you can improvise.

cards.q: Tannic red wine can taste metallic with oily ___.
cards.explain: Fish oils and tannin clash and leave a metallic taste. With oily fish pick a white, a rosé or a light low-tannin red such as Pinot Noir, chilled slightly.

units.title: Serving & storing
units.summary: Temperatures, glasses, opening bottles, storing wine and spotting faults.

cards.title: Not too cold, not too warm
cards.body:
Temperature changes how wine tastes. Too cold mutes aromas and makes tannins harsh; too warm makes alcohol stand out.

- **Sparkling & sweet**: well chilled, 6–10 °C
- **Light whites & rosé**: chilled, 7–10 °C
- **Full whites**: lightly chilled, 10–13 °C
- **Light reds**: 13 °C
- **Fuller reds**: room temperature, 15–18 °C

cards.q: At what temperature should sparkling wine be served?
cards.explain: Sparkling wine is served well chilled, about 6–10 °C. Cold keeps carbon dioxide dissolved, so the bubbles stay fine and lively and the wine tastes refreshing. Too warm and it foams over and tastes flabby; too cold and the aromas go silent.

cards.q: Light reds like Beaujolais can be served slightly chilled.
cards.explain: Light reds like Beaujolais (Gamay) have low tannin and juicy acidity, so around 13 °C brings out their fresh fruit. A slight chill stops the alcohol from tasting hot and makes them more refreshing.

cards.q: Serving a full-bodied red too cold will…
cards.explain: Cold emphasizes tannin and bitterness and mutes the aromas, so a full-bodied red tastes harsh and closed. Serve fuller reds at 15–18 °C: cooler than a warm room, which makes alcohol burn.

cards.q: Full-bodied whites such as oaked Chardonnay are best ___ chilled.
cards.explain: At 10–13 °C, richer whites such as oaked Chardonnay show their aromas and creamy texture. Straight from a very cold fridge, they taste thin and dull; a cool cellar temperature is better.

cards.title: The right glass
cards.body:
- **Reds**: a large bowl gives room to swirl and gather aromas.
- **Whites & rosé**: medium-sized, to keep them cool.
- **Sparkling**: a tall flute or tulip keeps the bubbles longer.

Fill only to the widest part of the bowl, or less, so there is room to swirl.

cards.title: Opening sparkling wine safely
cards.body:
The pressure in a Champagne bottle is about 5–6 atmospheres, roughly three times a car tire.

- Chill it well.
- Keep a thumb on the cork and point it away from people.
- Hold the cork and **turn the bottle**, easing it out with a gentle sigh, not a pop.

cards.q: Why do red wine glasses have a large bowl?
options: To allow swirling and gather aromas
cards.explain: The large bowl gives room to swirl, which releases aromas, and the wide shape concentrates them toward your nose as it narrows at the top. Big reds are rich in aromatic compounds, so they benefit most.

cards.q: When opening sparkling wine, you should twist the bottle, not the cork.
cards.explain: Hold the cork still and turn the bottle slowly: it gives you control and a quiet, safe opening. A cork can leave the bottle at around 25 mph, so keep a hand over it and point it away from people.

cards.q: Which glass is best for sparkling wine?
cards.explain: A tall, narrow flute or tulip reduces the surface area so bubbles last longer and the aroma stays concentrated. A wide coupe lets bubbles escape quickly, though a white-wine glass is a good all-round option for fine Champagne.

cards.title: Store wine like a cellar
cards.body:
- **Cool and steady**: about 10–15 °C, without big swings.
- **Dark**: light can damage wine.
- **On its side** for corked bottles, so the cork stays moist.
- Once open, re-seal and refrigerate. Most wines last 1–3 days; fortified wines last longer.

cards.title: Common faults
cards.body:
- **Cork taint (TCA)**: musty, damp cardboard, muted fruit.
- **Oxidation**: brownish color, bruised apple, flat.
- **Heat damage**: cooked, jammy flavors, sometimes a pushed-up cork.

cards.q: A wine smelling of damp cardboard is probably…
cards.explain: Cork taint is caused by TCA, a compound that can form in natural cork. It is not harmful, but it gives a musty, damp-cardboard smell and flattens the fruit. Around 1 in 20 bottles with natural cork used to be affected.

cards.q: Bottles with natural corks are best stored standing upright.
cards.explain: False: lie them on their side so the cork stays in contact with the wine, swells and keeps the seal. A dry cork can shrink and let air in, which would oxidize the wine. Screwcaps do not need this.

cards.q: Wine should be stored somewhere cool, dark and at a ___ temperature.
cards.explain: Wine should be stored somewhere cool, dark and at a constant temperature, ideally about 12–14 °C. Swings make the wine expand and contract, pushing air past the cork, and heat ages it quickly.

cards.q: A white wine that has turned brownish and smells of bruised apples is probably…
cards.explain: Too much oxygen dulls the fruit and browns the color. Some styles, like Oloroso Sherry, are deliberately oxidative.

cards.title: Opening and keeping
cards.body:
Once open, wine meets oxygen. Most still wines keep **2–5 days** with the cork back in, in the fridge. Sparkling wine keeps 1–3 days with a stopper.

Fortified wines like Tawny Port can keep for weeks.

cards.title: Decanting
cards.body:
**Decanting** means pouring wine into another vessel. It separates an old wine from its **sediment**, and lets young, tannic wines breathe so they taste softer.

Pour slowly and stop when you see sediment reach the neck.

cards.q: Why would you decant an old red wine?
cards.explain: Old reds throw a deposit of tannin and pigment as sediment; decanting separates the clear wine from it. Pour slowly with a light behind the neck, and stop when the sediment reaches the shoulder. Young wines are decanted for air instead.

cards.q: Sparkling wine should be served colder than full-bodied red wine.
cards.explain: Sparkling wine is best well chilled (6–10 °C), while full reds taste best around 15–18 °C. Cold keeps bubbles lively, while warmth lets a red's aromas open.

cards.q: How long does an opened bottle of still wine usually keep in the fridge?
cards.explain: Oxygen slowly flattens the fruit, so an opened still wine lasts 3–5 days in the fridge with the cork back in. Fortified wines like Port and Sherry last much longer because of their alcohol, though a fino is best within a week.

cards.q: Match the wine to its serving temperature
cards.explain: Too cold mutes aromas, and too warm makes alcohol stand out. Sparkling is chilled, light whites and rosés cold, full whites cool, light reds slightly cool and full reds just below room temperature.

cards.q: A wine that smells of wet cardboard is probably ___.
cards.explain: Cork taint (TCA) gives a musty, damp-cardboard smell and flattens the fruit. It is harmless but ruins the wine, and a bottle like this can be returned to the shop or restaurant.

units.title: Scores & critics
units.summary: What 92 points means, who gives the scores, and how to use them without being ruled by them.

cards.title: Why wine has scores
cards.body:
Shelf tags, apps and auction catalogs are full of numbers: **91 points**, **96 points**. They come from critics who taste thousands of wines a year and sum up each one in a single score.

The most common is the **100-point scale**, popularized in the 1980s by the American critic **Robert Parker** and his newsletter *The Wine Advocate*. It copies the grades of an American school report.

cards.title: Reading the numbers
cards.body:
Every wine starts at **50**. The rest rewards what is in the glass:

- **96–100 · Classic**: a great wine, complex and long. Rare.
- **90–95 · Outstanding**: real character and style.
- **85–89 · Very good**: well made, with something special.
- **80–84 · Good**: solid and pleasant.
- **Below 80**: plain, or with flaws.

In practice almost every score you see in a shop is between **85 and 100**: shops quote the good ones.

cards.title: What critics look at
cards.body:
A score is a judgment of **quality**, not of personal taste. Critics weigh the same things you learn in this course:

- **Balance**: fruit, acid, tannin and alcohol in harmony.
- **Length**: how long the flavor lasts after you swallow.
- **Intensity** and **complexity**: how much there is, and how many layers.
- **Typicity**: does it taste of its grape and place?

Many critics also give a **drinking window**, such as "2026–2040".

cards.q: On the 100-point scale, a wine scored 92 is…
cards.explain: On the 100-point scale, 90–95 is outstanding: a wine with real character and complexity. 96–100 is classic, 85–89 very good, and anything under 80 is generally not recommended. Remember that critics rarely publish scores below 80.

cards.q: On the 100-point scale, the lowest score a wine can get is 0.
cards.explain: Every wine starts at 50; the 50 points above that reward quality. In practice published scores sit mostly between 80 and 100.

cards.q: Who made the 100-point scale famous?
cards.explain: Robert Parker's newsletter The Wine Advocate used it from 1978, and his praise of the 1982 Bordeaux vintage made him the world's most influential critic.

cards.title: The big names
cards.body:
- **Robert Parker / The Wine Advocate** (USA): the critic who made scores matter. Parker retired in 2019; the Advocate goes on with a team.
- **Wine Spectator** (USA): a magazine scoring about 15,000 wines a year, tasted blind. Its **Top 100** list each November moves markets.
- **James Suckling** (USA/Asia): former Spectator critic, generous scores, big on Italy and Bordeaux.
- **Vinous** (Antonio Galloni, USA): detailed reviews, strong on Italy and California.
- **Wine Enthusiast** (USA): magazine scores on the 100-point scale, broad coverage.

cards.title: The 20-point school
cards.body:
Many European critics prefer **20 points**:

- **Jancis Robinson MW** (UK): one of the most respected voices in wine, co-author of *The World Atlas of Wine*. A 17/20 is a very good wine; 18.5+ is exceptional.
- **Decanter** (UK): the magazine now gives 100-point scores, and runs the **Decanter World Wine Awards**, the biggest wine competition, with medals instead of points.
- **La Revue du Vin de France** and **Bettane+Desseauve** (France) also score out of 20.

cards.title: Crowds and medals
cards.body:
**Vivino** gathers ratings from millions of drinkers on a **1–5 star** scale. A 4.2 is very good; it tells you what people enjoy, which is not always what critics praise.

**Medals** on a bottle come from competitions: a gold medal means a panel liked it more than the other wines in that flight. Useful, but there are hundreds of competitions.

cards.q: Match the critic to the scale they are known for
cards.explain: Parker made the 100-point scale famous, Jancis Robinson scores out of 20, Vivino uses 1–5 stars, and competitions such as the DWWA award medals.

cards.q: Which magazine publishes a famous 'Top 100' list every November?
cards.explain: Wine Spectator's Top 100 of the year, published every November, is one of the most watched lists in the trade. A wine that makes it can sell out within weeks, which is why price and availability matter as well as score.

cards.q: Jancis Robinson usually gives scores out of 20.
cards.explain: Like many European critics, Jancis Robinson scores out of 20: 17 is very good and 18.5 or higher is exceptional. The 100-point scale was popularized by American critic Robert Parker, and the two scales roughly translate: 17 is about 90.

cards.title: A number is not your taste
cards.body:
A 95-point Barolo is a great wine, but if you dislike firm tannin you may prefer an 89-point Pinot Noir. Use scores to **find well-made wines**, then trust your own palate.

Read the **note**, not just the number: "firm, needs time" tells you more than "94".

cards.title: Value hides below 90
cards.body:
Prices jump at **90 points**: shops love to quote them. Wines scored **87–89** are often the best value in the shop: very good wine without the score premium.

Also compare **like with like**: 90 points for a $12 Côtes du Rhône is a bigger achievement than 90 for a $200 Bordeaux.

cards.title: Scoring your own wines
cards.body: In the Journal, every tasting is scored on the **100-point scale**. Start at 50 and add points for balance, length, intensity and complexity. After a few tastings, your scores become a map of your own taste.

cards.q: Why are wines scored 87–89 often good value?
options: Prices jump once a wine reaches 90 points
They are made only in Europe
cards.explain: Shops and producers market 90+ scores heavily, so the price jumps at that line. A wine scoring 87–89 is often very similar in quality but noticeably cheaper, which is the sweet spot for value buyers.

cards.q: A high score means you will personally enjoy the wine.
cards.explain: A score judges quality and typicity. Your own taste for, say, tannin or oak may differ; read the tasting note too.

units.title: The story of wine
units.summary: From Georgian clay jars to phylloxera, the 1855 classification and the Judgment of Paris: how the wine world was made.

cards.title: Eight thousand years in clay
cards.body:
The oldest traces of grape wine, about **8,000 years** old, come from **Georgia** in the South Caucasus: residues inside clay jars. Georgians still ferment wine in buried clay vessels called **qvevri**, a method UNESCO lists as world heritage.

The oldest known winery, about **6,100 years** old, was found in the **Areni-1 cave** in Armenia, with a pressing floor and fermentation jars.

cards.title: Egypt, Phoenicia and Greece
cards.body:
In **ancient Egypt**, wine was for kings and priests; jars in Tutankhamun's tomb were labeled with the vintage, the estate and the chief winemaker, an early wine label.

**Phoenician** traders, from today's **Lebanon**, carried vines and wine across the Mediterranean. The **Greeks** planted vines in southern Italy, which they called **Oenotria**, "land of vines", and in Provence, at Marseille, around 600 BC.

cards.title: Rome builds Europe's vineyards
cards.body:
The **Romans** spread the vine wherever their legions went: up the **Rhône**, into **Bordeaux** (Burdigala), **Burgundy**, the **Mosel** and the **Rhine**. Many of Europe's great regions began as Roman vineyards along rivers, which carried both water for the vines and barrels to market.

Roman wine was often sweetened with honey or flavored with herbs and resin, and drunk mixed with water.

cards.q: Where do the oldest traces of grape wine (about 8,000 years old) come from?
cards.explain: Residues in clay jars in Georgia, in the South Caucasus, are the oldest evidence of grape wine. Georgians still use buried clay qvevri.

cards.q: What did the Greeks call southern Italy?
cards.explain: The Greeks called southern Italy Oenotria, the land of vines, because they planted vineyards there from about the 8th century BC. Burdigala was the Roman name for Bordeaux, and Roman legions spread vines through Gaul.

cards.q: The Romans spread vineyards along rivers such as the Rhône, Mosel and Rhine.
cards.explain: Rivers gave vines water, warmth from reflected sun, and a road for barrels to market. Many great regions began as Roman vineyards.

cards.title: The monks of Burgundy
cards.body:
After Rome fell, **monasteries** kept winemaking alive. In Burgundy, **Benedictine** monks of Cluny and **Cistercian** monks of Cîteaux (founded 1098) spent centuries tasting the wines of each plot, building walls around the best ones.

The **Clos de Vougeot**, walled by the Cistercians in the 14th century, is the most famous. Their idea that each **climat** (named plot) tastes different is the root of **terroir** and of Burgundy's Grands Crus.

cards.title: Bordeaux becomes English
cards.body:
In **1152** Eleanor of Aquitaine married **Henry Plantagenet**, soon King Henry II of England. Bordeaux became English for **three centuries**, until 1453.

English merchants shipped huge volumes of light red **clairet**, the origin of the British word **claret** for red Bordeaux. Trade, not monks, shaped Bordeaux: a merchant's city facing the sea.

cards.title: The Dutch drain the Médoc
cards.body:
In the **1600s**, **Dutch** engineers drained the marshy Médoc, revealing the **gravel ridges** where Cabernet Sauvignon would thrive. Dutch traders also wanted sweet whites and brandy, boosting Sauternes and Cognac.

By the 1700s, estates such as **Haut-Brion**, Lafite and Latour were selling their wine **by name** in London: the birth of the "château" brand.

cards.q: Which monks walled the Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy?
cards.explain: The Cistercians of Cîteaux, founded in 1098, studied Burgundy's plots for centuries and walled the Clos de Vougeot.

cards.q: Bordeaux belonged to England for three centuries after Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in ___.
cards.explain: The marriage in 1152 of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry Plantagenet made Bordeaux English until 1453. The English still call red Bordeaux claret, from the French clairet, a light red, and London became its biggest market.

cards.q: Dutch engineers drained the Médoc's marshes in the 1600s.
cards.explain: Dutch engineers drained the Médoc's marshes in the 1600s. Draining revealed the gravel ridges of the Left Bank, where Cabernet Sauvignon ripens on warm stones, and that created the region's great estates.

cards.title: The plague from America
cards.body:
In the **1860s**, vines in the southern Rhône began to wither and die. The culprit, identified in **1868** by the botanist **Jules-Émile Planchon**, was **phylloxera**: a tiny yellow aphid-like insect that feeds on vine **roots**.

It had crossed the Atlantic on American vines brought to Europe as botanical curiosities. Faster steamships meant the bugs survived the trip.

cards.title: A continent's vineyards destroyed
cards.body:
Over the next **thirty years**, phylloxera spread through almost every European vineyard: France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Germany, then Australia, South Africa and California.

France lost around **40% of its vines**. Growers tried everything: flooding vineyards, injecting carbon disulfide into the soil, even burying live toads under vines. Millions emigrated; some French winemakers moved to **Rioja**, raising its quality.

cards.title: The cure: grafting
cards.body:
American vines had evolved with phylloxera and their roots resist it. The solution, championed by Planchon and the American entomologist **Charles Valentine Riley**, was to **graft** European *Vitis vinifera* onto **American rootstocks**. **Thomas Munson** in Texas bred many of the rootstocks used.

Today almost every vine in the world grows on American roots. The fruit, and the wine, still come from the European vine on top.

cards.title: The survivors
cards.body:
A few places never had phylloxera, or it couldn't survive there:

- **Chile**, protected by the Andes, the Pacific and the Atacama desert.
- **Sandy soils** such as Colares in Portugal and parts of the Mosel; the insect can't move through sand.
- **Santorini**'s volcanic ash, and parts of **South Australia**, kept free by strict quarantine. Barossa has Shiraz vines from the **1840s**.

After phylloxera, fraud and fake wine were common; the **AOC** system (1935) was partly France's answer.

cards.q: What does phylloxera attack?
cards.explain: The insect feeds on roots; the vine slowly starves. American vines' roots can resist it, European vines' cannot.

cards.q: How did growers finally beat phylloxera?
options: Grafting European vines onto American rootstocks
cards.explain: Grafting keeps the European vine's fruit on resistant American roots. Almost every vineyard in the world is grafted today.

cards.q: Chile's vineyards were never hit by phylloxera.
cards.explain: Chile's vineyards were never hit by phylloxera, since the Andes, the Pacific and the Atacama desert isolate the country. Many Chilean vines still grow on their own roots, which is rare in the world.

cards.q: Which French botanist identified phylloxera in 1868?
cards.explain: Planchon found the insect on dying vines in the southern Rhône and helped promote grafting as the cure.

cards.title: A list for a world fair
cards.body:
For the **1855 Exposition Universelle** in Paris, Emperor **Napoleon III** wanted Bordeaux's best wines shown. The merchants of Bordeaux ranked the châteaux by **price**, the market's long verdict on quality.

The result: **61 red wines** in five tiers, from First to Fifth Growth, almost all from the **Médoc**, plus **Haut-Brion** from Graves; and a list of **Sauternes and Barsac**, with **Château d'Yquem** alone at the top as *Premier Cru Supérieur*.

cards.title: Almost unchanged since
cards.body:
The list has barely moved. **Cantemerle** was added in 1856, and in **1973** **Mouton Rothschild** was promoted to First Growth after Baron Philippe de Rothschild's fifty-year campaign. Its motto changed from "First I cannot be, second I do not deign to be, Mouton I am" to "**First I am, second I was, Mouton does not change**."

The five First Growths: **Lafite**, **Latour**, **Margaux**, **Haut-Brion** and **Mouton**.

cards.q: How did the merchants decide the 1855 ranking?
options: By the price the wines fetched
By the size of the estate
By the age of the château
cards.explain: Brokers took price over many years as the market's verdict on quality, so the ranking reflects reputation and market value. The brokers were practical: they knew what each château's wine had been fetching.

cards.q: Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
cards.explain: The only promotion of a First Growth in the list's history. Pétrus and Cheval Blanc are on the Right Bank and not in the 1855 list.

cards.title: A tasting nobody expected to matter
cards.body:
On **24 May 1976**, the English wine merchant **Steven Spurrier** held a blind tasting in Paris. Nine French experts (top chefs, sommeliers and the head of the Appellation authority) tasted top **Bordeaux** and **Burgundy** against unknown wines from **California**.

Only one journalist came: **George Taber** of *Time* magazine.

cards.title: California wins
cards.body:
The winners were both Californian:

- **Reds**: **Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973** Cabernet Sauvignon, ahead of Mouton Rothschild and Haut-Brion.
- **Whites**: **Chateau Montelena 1973** Chardonnay, ahead of top white Burgundies such as Meursault-Charmes.

Taber's story, "Judgment of Paris", went around the world. One judge asked for her scorecard back.

cards.title: Why it changed everything
cards.body:
The result proved that great wine could be made **outside France**. Investment poured into **Napa**, then Oregon, Australia, Chile and beyond. French producers began investing abroad: Mouton Rothschild partnered with Robert Mondavi to create **Opus One** (1979).

French critics said red Bordeaux needs time. A **rematch in 2006**, thirty years on, again put California reds on top, led by **Ridge Monte Bello 1971**.

cards.q: Which red won the 1976 Judgment of Paris?
cards.explain: A Napa Cabernet from Stag's Leap Wine Cellars beat the best of Bordeaux in 1976, judged blind by French experts. The Judgment of Paris proved that great wine could be made outside France, and changed the wine world.

cards.q: Which wine won the white flight?
cards.explain: Chateau Montelena, from Calistoga in northern Napa, beat top white Burgundies in the 1976 Judgment of Paris. It was a Chardonnay, and the result stunned French critics.

cards.q: The 1976 tasting was judged by Californian experts.
cards.explain: All nine judges were French, which is what made the result so shocking. The wines were tasted blind, so the judges thought they were picking French wine, and the Californian winners were a surprise.

cards.q: The English merchant who organized the 1976 tasting was Steven ___.
cards.explain: Steven Spurrier ran a wine shop and school in Paris; George Taber was the Time journalist who reported it.

cards.title: Scientists in the cellar
cards.body:
After the war, **Émile Peynaud** in Bordeaux and others brought science to winemaking: clean cellars, control of **malolactic** conversion and **temperature-controlled** fermentation in steel. Wine became more reliable everywhere.

**Stainless steel** tanks with cooling jackets made fresh, fruity whites possible in warm places like Australia and Spain.

cards.title: Critics and the globe
cards.body:
**Robert Parker**'s praise of the **1982 Bordeaux** vintage, when others doubted it, made him the world's most powerful critic, and made ripe, rich styles fashionable in the 1990s.

**Flying winemakers** from Australia and Bordeaux consulted around the world; **Malbec** turned Argentina into a star; New Zealand's **Sauvignon Blanc** (Cloudy Bay, 1985) created a new classic.

cards.title: Today and tomorrow
cards.body:
The pendulum has swung back toward **freshness**, less new oak, organic and biodynamic farming, natural wines, and old local grapes rescued from extinction.

**Climate change** is moving the map: English sparkling wine now wins blind tastings, harvests in Champagne are weeks earlier than 30 years ago, and growers plant higher and cooler.

cards.q: Which vintage made Robert Parker famous?
cards.explain: Robert Parker called 1982 a great Bordeaux vintage when others were cautious; he was right, and his influence soared. His 100-point scale then shaped what wine was made and what it cost.

cards.q: Climate change is making harvests earlier in regions such as Champagne.
cards.explain: Warmer seasons ripen grapes sooner; Champagne now picks weeks earlier than a generation ago, and cooler places such as England are rising.

units.title: Appellations to know
units.summary: Every Level 2 region on a card, with its map, grapes and climate.

cards.title: France
cards.body:
The benchmark for almost every classic style. France's regions gave the world its most imitated grapes, its appellation system and the very idea of terroir.

- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah.
- **Climate:** Cool continental in the north and east, maritime on the Atlantic coast, Mediterranean in the south.
- **Quality system:** AOC/AOP (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée/Protégée) rules control where grapes grow, which varieties are allowed, yields and winemaking. IGP (Vin de Pays) gives more freedom; Vin de France is the most basic category.
- Labels usually name the place, not the grape: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc, red Burgundy is Pinot Noir.
- Champagne, Bordeaux and Burgundy are among the most valuable wine regions on earth.

cards.title: Bordeaux
cards.body:
The world's most famous red wine region: blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from châteaux on either side of the Gironde estuary, plus great sweet and dry whites.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Sauvignon Blanc.
- **Climate:** Moderate maritime, moderated by the Atlantic and the Gironde estuary; vintages vary with autumn rain.
- **Quality system:** The 1855 Classification ranked Médoc (and one Graves) châteaux from First to Fifth Growth; Sauternes was ranked too. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years. Pomerol has none.
- Blending spreads risk: Merlot ripens early, Cabernet Sauvignon late.
- The five First Growths are Lafite, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion and Mouton Rothschild (promoted in 1973).

cards.title: Burgundy
cards.body:
Terroir taken to its extreme: a narrow strip of slopes where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay change character from one vineyard to the next.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gamay.
- **Climate:** Cool continental: cold winters, warm summers, risk of spring frost and hail. Vineyards face east and south-east for morning sun.
- **Quality system:** A pyramid: Regional (Bourgogne) → Village (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin) → Premier Cru → Grand Cru (33 vineyards, about 1–2% of production).
- Vineyards are split between many owners, so a Grand Cru like Clos de Vougeot has more than 80 producers.
- A 'climat' is a precisely named vineyard plot; Burgundy's climats are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

cards.title: Rhône Valley
cards.body:
Two regions in one: the narrow, steep Northern Rhône devoted to Syrah, and the broad, sunny Southern Rhône of Grenache-based blends.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier, Marsanne & Roussanne.
- **Climate:** North: moderate continental, steep granite slopes. South: Mediterranean, hot and dry, swept by the cold Mistral wind.
- **Quality system:** Côtes du Rhône → Côtes du Rhône Villages → named villages → crus such as Gigondas and Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
- Châteauneuf-du-Pape allows 13 grape varieties.
- Côte-Rôtie means 'roasted slope', after its steep sun-baked terraces.

cards.title: Loire Valley
cards.body:
France's longest river and a paradise of fresh, high-acid wines: Muscadet, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Melon de Bourgogne, Gamay.
- **Climate:** Cool: maritime near the Atlantic, becoming continental inland.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Bordeaux**?
cards.explain: Bordeaux: The world's most famous red wine region: blends of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from châteaux on either side of the Gironde estuary, plus great sweet and dry whites.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Burgundy**?
cards.explain: Burgundy: Terroir taken to its extreme: a narrow strip of slopes where Pinot Noir and Chardonnay change character from one vineyard to the next.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Champagne
cards.body:
The home of the world's most celebrated sparkling wine, made by the traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Meunier.
- **Climate:** Cool continental at the northern limit of grape growing; chalk subsoil stores water and reflects light.
- **Quality system:** Villages are rated: 17 Grand Cru and 42 Premier Cru villages.
- Non-vintage Champagne must spend at least 15 months in bottle, 12 of them on lees; vintage at least 3 years.
- Most Champagne is a blend of many villages and years, assembled by large houses.

cards.title: Chablis
cards.body:
Steely, unoaked or lightly oaked Chardonnay: green apple, lemon and wet stones with high acidity. Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** The northernmost part of Burgundy: cool, with frost risk. Kimmeridgian limestone full of fossil oyster shells.

cards.title: Côtes du Rhône
cards.body:
The big regional appellation, mostly in the south: juicy, spicy red blends with great value.

- **Where:** Rhône Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre.

cards.title: Sancerre
cards.body:
The classic Sauvignon Blanc: citrus, gooseberry and flinty minerality, with high acidity. Also light Pinot Noir reds and rosés.

- **Where:** Loire Valley, France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir.
- **Climate:** Cool continental; chalk, flint (silex) and limestone soils.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Champagne**?
cards.explain: Champagne: The home of the world's most celebrated sparkling wine, made by the traditional method from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Chablis**?
cards.explain: Chablis: Steely, unoaked or lightly oaked Chardonnay: green apple, lemon and wet stones with high acidity. Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Italy
cards.body:
Wine is made in every one of Italy's 20 regions, with hundreds of native grapes. Its wines are made for the table: high acidity, savory and food-friendly.

- **Grapes:** Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Pinot Grigio, Glera, Corvina.
- **Climate:** Alpine north, Mediterranean south; the Apennine mountains and the sea moderate the heat almost everywhere.
- **Quality system:** DOCG (strictest, guaranteed) → DOC → IGT (regional, more flexible, home of many Super Tuscans) → Vino. Classico marks a historic heartland; Riserva means longer ageing; Superiore, higher alcohol or stricter rules.

cards.title: Spain
cards.body:
The country with the most vineyard area in the world: Rioja and Ribera del Duero reds, Cava, Albariño and the unique fortified Sherry.

- **Grapes:** Tempranillo, Grenache, Albariño, Verdejo, Macabeo.
- **Climate:** Mostly hot and dry; the central plateau (Meseta) is high and continental; green, rainy Atlantic north-west.
- **Quality system:** DOCa/DOQ (Rioja, Priorat) → DO → Vino de la Tierra. Age terms: Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva (longer ageing in oak and bottle).

cards.title: United States
cards.body:
Wine is made in all 50 states, but the West Coast leads: Napa Cabernet, Sonoma Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Oregon Pinot and Washington's Bordeaux varieties.

- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot.
- **Climate:** California: Mediterranean, cooled by Pacific fog and breezes. Oregon: cool and wet. Eastern Washington: hot, dry desert irrigated by rivers.
- **Quality system:** Wines are labeled by grape. AVAs (American Viticultural Areas) define places; a varietal wine must contain at least 75% of the named grape.

cards.title: Australia
cards.body:
Bold, fruit-driven Shiraz made Australia famous, but its cool regions now shine for Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling.

- **Grapes:** Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sémillon.
- **Climate:** Mostly warm to hot; quality regions are in the cooler south, near the coast or at altitude.
- **Quality system:** Labeled by grape; Geographical Indications (GIs) define zones, regions and subregions.
- Some of the world's oldest vines, ungrafted Shiraz and Grenache from the 1840s, still grow in the Barossa.
- South Australia has never had phylloxera.

cards.title: New Zealand
cards.body:
Intense, pure-fruited wines. Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became a global style; Central Otago and Martinborough make fine Pinot Noir.

- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Grigio, Syrah.
- **Climate:** Cool maritime: no vineyard is more than about 130 km from the sea. Long, sunny days with cool nights.

cards.title: Marlborough
cards.body:
New Zealand's largest region: pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit, gooseberry and grassy notes.

- **Where:** New Zealand.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.
- **Climate:** Sunny and dry with cold nights, ideal for aromatic intensity and high acidity.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Marlborough**?
cards.explain: Marlborough: New Zealand's largest region: pungent Sauvignon Blanc with passion fruit, gooseberry and grassy notes.

units.title: In the vineyard
units.summary: The vine's year, climate and weather, and what terroir really means.

cards.title: A year in the vineyard
cards.body:
A grapevine follows the same cycle every year:

- **Budburst**: green shoots emerge in spring.
- **Flowering & fruit set**: tiny flowers become berries.
- **Véraison**: berries soften and change color.
- **Harvest**: in autumn, when sugar, acid and flavor are in balance: **September and October** in the Northern Hemisphere, **March and April** in the Southern.
- **Dormancy**: the vine rests in winter and is pruned.

cards.title: What a grape needs
cards.body: Vines need **sunlight** (to make sugar), **warmth** (to ripen), **water** and **nutrients**. Most quality vineyards lie between **30° and 50°** latitude in both hemispheres.

cards.q: What is véraison?
options: When grapes change color and start to ripen
cards.explain: At véraison black grapes turn from green to purple, white grapes become translucent, and sugar starts to build fast.

cards.q: Most of the world's vineyards lie between which latitudes?
cards.explain: Closer to the equator it is too hot (no winter rest); closer to the poles it is too cold to ripen grapes.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, harvest usually happens in September and ___.
cards.explain: In the Northern Hemisphere, harvest usually happens in September and October, though warm regions start in August. In the Southern Hemisphere the seasons flip: harvest falls around February to April.

cards.q: Put each stage with its season (Northern Hemisphere)
cards.explain: The vine's year: budburst in spring, flowering in late spring, fruit set in early summer, véraison in late summer, harvest in autumn, and dormancy in winter. This cycle drives the whole calendar of a wine region.

cards.title: Cool vs warm climates
cards.body:
**Climate** is a region's long-term average; **weather** is what happens in a given year.

- **Cool climates**: higher acidity, lower alcohol, lighter body, green and citrus fruit (or red fruit in reds).
- **Warm climates**: lower acidity, higher alcohol, fuller body, stone, tropical and black fruit.

cards.title: Natural air conditioning
cards.body:
Warm regions can still make fresh wines thanks to:

- **Altitude**: temperatures drop about 0.6 °C every 100 m.
- **Ocean currents and fog**: California's Pacific fog, Chile's Humboldt Current.
- **Large rivers and lakes**, which moderate temperatures.

cards.q: A cool-climate wine typically has…
cards.explain: Less heat means less sugar (so less alcohol) and more acid retained in the grapes. Cool-climate wines tend to be lighter, crisper and more aromatic, such as Chablis or Mosel Riesling.

cards.q: Weather explains why the same wine can vary from vintage to vintage.
cards.explain: A cold spring, a hot summer or autumn rain can change a vintage. That is why vintages matter most in marginal climates.

cards.q: How do high-altitude vineyards in hot countries keep wines fresh?
cards.explain: High-altitude vineyards stay cooler: Argentina's Mendoza vineyards sit at 800–1,500 m, where cool nights preserve acidity and color, even though days are hot. Every 100 m of altitude cools it by about 0.6 °C.

cards.q: Warm-climate Chardonnay tastes of tropical fruit; cool-climate Chardonnay tastes of green ___ and citrus.
cards.explain: The same grape can taste very different depending on how much warmth it receives: cool-climate Chardonnay shows green apple and citrus, while warm-climate Chardonnay tastes of peach and tropical fruit.

cards.title: A sense of place
cards.body: **Terroir** is everything about a site: soil, slope, aspect, altitude, climate and water. In Burgundy, neighboring vineyards a few meters apart can make very different wines.

cards.title: Slopes, soil and water
cards.body:
- **Slopes** facing the sun (south in the north, north in the south) get more heat.
- **Well-drained soils** (gravel, slate, chalk) stress vines gently, giving smaller, more concentrated berries.
- **Stony soils** store heat and release it at night.
- Too much water gives big, diluted grapes.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, which slope direction receives the most sun?
cards.explain: South-facing slopes catch more direct sunlight, which is vital in cool regions like the Mosel and Burgundy.

cards.q: Terroir includes soil, slope and local climate.
cards.explain: Terroir is the whole natural environment of a vineyard: soil, slope, aspect and climate, and many add the human traditions of a place. It is the reason the same grape tastes different from one hillside to the next.

cards.q: Why are well-drained gravel soils prized in the Médoc?
options: They drain water and store heat
cards.explain: Gravel warms up and drains quickly, which helps late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon ripen fully and keeps the vine's roots from sitting in water. That is why the best Médoc châteaux sit on the gravel mounds beside the Gironde.

cards.q: The Mosel's steep slate slopes absorb and reflect ___ onto the vines.
cards.explain: The Mosel's steep slate slopes absorb and reflect heat onto the vines. In such a northerly region, every bit of warmth counts, so the best vineyards face south, along the river.

lessons.title: Deep dive: a year in the vineyard

cards.title: Winter: pruning
cards.body:
While the vine sleeps, growers **prune** last year's canes. Pruning decides how many buds, and so how many bunches, the vine will carry.

- **Cane pruning** (Guyot): one or two long canes are kept and tied along a wire. Common in Bordeaux and Burgundy.
- **Spur pruning** (cordon, gobelet): many short two-bud spurs on a permanent arm or trunk.

Fewer buds usually means fewer but more concentrated grapes.

cards.title: Spring: budburst, frost and flowering
cards.body:
As soils warm past about **10 °C**, buds swell and burst. Young shoots are fragile: one clear, still night below freezing can kill them. Growers fight **spring frost** with candles, wind machines or sprinklers that coat buds in protective ice.

Around **June**, tiny flowers self-pollinate. Cold, wet or windy weather at flowering causes **coulure** (flowers fail) and **millerandage** (uneven small berries), cutting the crop.

cards.title: Summer: fruit set and véraison
cards.body:
After flowering, berries form and grow while hard and green. Mid-summer brings **véraison**: black grapes change color, all grapes soften and start piling up sugar while acid falls.

Growers trim shoots, remove leaves around bunches for sun and air, and sometimes **green harvest** (cut some bunches) so the rest ripen better.

cards.title: Autumn: harvest
cards.body:
Picking day is a balance of **sugar** (future alcohol), **acidity** (freshness) and **ripe tannins and flavors**.

- **Hand picking** allows selection of whole bunches; essential on steep slopes and for sparkling wine, sweet wine and whole-bunch ferments.
- **Machine harvesting** shakes berries off at night, quickly and cheaply, when grapes are cool.

cards.title: Phenolic ripeness
cards.body:
Sugar ripeness and **phenolic ripeness** are not the same thing. Phenolics are the skin and seed compounds that give color, tannin and flavor.

In hot places sugar races ahead; picking early keeps alcohol down but tannins taste green. In cool places the grapes may never get enough sugar. Great sites let both arrive together.

cards.q: What is véraison?
options: When grapes change color and start to ripen
cards.explain: At véraison black grapes turn purple, all grapes soften, sugar rises and acidity falls. It marks the start of ripening, about six weeks before harvest.

cards.q: Why do growers light candles or run wind machines in spring?
options: To protect young shoots from frost
cards.explain: Cold air is heavy and pools in low spots on still frosty nights, so growers light candles or run wind machines to mix in warmer air from above. Spring frost can destroy a year's crop in hours.

cards.q: Cold, wet weather at flowering can reduce the size of the crop.
cards.explain: Poor flowering (coulure) and uneven berry set (millerandage) both cut yields, and cold, wet weather at flowering causes them. A smaller crop can mean more concentrated wine, but also higher prices.

cards.q: Match the season to the vineyard job
cards.explain: The vineyard calendar runs from pruning in winter to picking in autumn (reversed in the Southern Hemisphere).

cards.q: Picking ___ of whole bunches is needed for traditional-method sparkling wine.
cards.explain: For traditional-method sparkling wine, whole undamaged bunches are picked by hand and pressed gently so the juice of black grapes stays pale. That is why Champagne must be hand-harvested.

lessons.title: Deep dive: soil, slope and water

cards.title: What soil really does
cards.body:
Soil matters less for "flavor" than for **water and heat**.

- **Free-draining** soils (gravel, sand, slate) keep roots searching deep and limit vigor: smaller berries, more concentration.
- **Water-holding** soils (clay) keep vines going in drought but can be cold and late in wet years.
- **Limestone** and chalk drain well yet hold water in their pores, keeping acidity fresh. Champagne, Chablis and Saint-Émilion sit on it.

cards.title: Stones that store heat
cards.body:
Dark **slate** in the Mosel and big rounded **galets** in Châteauneuf-du-Pape soak up the sun by day and give warmth back at night, helping grapes ripen in marginal places.

Light-colored chalk does the opposite: it reflects light up into the canopy.

cards.title: Slope, aspect and water
cards.body:
In cool regions, a **south-facing slope** (north-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) catches more sun at a better angle. Slopes also drain cold air and water away.

Nearby **rivers and lakes** reflect light and soften temperature swings: the Mosel, Rhine, Loire and Douro are lined with vineyards for a reason.

cards.title: Altitude and fog
cards.body:
Temperature falls about **0.6 °C every 100 m** you climb. Argentina's Mendoza and Salta grow fresh wines at 1,000–3,000 m in otherwise hot latitudes.

Cold ocean currents and **fog** do the same job near the coast: California's Sonoma Coast, Chile's Casablanca and South Africa's Elgin all rely on them.

cards.q: Why are south-facing slopes prized in cool Northern Hemisphere regions?
options: They get more and stronger sunlight
cards.explain: The sun hits a south-facing slope at a steeper angle, so more energy reaches each vine, and the slope warms faster in spring. In cool Northern Hemisphere regions the best vineyards face south.

cards.q: Which soil drains well but still holds water for dry spells?
cards.explain: Porous chalk acts like a sponge: it stores water in its pores and releases it in dry spells, but still drains well. That is why Champagne's vines rarely suffer drought.

cards.q: Vineyards at high altitude are cooler than low ones at the same latitude.
cards.explain: Vineyards at altitude are roughly 0.6 °C cooler for every 100 m, so high sites in hot countries keep acidity and freshness. Mendoza and Salta in Argentina plant at 1,500 to 3,000 m.

cards.q: Match the region to its signature soil
cards.explain: Each soil helps vines cope with that place's climate: chalk in Champagne stores water, gravel in the Médoc stores heat, slate in the Mosel warms the slopes and limestone in Burgundy drains well.

cards.title: Gravel
cards.body: Loose stones that drain fast and store the day's heat. The Left Bank of **Bordeaux** (the Médoc and Graves) is built on gravel banks left by ancient rivers, perfect for late-ripening **Cabernet Sauvignon**.

cards.title: Clay
cards.body: Cool and water-holding, so vines never go thirsty but ripen later. **Pomerol** and Saint-Émilion's clay suits early **Merlot**; clay often gives fuller, rounder wines.

cards.title: Limestone and chalk
cards.body: Porous white rock that holds water like a sponge yet drains well and keeps acidity bright. **Champagne**, **Chablis**, the Côte d'Or and Saint-Émilion's plateau all sit on it.

cards.title: Slate and schist
cards.body: Dark, flaky rock that soaks up sun and splits so roots can dive deep. The **Mosel** (slate) and the **Douro** (schist) grow some of the world's most striking wines on almost no soil at all.

cards.title: Volcanic
cards.body: Ash, pumice and basalt: poor, free-draining and rich in minerals. **Santorini**, **Etna**, the Canary Islands and parts of Campania make tense, smoky, saline wines.

cards.title: Granite
cards.body: Crumbly, acidic and warm. The crus of **Beaujolais** and the northern Rhône's **Côte-Rôtie** and **Hermitage** owe their perfumed, structured wines to granite.

cards.title: Special soils
cards.body:
- **Albariza** (Jerez): blinding white chalk that holds winter rain through the summer, the home of Sherry's Palomino.
- **Terra rossa** (Coonawarra): red iron-rich clay over limestone, famous for Cabernet.
- **Loess** (Austria's Wagram and Kremstal): fine wind-blown silt loved by Grüner Veltliner.

cards.q: Match the soil to its famous region
cards.explain: Each soil shaped a classic: drainage, heat and water retention are what matter most. Gravel suits Cabernet in the Médoc, clay suits Merlot in Pomerol and chalk shapes Champagne.

cards.q: Which soil holds water like a sponge yet still drains well?
cards.explain: Porous chalk stores water in its pores yet still drains, so vines in Champagne rarely suffer drought. It also reflects light and keeps roots cool, which helps retain acidity.

cards.q: Clay soils tend to be cool and late-ripening.
cards.explain: Clay soils hold water and warm up slowly, so they tend to be cool and late-ripening. That suits early ripeners like Merlot, which is why it thrives on the clay of Pomerol.

cards.title: The growing season
cards.body:
In the Northern Hemisphere: **budburst** in spring (March–April), **flowering** in early summer, **véraison** (grapes soften and change color) in midsummer, and **harvest** from September to October.

Spring frost at budburst and rain at flowering are among the biggest risks to a crop.

cards.title: Sun, slope and water
cards.body:
South-facing slopes (north-facing in the Southern Hemisphere) catch more sun. Rivers and lakes reflect light and moderate temperature extremes.

Poor, well-drained soils make vines struggle a little, giving smaller crops with more concentrated flavor.

cards.q: What is 'véraison'?
options: When grapes soften and change color
cards.explain: Véraison is when black grapes turn from green to purple and sugar starts to build, about 40 to 50 days before harvest. Growers often thin crops then, to concentrate flavor in the remaining bunches.

cards.q: Spring frost is a major risk around budburst.
cards.explain: Young shoots are easily killed by frost; growers use wind machines, sprinklers or candles to protect them.

cards.q: Match the stage to its season (Northern Hemisphere)
cards.explain: The vine's yearly cycle drives the whole calendar of a wine region: budburst in spring, flowering in late spring, véraison in late summer and harvest in autumn. Frost in spring and rain at harvest are the biggest risks.

cards.q: Why are poor, well-drained soils often prized for vines?
options: Lower yields with more concentrated grapes
They add sugar to the grapes
cards.explain: Vines that struggle a little put their energy into fewer, more flavorful grapes. Rich, fertile soil makes leafy vines and diluted fruit, while poor, well-drained soils such as gravel or slate stress the vine in a good way.

cards.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the best vineyard slopes usually face ___.
cards.explain: In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes get the most sun, helping grapes ripen in cool climates. In the Southern Hemisphere, it is the reverse: north-facing slopes get the most sun.

units.title: In the winery
units.summary: How white, red and rosé wines are made, and what oak, lees and malolactic conversion add.

cards.title: Fresh and fruity
cards.body:
For white wine, grapes are crushed and **pressed straight away**. Only the juice is fermented, usually **cool (12–22 °C)** in stainless steel, to keep delicate fruit aromas.

Richer whites, above all **Chardonnay** in Burgundy and California, may be **fermented in oak barrels** instead: the wood and the lees add **richness, a creamy texture and toasty flavors**.

cards.q: When are white grapes pressed?
cards.explain: White grapes are pressed before fermentation, separating juice from skins early, which keeps the wine pale and low in tannin. Red wines do the opposite: they ferment on their skins, then are pressed.

cards.q: White wines are usually fermented at cooler temperatures than reds.
cards.explain: White wines are usually fermented cooler (12–18 °C) than reds, which preserves fresh, fruity and floral aromas. Warm fermentation would blow those delicate aromas away.

cards.q: Most white wines are fermented in stainless ___ tanks.
cards.explain: Steel is neutral and easy to keep cool. Oak barrels or concrete add texture and flavor for richer styles.

cards.q: Why might a winemaker ferment Chardonnay in oak barrels?
options: To add richness, texture and toasty flavors
cards.explain: Barrel fermentation integrates oak flavors and adds weight and creaminess. It is classic in Burgundy and California, and the yeast lees in the barrel add texture too.

cards.title: Skins make the difference
cards.body:
For red wine, black grapes ferment **with their skins** at **20–32 °C**. Warmth and contact extract color and tannin. The floating cap of skins is punched down or pumped over to keep it in contact with the wine.

After fermentation, the wine is drained and the skins pressed.

cards.title: Rosé
cards.body: Rosé uses black grapes but only **brief skin contact**, a few hours to two days, then ferments cool like a white.

cards.q: Why are red wines fermented warmer than whites?
cards.explain: Red wines ferment warmer (25–30 °C) because higher temperatures help pull pigments and tannins out of the skins. Too hot, though, and the delicate aromas are lost.

cards.q: The layer of skins floating on fermenting red wine is called the ___.
cards.explain: The layer of skins floating on fermenting red wine is called the cap. Winemakers punch it down or pump wine over it to extract color and tannin, and to keep it from drying out and growing bacteria.

cards.q: Rosé is made by fermenting black grapes on their skins for several weeks.
cards.explain: That is red winemaking. Rosé gets only hours to a couple of days of skin contact, just enough for a pink hue, then the juice is drawn off and fermented like a white.

cards.q: Match the process to the wine
cards.explain: Skin contact is what separates the three: white has none, rosé has a few hours, and red has days to weeks. Orange wine is white grapes fermented on their skins.

cards.title: Shaping the style
cards.body:
After fermentation, winemakers can add layers:

- **Oak**: new barrels add vanilla, toast, smoke and spice; any barrel lets in tiny amounts of oxygen that soften tannin.
- **Lees ageing**: contact with dead yeast adds texture and bready notes.
- **Malolactic conversion**: turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid and can add butter.

Barrels are expensive: cheaper wines get their oak flavor from **oak chips or staves** soaked in a tank.

cards.q: Which flavor does new oak typically add?
cards.explain: Toasted oak adds vanilla, clove, coconut (especially American oak) and smoke. The more toasted and newer the barrel, the stronger the flavor, so winemakers choose barrels like seasoning.

cards.q: American oak typically gives stronger coconut and vanilla flavors than French oak.
cards.explain: American oak has more lactones, which smell of coconut and vanilla, while French oak is more subtle and spicy. That is why traditional Rioja, aged in American oak, often smells of coconut and vanilla.

cards.q: Ageing wine on dead yeast cells, called the ___, adds texture and bready flavors.
cards.explain: Ageing wine on dead yeast cells, the lees, adds texture and bready flavors. Muscadet sur lie and Champagne are classic examples of lees influence, and stirring the lees (bâtonnage) adds creaminess.

cards.q: Malolactic conversion makes a wine taste…
cards.explain: Malic acid (think green apple) is converted into milder lactic acid (think milk). Almost all reds and many Chardonnays go through it.

cards.q: What is the cheaper alternative to aging in oak barrels?
options: Oak chips or staves in a tank
cards.explain: Oak chips or staves are the cheaper alternative to barrels. They add oak flavor quickly, but without the slow oxygen exposure of a barrel, so the wine does not develop in the same way.

lessons.title: Deep dive: from grape to red wine

cards.title: Sorting and crushing
cards.body:
At the winery, bunches go over a **sorting table** to remove leaves and bad berries. A **destemmer** pulls the berries off the stems; rollers then crack the skins.

Some winemakers keep **whole bunches** (stems and all) for a fresher, spicier, more aromatic red: common in Burgundy and northern Rhône.

cards.title: Fermentation on the skins
cards.body:
Red wine ferments **with the skins**, at about **20–32 °C**, warmer than whites. Heat and alcohol pull color, tannin and flavor out of the skins.

Carbon dioxide pushes the skins up into a thick **cap**. It must be kept wet:
- **Pump-over** (remontage): juice from the bottom is sprayed over the cap.
- **Punch-down** (pigeage): the cap is pushed down by hand or machine.

cards.title: Extraction and pressing
cards.body:
After fermentation the wine may sit on the skins for days or weeks (**post-fermentation maceration**) to soften and build tannin.

The free-run wine is drained off, then the skins are pressed. **Press wine** is darker and more tannic; the winemaker blends some back in for structure.

cards.title: Malolactic conversion
cards.body:
Almost all reds then go through **malolactic conversion** (MLC): bacteria turn sharp **malic acid** (green apple) into softer **lactic acid** (milk).

It makes wine rounder and more stable and can add a buttery note. For whites it is a choice: Burgundy Chardonnay often does it, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc usually do not.

cards.title: Oak or not?
cards.body:
- **New oak** adds vanilla, toast, clove, coconut (American oak) and smooths tannins through slow oxygen exchange.
- **Old oak** gives gentle oxygen without much flavor.
- **Stainless steel** and concrete keep fruit pure.

Barrels are toasted over fire; the **toast level** (light, medium, heavy) changes the flavors.

cards.q: Why does red wine ferment with the grape skins?
options: To extract color, tannin and flavor
cards.explain: Red wine ferments with the grape skins because the juice of almost all black grapes is clear; the color and tannin are in the skins. Fermenting on the skins is what makes red wine red.

cards.q: What does malolactic conversion do?
options: Turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid
cards.explain: Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, which softens acidity and can add buttery notes (diacetyl). It is allowed in most reds and full-bodied whites, but blocked in crisp whites.

cards.q: Match the technique to what it means
cards.explain: These are the winemaker's main tools for managing extraction: cold soak before fermentation, punch-downs and pump-overs during it, and extended maceration after. Each pulls more or less color and tannin from the skins.

cards.q: American oak tends to give stronger coconut and vanilla notes than French oak.
cards.explain: American oak is wider-grained and richer in the compounds behind coconut and vanilla aromas, which is why traditional Rioja smells of them. French oak is tighter-grained and gives more subtle spice and toast.

cards.q: The layer of skins floating on fermenting red wine is called the ___.
cards.explain: The cap is pushed up by carbon dioxide and must be kept moist, or it dries out and grows bacteria. Punching it down or pumping juice over it keeps the skins in contact with the fermenting wine.

lessons.title: Deep dive: whites, rosés and finishing touches

cards.title: White wine: cool and clean
cards.body:
For white wine, grapes are **pressed first** and the skins removed. The juice is cooled and allowed to settle so it ferments clean.

Fermentation is cool, about **12–22 °C**, to keep delicate fruit and floral aromas. Many aromatic whites stay in stainless steel; rich Chardonnay may ferment in barrel.

cards.title: Lees and bâtonnage
cards.body:
After fermentation, dead yeast cells, the **lees**, settle out. Leaving wine on fine lees adds texture and bready, nutty notes. Stirring them up is **bâtonnage**.

Muscadet *sur lie* and white Burgundy are classic examples.

cards.title: Rosé, three ways
cards.body:
- **Short maceration**: black grapes soak on their skins for a few hours, then the pink juice is fermented like a white.
- **Direct pressing**: whole black grapes pressed gently; very pale rosé (Provence style).
- **Saignée**: some juice is "bled" from a red ferment, concentrating the red and making a deeper rosé.

Blending red and white wine is only allowed in a few cases, such as rosé Champagne.

cards.title: Clarifying, stabilizing, bottling
cards.body:
Before bottling, wine is **fined** (proteins such as egg white or bentonite clay grab haze-causing particles) and often **filtered**.

**Cold stabilization** prevents harmless tartrate crystals ("wine diamonds"). A little **sulfur dioxide** protects against oxygen and microbes.

Closures: natural cork, technical cork, screw cap (keeps fruit fresh, no cork taint) or glass stopper.

cards.q: Why are most white wines fermented cooler than reds?
cards.explain: Low temperatures preserve volatile aromas, so whites ferment cool, around 12–18 °C. Reds need warmth to extract color and tannin from the skins, and ferment at 25–30 °C.

cards.q: Which rosé method bleeds juice from a red wine tank?
cards.explain: Saignée, French for bleeding, is the method of draining some juice from a red wine tank early to make rosé. The red left behind becomes more concentrated, so rosé is a useful by-product.

cards.q: Tartrate crystals in a bottle mean the wine has spoiled.
cards.explain: Tartrates are harmless crystals of potassium bitartrate, sometimes called wine diamonds. They form when wine is cold, and are not a fault, though cold stabilization removes them for appearance.

cards.q: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Removing haze with a binding agent
cards.explain: These terms are all about texture and clarity: fining removes unwanted particles, filtration removes yeast and bacteria, and racking moves wine off the lees. A wine can be bottled unfined and unfiltered for more texture.

cards.title: Making red wine
cards.body:
Black grapes are crushed and fermented **with their skins**. The skins give color, tannin and flavor. Winemakers punch down or pump over the cap of skins to extract them.

After fermentation the wine is pressed off the skins, then usually aged before bottling.

cards.title: Oak or stainless steel?
cards.body:
**Stainless steel** keeps fruit pure and fresh. **Oak barrels** let in a little oxygen, soften tannins and, when new, add vanilla, toast and spice.

Small new barrels give the most flavor; large old casks give texture with little oak taste.

cards.q: Where does red wine get its color?
cards.explain: The juice of almost all black grapes is clear; color comes from contact with the skins during fermentation. The longer the contact, the deeper the color and the greater the tannin.

cards.q: Small new oak barrels add more oak flavor than large old ones.
cards.explain: New small barrels add more oak flavor than large old ones because there is more wood surface per liter of wine, and fresh wood has more flavor compounds. After 4–5 years, a barrel gives mainly oxygen, not flavor.

cards.q: What does 'punching down' do?
options: Pushes the skins back into the fermenting wine
cards.explain: The skins float up as a cap; pushing them down (punching down) extracts color and tannin, and keeps the cap wet. Gentle punching makes elegant Pinot Noir, while more vigorous extraction makes Cabernet.

cards.q: Match the choice to its effect
cards.explain: Each winemaking decision leaves a mark on the final wine: stainless steel keeps freshness, oak adds spice, lees add texture, and malolactic fermentation adds creaminess.

cards.q: After fermentation, red wine is separated from the skins by ___.
cards.explain: After fermentation, red wine is separated from the skins by pressing. The free-run wine drains first, and the press wine, which is darker and more tannic, can be blended back for structure.

units.title: More white grapes
units.summary: Chenin Blanc, Sémillon, the aromatic grapes and Europe's crisp coastal whites.

cards.title: Chenin Blanc
cards.body: High acidity, apple, quince and honey. The **Loire** makes it in every style: dry, off-dry, sweet and sparkling (**Vouvray**, **Savennières**). **South Africa** grows more Chenin than anywhere else, with riper, often oaked styles.

cards.title: Sémillon
cards.body: Thin-skinned and prone to **noble rot**, Sémillon is the heart of **Sauternes**. In Australia's **Hunter Valley** it is picked early for a light, lemony dry wine that ages into toast and honey.

cards.q: Vouvray is made from which grape?
cards.explain: Vouvray, near Tours, makes Chenin Blanc from dry (sec) to sweet (moelleux), plus sparkling. Chenin's high acidity keeps even sweet versions fresh, and they can age for decades, with notes of quince, honey and wet wool.

cards.q: Which country has the most Chenin Blanc vineyards?
cards.explain: Chenin Blanc (also called Steen) is South Africa's most planted grape, with more vineyards there than in its native Loire. Old bush vines make some of the Cape's best and best-value whites.

cards.q: Sémillon is the main grape of sweet Sauternes.
cards.explain: Sémillon is the main grape of sweet Sauternes, where its thin skins are susceptible to Botrytis cinerea, noble rot, which concentrates the sugar. The fog from the Ciron river encourages it on autumn mornings.

cards.q: Hunter Valley Sémillon is light when young but ages to flavors of ___ and honey.
cards.explain: Hunter Valley Sémillon is light, low in alcohol and lemony when young, yet ages to flavors of toast and honey after a decade, even though it sees no oak. It is a favorite of connoisseurs.

cards.title: Perfume in a glass
cards.body:
- **Gewürztraminer**: rose, lychee, ginger; low acidity, oily texture (Alsace).
- **Muscat**: smells of fresh grapes, orange blossom and peach (Moscato d'Asti, Alsace).
- **Viognier**: apricot, peach, honeysuckle; full and silky (Condrieu).

cards.q: Lychee and rose petal aromas are typical of…
cards.explain: Gewürztraminer is one of the most aromatic grapes in the world: lychee, rose petals and ginger. Alsace makes the classic examples, rich and low in acidity, perfect with spicy food.

cards.q: Which grape smells most like fresh grapes?
cards.explain: Muscat is famous for actually tasting grapey, along with orange blossom and peach. It is one of the oldest grape families, and the parent of many others, and it makes everything from sparkling Moscato d'Asti to fortified Muscat.

cards.q: Condrieu, in the Northern Rhône, is made from…
cards.explain: Condrieu is Viognier's spiritual home in the Northern Rhône: apricot, peach and blossom with a rich, silky texture and low acidity. The steep granite terraces are tiny, so the wine is rare and expensive.

cards.q: Gewürztraminer typically has high acidity.
cards.explain: Gewürztraminer is notably low in acidity, with a rich, almost oily texture. That is why it can taste heavy, and why it works best with spicy or rich food that needs a full, aromatic wine.

cards.q: Match the aromatic grape to its classic note
