cards.body: The finest sparkling wines are made by the **traditional method**: a still base wine gets yeast and sugar, then ferments **a second time inside its own bottle**. The trapped CO₂ makes the bubbles.

cards.title: The magic of lees
cards.body:
The wine then rests on its dead yeast (**lees**) for months or years. As the yeast breaks down (**autolysis**), it gives **biscuit, bread and brioche** aromas and finer bubbles.

To remove the yeast, bottles are slowly turned and tilted neck-down so it slides into the neck (**riddling**), then frozen out (**disgorgement**). A little wine and sugar, the **dosage**, sets the final sweetness.

cards.q: In the traditional method, where does the second fermentation happen?
cards.explain: In the traditional method, the second fermentation happens inside the bottle itself. Sugar and yeast are added to a still base wine, the bottle is capped, and the CO₂ stays trapped as bubbles. It is labor-intensive, which is part of why Champagne, Cava and Crémant cost more.

cards.q: Brioche and biscuit aromas in Champagne come from…
cards.explain: Autolysis, the breakdown of dead yeast cells (lees) over months and years, releases bready, toasty notes such as brioche and biscuit. The longer a Champagne rests on its lees, the more of these flavors it develops.

cards.q: Turning bottles so the yeast slides into the neck is called ___.
cards.explain: Riddling (remuage) used to be done by hand on wooden racks; today machines called gyropalettes do most of it.

cards.q: Dosage is the mix of wine and sugar added after disgorgement.
cards.explain: Dosage is the mix of wine and sugar added after disgorgement. It sets the final sweetness, from Brut Nature (no added sugar) to Doux (over 50 g/L), and balances Champagne's very high acidity.

cards.title: The original
cards.body:
A cold, northerly region with **chalk** soils. Three main grapes:

- **Chardonnay**: finesse and citrus.
- **Pinot Noir**: body and red fruit.
- **Meunier**: fruity roundness.

Most Champagne is a **non-vintage** blend of many villages and years, made in a consistent house style.

cards.q: Which three grapes dominate Champagne?
cards.explain: Champagne is made mainly from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier. Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada make Cava; Glera makes Prosecco. Two black grapes and one white make most Champagne, which is why Blanc de Blancs is the exception.

cards.q: A Champagne labeled Blanc de Blancs is made from…
cards.explain: A Blanc de Blancs is made from Chardonnay only: white from whites, usually fine, citrusy and long-lived. Blanc de Noirs is white wine from black grapes (Pinot Noir and Meunier), fuller and richer.

cards.q: Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months before release.
cards.explain: Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months before release, with at least 12 months of that on lees. Vintage Champagne needs at least three years, and most houses age it much longer.

cards.q: Match the Champagne district to its main grape
cards.explain: Each district is known for the grape that best suits its soils and frost risk: Montagne de Reims for Pinot Noir, the Côte des Blancs for Chardonnay, and the Vallée de la Marne for Meunier, which ripens earlier and resists spring frost.

cards.title: The tank method
cards.body: **Prosecco** (from the **Glera** grape) gets its second fermentation in a large **pressure tank**. It's faster and cheaper, and keeps fresh **pear, apple and blossom** aromas without the bready notes.

cards.title: Other traditional-method wines
cards.body:
- **Cava** (Spain): Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada; citrus and almond.
- **Crémant** (France): Loire, Alsace and Burgundy.
- **Franciacorta** (Italy), **English sparkling**, **Tasmania**, **Cap Classique** (South Africa).

cards.q: Prosecco is mostly made by…
cards.explain: Prosecco is mostly made by the tank method (Charmat), where the second fermentation happens in a large pressurized tank. This preserves Glera's fresh, fruity, floral character and keeps it cheaper than traditional-method wines.

cards.q: Cava comes from which country?
cards.explain: Cava comes from Spain, mostly from Penedès near Barcelona, and is made by the traditional method, like Champagne, usually from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. It is one of the best-value sparkling wines in the world.

cards.q: Crémant is a French traditional-method sparkling wine made outside Champagne.
cards.explain: Crémant uses the same method as Champagne but in other places and often with local grapes: Crémant d'Alsace, de Loire, de Bourgogne. It is often great value, since the land is cheaper.

cards.q: Prosecco is made from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: Glera grows in the Veneto and Friuli. The best Prosecco comes from the steep hills of Conegliano-Valdobbiadene, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and is labeled DOCG.

cards.q: Which sparkling wine label term is drier: Brut or Extra Dry?
cards.explain: Confusingly, Extra Dry (12–17 g/L) is sweeter than Brut (under 12 g/L). The sparkling sweetness scale runs Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut, Extra Dry, Sec, Demi-sec, Doux: dry is not the driest.

lessons.title: Deep dive: the traditional method step by step

cards.title: 1. The base wine
cards.body:
Grapes are picked early for high acidity and pressed gently as **whole bunches**. The first, purest juice is the *cuvée*; later pressings (*taille*) are fuller and less fine.

The juice ferments into a dry, sharp, low-alcohol **base wine**. Many base wines from different villages, grapes and years are blended into the house style: this is the **assemblage**.

cards.title: 2. Second fermentation in bottle
cards.body:
The blend is bottled with the **liqueur de tirage**: wine, sugar and yeast. A crown cap seals it.

Yeast eats the sugar, making about **1.5% more alcohol** and carbon dioxide that cannot escape: around **6 atmospheres** of pressure, three times a car tire.

cards.title: 3. Ageing on the lees
cards.body:
Dead yeast cells (lees) slowly break down (**autolysis**), giving bread, brioche, biscuit and toast notes and a finer, creamier mousse.

Champagne rules: at least **15 months** for non-vintage (12 on the lees) and **3 years** for vintage. Top houses go much longer, in cool chalk cellars under Reims and Épernay.

cards.title: 4. Riddling and disgorging
cards.body:
**Riddling** (*remuage*) turns and tilts bottles day by day until the sediment slides into the neck. Once done by hand on wooden *pupitres*, it is now mostly done by **gyropalettes**.

The neck is frozen, the cap removed, and pressure pops out the plug of ice and yeast: **disgorgement**.

cards.title: 5. Dosage and sweetness
cards.body:
The bottle is topped up with **liqueur d'expédition**, wine with a little sugar. This **dosage** sets the style:

- **Brut Nature**: 0–3 g/L
- **Extra Brut**: 0–6 g/L
- **Brut**: under 12 g/L (most Champagne)
- **Extra Dry**: 12–17 g/L (sweeter than Brut!)
- **Demi-Sec**: 32–50 g/L

cards.q: What creates the bubbles in traditional-method sparkling wine?
options: A second fermentation in the bottle
cards.explain: In traditional-method wine, sugar and yeast are added at bottling and the second fermentation happens inside the sealed bottle. The CO₂ it makes cannot escape, so it dissolves in the wine and becomes the bubbles.

cards.q: Which is sweeter?
cards.explain: Confusingly, Extra Dry (12–17 g/L) is sweeter than Brut (under 12 g/L). The scale runs Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut, Extra Dry, Sec, Demi-sec, Doux, so the word dry does not mean the driest.

cards.q: Breakdown of dead yeast cells that gives brioche notes is called ___.
cards.explain: Autolysis is the breakdown of dead yeast cells, which releases bready, toasty notes such as brioche. The longer the wine rests on its lees, the toastier and creamier it becomes.

cards.q: Put the steps with their French names
cards.explain: These words appear on back labels and in every Champagne cellar tour: tirage (bottling with sugar and yeast), remuage (riddling), dégorgement (disgorgement) and dosage (the final sugar top-up).

cards.q: Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months before release.
cards.explain: Non-vintage Champagne must age at least 15 months, with at least 12 on lees. Vintage Champagne needs at least three years, though many houses give it much longer.

lessons.title: Deep dive: the world of bubbles

cards.title: Champagne's grapes and villages
cards.body:
Three main grapes: **Chardonnay** (finesse, citrus, the Côte des Blancs), **Pinot Noir** (body, red fruit, the Montagne de Reims) and **Meunier** (fruity, early-drinking, the Vallée de la Marne).

Villages are rated: 17 are **Grand Cru**, 42 **Premier Cru**.

cards.title: Who makes it
cards.body:
Labels carry a code:
- **NM** (négociant-manipulant): a house that buys grapes, like Moët or Bollinger.
- **RM** (récoltant-manipulant): a grower making wine only from their own vines, "grower Champagne".
- **CM**: a cooperative.

cards.title: Tank method: Prosecco and Asti
cards.body:
In the **tank method** (Charmat), the second fermentation happens in a big pressurized tank. It is fast and keeps the grape's fresh fruit and floral aromas.

**Prosecco** (Glera, Veneto and Friuli) is the best known; Conegliano Valdobbiadene is its hilly heartland. **Asti** and **Moscato d'Asti** use a single fermentation stopped early, so they stay sweet and low in alcohol.

cards.title: Other great sparklers
cards.body:
- **Cava** (Spain, mostly Penedès): traditional method with Macabeo, Xarel·lo, Parellada.
- **Crémant** (France: Loire, Alsace, Burgundy, Limoux…): traditional method, at least 9 months on lees.
- **Franciacorta** (Lombardy) and **Trentodoc**: Italy's traditional-method stars.
- **English sparkling wine**: chalk soils like Champagne's, booming since the 1990s.
- **Pét-nat** (*pétillant naturel*): bottled before the first fermentation finishes; cloudy and rustic.

cards.q: Which grape is the specialty of the Côte des Blancs?
cards.explain: Blanc de Blancs means white from whites: 100% white grapes, in Champagne usually Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs. These are typically the lightest, most citrusy and most age-worthy wines.

cards.q: What does 'RM' on a Champagne label tell you?
options: A grower made it from their own grapes
cards.explain: RM is Récoltant-Manipulant: grower Champagne, made by the family that owns the vines. It often shows more terroir than a blended house wine, and is usually better value.

cards.q: Match the sparkling wine to its method
cards.explain: Method shapes texture and flavor as much as the grape: the traditional method gives fine bubbles and toasty notes, the tank method keeps fresh fruit, and the ancestral method leaves a cloudy, lightly sparkling wine.

cards.q: Moscato d'Asti is fully sparkling and around 12% alcohol.
cards.explain: Moscato d'Asti is gently sparkling (frizzante), sweet and only about 5% alcohol, which makes it a light, grapey dessert wine. Fully sparkling, higher-alcohol wine would be Asti Spumante.

cards.title: Bubble methods
cards.body:
**Traditional method**: second fermentation in the bottle, ageing on lees for toasty, fine-bubbled wines (Champagne, Cava, Crémant).

**Tank method**: second fermentation in a sealed tank for fresh, fruity wines (Prosecco).

cards.title: How sweet is Brut?
cards.body:
Sparkling sweetness runs from **Brut Nature** (no added sugar) through **Extra Brut** and **Brut** (the most common, dry) to **Extra Dry**, **Dry**, **Demi-Sec** and **Doux** (sweet).

Confusingly, Extra Dry is slightly sweeter than Brut.

cards.q: Which wine is usually made by the tank method?
cards.explain: Prosecco's second fermentation happens in pressurized tanks, keeping fresh pear and apple fruit. This gives a light, fruity wine, unlike the toasty notes of bottle-fermented Champagne.

cards.q: Extra Dry sparkling wine is drier than Brut.
cards.explain: A historical quirk: Extra Dry has a little more sugar than Brut, because in the 19th century sparkling wines were much sweeter, and Brut was invented as a new, drier style.

cards.q: Match the sparkling wine to its country
cards.explain: Most wine countries have a sparkling tradition: Champagne in France, Cava in Spain, Prosecco and Franciacorta in Italy, Sekt in Germany, Cap Classique in South Africa. The method varies, the bubbles do not.

cards.q: Where does Champagne's toasty, bready character come from?
cards.explain: Dead yeast cells break down over months or years, giving brioche, biscuit and toast notes. That is autolysis, and it is why a long-aged Champagne tastes richer and creamier than a young one.

cards.q: Removing the yeast plug from the neck of the bottle is called ___.
cards.explain: Disgorgement: the neck is frozen, the cap removed, and the pressure pushes out the plug of dead yeast. The bottle is then topped up with dosage and corked.

units.title: Sweet & fortified
units.summary: Noble rot, icewine, Port and Sherry.

cards.title: Concentrate the sugar
cards.body:
To make a sweet wine you need more sugar than yeast can ferment, or you stop fermentation early. Winemakers concentrate grapes by:

- **Late harvest**: leaving them to ripen and shrivel on the vine.
- **Noble rot**: Botrytis cinerea pierces the skins: Sauternes in Bordeaux, **Tokaji Aszú** in Hungary.
- **Freezing**: icewine.
- **Drying** after harvest: passito.

cards.q: What is Botrytis cinerea?
options: A type of yeast for Champagne
cards.explain: Under the right conditions (misty mornings, dry afternoons) it is 'noble rot', making wines like Sauternes and Tokaji.

cards.q: Icewine is made from grapes that are…
cards.explain: Pressed while frozen, only a little concentrated, sugary juice is released. Canada and Germany are famous for it.

cards.q: Sauternes is a sweet wine made with grapes affected by noble rot.
cards.explain: Sauternes and Barsac in southern Bordeaux make sweet wines from Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc affected by noble rot (Botrytis). The fungus shrivels the grapes and concentrates sugar, acidity and flavors like honey and saffron.

cards.q: Hungary's famous noble rot wine is Tokaji ___.
cards.explain: Botrytized aszú berries are soaked in base wine or must, giving luscious, high-acid wines that live for decades.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to its method
cards.explain: Three different routes to sweetness: noble rot concentrates sugar in Sauternes, drying grapes does it in Vin Santo or Tokaji, and freezing grapes on the vine does it in Icewine. Each method leaves a distinct flavor.

cards.title: Fortified mid-fermentation
cards.body: Port comes from Portugal's **Douro Valley**. Halfway through fermentation, **grape spirit** is added. This kills the yeast, leaving a **sweet, strong (about 20% abv)**, deeply colored wine.

cards.title: Ruby vs tawny
cards.body:
- **Ruby** styles (Ruby, Reserve, LBV, Vintage): aged to keep fresh black fruit.
- **Tawny** styles: aged for years in small casks, becoming brownish with nutty, caramel notes.

cards.q: When is grape spirit added to Port?
cards.explain: Port is fortified during fermentation: adding grape spirit early kills the yeast and keeps natural grape sugar, giving a sweet, strong wine. Sherry is the reverse, fortified after fermentation, which is why it can be dry.

cards.q: Port comes from which river valley?
cards.explain: Grapes grow on steep schist terraces; wines were traditionally shipped down to Porto's lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia.

cards.q: Tawny Port gets its nutty flavors from long ageing in small wooden casks.
cards.explain: Oxygen seeping through the small old casks turns the wine tawny and develops walnut, toffee and caramel notes. Ruby Port ages in large vats or the bottle, so it stays red and fruity.

cards.q: Port is typically about ___% alcohol.
cards.explain: Port is usually 19–22% abv, since grape spirit of about 77% is added to fermenting wine. That is more alcohol than most wines, so serve it in small glasses.

cards.title: The world's most misunderstood wine
cards.body:
Sherry comes from the hot south of Spain around **Jerez**. Most is made from **Palomino** and is **dry**.

- **Fino & Manzanilla**: aged under **flor** (a layer of yeast); pale, bone dry, tangy, almond and bread. Manzanilla is Fino aged by the sea in **Sanlúcar de Barrameda**, saltier still.
- **Oloroso**: aged with oxygen; dark, nutty, dry.
- **Pedro Ximénez**: from sun-dried grapes; black, raisiny, very sweet.

cards.title: The solera
cards.body: Sherry ages in a **solera**, tiers of barrels where younger wine gradually refreshes older wine. The result is consistent year after year, so most Sherry has no vintage.

cards.q: What is flor?
options: A layer of yeast that protects Fino from oxygen
cards.explain: It grows on the wine's surface in partly filled barrels, keeping it pale and adding bready, salty notes.

cards.q: Most Sherry is sweet.
cards.explain: Fino, Manzanilla, Amontillado and Oloroso are naturally dry. Sweet styles are Pedro Ximénez, Moscatel and blended Cream Sherry.

cards.q: Which Sherry is darkest and sweetest?
cards.explain: Pedro Ximénez (PX) is made from sun-dried grapes: syrupy, raisined and almost black, with flavors of fig and molasses. It is so sweet that it is often poured over vanilla ice cream.

cards.q: Manzanilla is a Fino-style Sherry aged in which seaside town?
cards.explain: Manzanilla is a Fino-style Sherry aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, on the coast. The sea air helps flor grow thickly, giving an extra-salty tang, and it is the classic partner for tapas and shellfish.

cards.q: Sherry is aged in a fractional blending system called a ___.
cards.explain: Sherry is aged in a fractional blending system called a solera. Wine is drawn from the oldest tier and replaced from the next-oldest, and so on, so each bottle holds traces of very old wine.

lessons.title: Deep dive: how sweetness is made

cards.title: Concentrate the sugar
cards.body:
Sweet wine needs grapes so sugary that yeast cannot (or is not allowed to) ferment it all. Four ways:

- **Noble rot** (*Botrytis cinerea*): misty mornings, sunny afternoons; the fungus pierces skins and water evaporates. Sauternes, Tokaji, Trockenbeerenauslese.
- **Drying**: grapes dry on mats or in lofts (*appassimento*, *passito*). Recioto, Vin Santo.
- **Freezing**: grapes freeze on the vine; water stays behind as ice when pressed. Icewine, Eiswein.
- **Late harvest**: simply leave grapes to shrivel on the vine.

cards.title: Icewine
cards.body:
Grapes must be picked frozen, at about **-8 °C** or colder, usually at night in December or January. Only a few drops of syrupy juice come from each bunch.

Canada (Ontario, often **Vidal** or Riesling) and Germany/Austria (Eiswein) are the leaders. The style is intensely sweet with piercing acidity.

cards.title: Stop the fermentation
cards.body:
Another route is to **stop** fermentation while sugar remains:
- Chilling and filtering out the yeast (Moscato d'Asti, many German Kabinett and Spätlese).
- Adding grape spirit, which kills the yeast: **fortification** (Port, Vins Doux Naturels).

cards.title: Tokaji Aszú
cards.body:
In Hungary's Tokaj, botrytized **aszú** berries (mainly **Furmint**) are picked one by one and soaked in fermenting wine. Sweetness used to be measured in **puttonyos**, the baskets of aszú added; today the minimum is 120 g/L of sugar.

**Eszencia** is the free-run syrup alone: so sweet it barely ferments, reaching just a few % alcohol.

cards.q: What does noble rot do to grapes?
options: Shrivels them and concentrates sugar and acid
cards.explain: Botrytis pierces the grape skin so water evaporates and the sugar, acid and flavor concentrate. It also adds its own flavors of honey, marmalade and saffron, which is why Sauternes tastes more than just sweet.

cards.q: How cold must grapes be for icewine?
cards.explain: Icewine grapes are picked at about −8 °C or colder, when most of the water is frozen and pressing yields only a few drops of intensely sweet juice. Canada and Germany (Eiswein) are the main producers.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to its method
cards.explain: Four different routes to sweetness: noble rot (Sauternes), freezing (Icewine), drying (Vin Santo, Recioto) and fortification (Port). Each leaves a distinct flavor.

cards.q: Furmint is the main grape of Tokaji.
cards.explain: Furmint is the main grape of Tokaji. Its high acidity balances the huge sweetness, and Hárslevelű, its partner, adds a floral, honeyed perfume.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Port, Sherry and Madeira

cards.title: Port: the Douro and Gaia
cards.body:
Port grapes (Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz and others) grow on steep **schist terraces** of the Douro. Fermentation lasts only two or three days before **grape spirit at 77%** is added, leaving a sweet wine of about **19–22%**.

Traditionally the young wine went downriver to the lodges of **Vila Nova de Gaia**, opposite Porto, to age.

cards.title: Ruby or tawny?
cards.body:
- **Ruby styles** age in big vats or bottle; fruit stays deep red and fresh. Ruby, Reserve, LBV (4–6 years in wood), and **Vintage Port**, made only in declared years and aged for decades in bottle.
- **Tawny styles** age in small casks; oxygen fades the color to amber and builds nutty, caramel notes. 10, 20, 30, 40 Year Old, and **Colheita** (single harvest).

cards.title: Sherry: flor or no flor
cards.body:
Sherry is made from **Palomino** in the chalky *albariza* soils around **Jerez**. The base wine is dry; it is fortified and aged in a **solera**, a stack of casks where young wine refreshes older wine.

- **Fino / Manzanilla**: fortified to about 15%, so a layer of yeast, **flor**, grows on top and protects it from air. Pale, salty, bone dry.
- **Oloroso**: fortified to about 17%, too strong for flor; ages with oxygen into a dark, nutty wine.
- **Amontillado** and **Palo Cortado** sit in between.
- **Pedro Ximénez**: sun-dried grapes, syrupy sweet.

cards.title: Madeira: cooked and immortal
cards.body:
On the Portuguese island of Madeira, wines are deliberately **heated**: in tanks (*estufagem*) or for years in warm attics (*canteiro*). The result tastes of caramel and walnut with soaring acidity, and can last for centuries once opened.

Styles follow the grapes, dry to sweet: **Sercial**, **Verdelho**, **Bual**, **Malmsey** (Malvasia).

cards.q: Why is fino sherry so pale?
options: A layer of flor yeast protects it from oxygen
It is made from white grapes only
cards.explain: Fino is aged under flor, a layer of yeast that keeps the wine from contact with air. Without oxidation it stays pale and fresh, with salty, almondy, bready notes.

cards.q: Where do the big Port houses traditionally age their wines?
cards.explain: Port is aged in lodges in Vila Nova de Gaia, across the Douro from Porto, because the cool, humid air by the sea suits slow aging. The big houses' names still line the riverfront.

cards.q: Match the Madeira style to its sweetness
cards.explain: The grape names on a Madeira label tell you the sweetness: Sercial is driest, Verdelho is medium-dry, Bual is medium-sweet and Malvasia (Malmsey) is the sweetest. Madeira's heating makes it almost indestructible.

cards.q: Tawny Port gets its color from ageing in small casks.
cards.explain: Slow oxidation in small casks turns Tawny Port from red to amber-brown and gives it nutty, caramel flavors. Ruby Port avoids this and stays red and fruity.

cards.q: A tiered system of casks where young sherry refreshes older sherry is a ___.
cards.explain: In a solera, wine is drawn from the oldest casks and topped up from the next oldest, and so on. Each bottle holds traces of very old wine, so the style stays consistent from year to year.

cards.title: Three roads to sweetness
cards.body:
1. **Noble rot** (botrytis) shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar: Sauternes, Tokaji.
2. **Freezing**: grapes picked frozen give Icewine/Eiswein.
3. **Drying**: grapes dried after picking make Recioto and Vin Santo.

Stopping fermentation early, as in Port, is a fourth route.

cards.title: Sherry styles
cards.body: **Fino** and **Manzanilla** age under a layer of yeast called **flor**: pale, dry, salty, almond. **Oloroso** ages without flor, in contact with air: dark, nutty, dry. **Pedro Ximénez** is a dark, raisin-sweet dessert sherry.

cards.q: What is 'flor' in sherry-making?
options: A layer of yeast on the wine
cards.explain: Flor is a layer of yeast that grows on the surface of Fino and Manzanilla. It protects the wine from oxygen and gives a tangy, bready, almond character, which is why those wines are pale and dry.

cards.q: Match the sweet wine to how it's made
cards.explain: Different routes to sugar create very different sweet wines: noble rot (Sauternes), dried grapes (Vin Santo), frozen grapes (Icewine) and fortification (Port). Each leaves a signature flavor.

cards.q: Oloroso sherry ages under flor.
cards.explain: Oloroso is fortified to about 17–18% alcohol, a strength where flor can not survive, so it ages oxidatively and darkens, with walnut and dried fruit flavors. Fino stays under flor and stays pale.

cards.q: Which wine is fortified during fermentation, keeping natural sweetness?
cards.explain: Port is fortified during fermentation: adding grape spirit stops the yeast, leaving natural sugar in the wine. If the spirit were added after fermentation, as with dry Sherry, the wine would be dry.

cards.q: Noble rot is caused by a fungus called ___.
cards.explain: Botrytis cinerea, the noble rot, in the right conditions of damp mornings followed by sunny afternoons, shrivels grapes and concentrates sugar and acid. In wet weather, the same fungus becomes grey rot and ruins the crop.

units.title: Viticulture in depth
units.summary: Site selection, training and pruning, vineyard threats, yields and harvest decisions.

cards.title: Temperature is king
cards.body:
The growing season needs a mean temperature of roughly **13–21 °C**. Growers fine-tune heat with:

- **Latitude**: further from the equator is cooler.
- **Altitude**: about 0.6 °C cooler per 100 m.
- **Aspect**: slopes facing the equator get more sunlight.
- **Water bodies**: oceans, lakes and rivers moderate extremes and reflect light.
- **Diurnal range**: cool nights preserve acidity and aroma.

cards.title: Sunlight, wind and fog
cards.body: Coastal fog and wind cool California's Sonoma Coast and Carneros, while inland Napa warms up. Chile's Humboldt Current and South Africa's Benguela Current do the same.

cards.q: Why is a large diurnal range valuable?
options: Cool nights preserve acidity and aromas
It speeds up ripening at night
cards.explain: Warm days ripen sugar; cool nights slow the loss of acid. High-altitude Argentina and Washington State rely on it.

cards.q: Approximately how much does temperature drop per 100 m of altitude?
cards.explain: Temperature drops about 0.6 °C per 100 m of altitude, so a vineyard at 1,000 m is about 6 °C cooler than one at sea level, other things being equal. That is how high-altitude vineyards in hot countries make fresh wines.

cards.q: The cold Humboldt Current cools Chile's coastal vineyards.
cards.explain: The cold Humboldt Current flows north along Chile's coast, bringing cool air and morning fog to regions like Casablanca and San Antonio. That is why Chile can make cool-climate wines at a warm latitude.

cards.q: In the Southern Hemisphere, the warmest slopes face ___.
cards.explain: Slopes facing the equator get the most direct sun: south in the Northern Hemisphere, north in the Southern.

cards.title: Shaping the vine
cards.body:
- **Bush vines** (gobelet): free-standing, low, for hot, dry, windy sites (Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Barossa old vines).
- **Cane pruning** (e.g. Guyot): one or two long canes tied to a wire each year (Burgundy, Bordeaux).
- **Spur pruning** (cordon): short spurs on a permanent arm, easier to mechanize.
- **VSP**: shoots trained upwards between wires for an even, sunny canopy.

cards.title: Canopy management
cards.body: Leaf removal, shoot positioning and trimming balance **sunlight** on the grapes (for ripeness and color) with **shade** (to prevent sunburn), and improve **airflow** to reduce disease.

cards.q: Bush vines are best suited to…
cards.explain: Low and sturdy with their own shade, they need no trellis and little water, as in the Southern Rhône and Spain.

cards.q: Guyot is a cane-pruned training system.
cards.explain: Guyot is a cane-pruned training system: one or two long canes are kept each year. Single or double Guyot is common in Burgundy and Bordeaux, and gives precise control of yield.

cards.q: Which is a main aim of canopy management?
options: Balancing sunlight and airflow around the grapes
cards.explain: The aim of canopy management is good leaf exposure to the sun, and airflow to reduce fungal disease. It shapes the leaves around the bunches so that grapes ripen well and stay healthy.

cards.q: Shoots trained vertically upward between wires is called ___.
cards.explain: Vertical Shoot Positioning (VSP) trains shoots upward between wires. It is widely used in the New World and much of Europe, since it exposes the bunches and suits mechanical harvesting.

cards.title: Pests and diseases
cards.body:
- **Phylloxera**: an aphid-like louse that kills vine roots. Grafting onto **American rootstock** is the main defense.
- **Powdery mildew** (oidium) and **downy mildew**: fungal diseases.
- **Grey rot** (botrytis in wet weather): destroys bunches.
- **Viruses**, birds and animals.

cards.title: Weather hazards
cards.body:
- **Spring frost** kills young shoots: use wind machines, heaters or sprinklers.
- **Hail** shreds leaves and bunches: use nets.
- **Drought** and **heatwaves** stop ripening or sunburn grapes.
- **Rain at harvest** dilutes and rots grapes.

cards.q: How do most vineyards protect against phylloxera?
cards.explain: Most vineyards protect against phylloxera by grafting: American vine species tolerate the louse on their roots, and European vines are grafted on top. This saved the world's wine industry in the late 1800s.

cards.q: Sprinklers can protect buds from spring frost.
cards.explain: As water freezes on the buds it releases heat, holding them at about 0 °C inside a protective ice shell.

cards.q: Which region has never been affected by phylloxera?
cards.explain: Protected by the Andes, the Atacama Desert, the Pacific and Patagonian ice, Chile has never had it. South Australia is also free.

cards.q: Match the hazard to the defense
cards.explain: Growers combine many tools to protect a year's crop: wind machines and heaters against frost, nets against hail and birds, and sprays or canopy work against mildew. Each hazard has its own defense.

cards.title: Less is often more
cards.body:
Lower **yields** often mean more concentrated grapes, especially from **old vines**. But very low yields are not always better, and balance matters.

Harvest timing balances **sugar**, **acidity**, **tannin ripeness** and **flavor**. Pick early for freshness and sparkling base wines; pick late for richness or sweet wines.

cards.title: Hand or machine?
cards.body:
- **Hand harvesting**: selective, gentle, keeps whole bunches (essential for Champagne and carbonic maceration); slow and costly.
- **Machine harvesting**: fast and cheap, can pick at night when it's cool; less selective, needs flat land and trellised vines.

cards.q: Why are grapes for sparkling base wine picked early?
options: To keep high acidity and moderate alcohol
cards.explain: Fresh, high-acid, relatively neutral base wines are ideal, since the second fermentation adds more alcohol.

cards.q: Machine harvesters can work at night, when grapes are cool.
cards.explain: Machine harvesters can work at night, when grapes are cool. Night picking keeps fruit fresh and reduces oxidation, which is useful in hot regions like Australia and California.

cards.q: Which wine style requires whole bunches, so hand harvesting is essential?
cards.explain: Whole-bunch pressing gives clean, pale juice, and Champagne rules require hand harvesting, because crushed grapes would stain the juice red or add tannin. Hand-picking keeps the bunches intact.

cards.q: Vines that are decades old usually give lower ___ of more concentrated fruit.
cards.explain: 'Old vines' (vieilles vignes) is a common label term, though it has no legal definition in most places.

lessons.title: Deep dive: farming philosophies and climate change

cards.title: Organic, biodynamic, sustainable
cards.body:
- **Organic**: no synthetic herbicides, pesticides or fertilizers. Copper and sulfur are allowed against mildew.
- **Biodynamic**: organic plus a whole-farm system from Rudolf Steiner's 1924 lectures: herbal preparations and a calendar following the moon. Followers include Domaine Leflaive and Zind-Humbrecht.
- **Sustainable**: certified programs balancing environment, people and cost (Napa Green, Sustainable Wine South Africa, HVE in France).

cards.title: Yield and quality
cards.body:
Yields are measured in **hectoliters per hectare** (hl/ha). Grand Cru Burgundy is limited to about 35 hl/ha; bulk vineyards can exceed 150.

Lower yields often mean more concentrated grapes, but a healthy, balanced vine matters more than any number. Old vines naturally give small crops of small berries.

cards.title: Climate change in the vineyard
cards.body:
Harvests in Europe now come two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s. Riper grapes mean **higher alcohol** and **lower acidity**.

Growers respond by planting on **higher, cooler sites**, facing slopes away from the sun, keeping more leaves for shade, and trying heat-tolerant grapes. England, Tasmania and southern Chile are booming as cool places get warm enough.

cards.q: What does biodynamic farming add to organic farming?
options: Herbal preparations and a lunar calendar
cards.explain: Biodynamic farming adds to organic farming a view of the vineyard as a self-sustaining farm organism, with preparations and a lunar calendar. Evidence for the calendar is limited, but many top estates use it.

cards.q: How is yield usually measured?
cards.explain: Yield is measured in hectoliters per hectare (hl/ha), where 1 hl = 100 liters, or about 133 standard bottles. Lower yields usually mean more concentrated grapes, and appellations set maximum limits.

cards.q: Climate change has made European harvests later.
cards.explain: They now start two to three weeks earlier than in the 1980s.

cards.title: Training and canopy
cards.body:
Vines are trained to control sun and air. **Bush vines** (gobelet) suit hot, dry places such as old Grenache in Châteauneuf. **Trellised** systems like Guyot and VSP spread leaves for sun in cool climates.

Removing leaves around the bunches improves ripening and airflow, cutting disease.

cards.title: Threats in the vineyard
cards.body:
**Phylloxera**, a root-eating aphid, destroyed most of Europe's vineyards in the late 1800s. The fix: graft vines onto American rootstock.

Fungal diseases like **powdery** and **downy mildew** thrive in damp weather; **grey rot** spoils grapes unless conditions turn it into noble rot.

cards.q: How did growers defeat phylloxera?
cards.explain: American vine roots resist phylloxera, so European vines are grafted onto them. The louse, from North America, destroyed most European vineyards in the 1860s–1890s before this solution.

cards.q: Bush vines are typical of hot, dry vineyards.
cards.explain: The leafy bush shades the grapes from harsh sun; they are common in the southern Rhône, Spain and Australia.

cards.q: Match the threat to what it attacks
cards.explain: Growers fight each threat in a different way: mildew and oidium are fungi sprayed with sulfur or copper, phylloxera is a root insect beaten by grafting, and frost is beaten by heaters.

cards.q: Why do growers remove leaves around the bunches in cool climates?
options: More sun and air on the grapes
To make the vine grow taller
cards.explain: Removing leaves around the bunches in cool climates helps ripening and reduces rot, because sun and air reach the fruit. Too much can sunburn grapes, so it is a careful balance.

cards.q: Phylloxera is a tiny insect that feeds on vine ___.
cards.explain: Phylloxera is a tiny insect that feeds on vine roots. It sucks sap from the roots and slowly kills un-grafted European vines, as it did in the 19th century.

units.title: Winemaking in depth
units.summary: Before, during and after fermentation: the choices that define style.

cards.title: Preparing the must
cards.body:
- **Sorting**: removing rotten or unripe fruit.
- **Destemming and crushing**, or keeping whole bunches.
- **SO₂**: added to protect against oxygen and bacteria.
- **Must adjustments**: in cool places, **chaptalization** (adding sugar to raise alcohol); in hot places, **acidification**.
- **Cold soak**: macerating black grapes before fermentation for color and fruit.

cards.q: What is chaptalization?
options: Adding sugar to the must to raise alcohol
cards.explain: Named after Jean-Antoine Chaptal. It is allowed in cooler regions such as Burgundy and Germany (with limits) and banned in many warm regions.

cards.q: Acidification is most common in hot regions.
cards.explain: Grapes from hot climates lose acidity as they ripen, so winemakers add tartaric acid to restore balance.

cards.q: Why is sulfur dioxide (SO₂) used in winemaking?
cards.explain: Small amounts of sulfur dioxide protect wine from oxidation and spoilage. Almost all wines contain some, including natural wines in tiny amounts, and it has been used since Roman times.

cards.q: Soaking black grapes before fermentation at low temperature is called a cold ___.
cards.explain: A cold soak is soaking black grapes before fermentation at low temperature. It is popular for Pinot Noir to extract color and fruit before alcohol forms, as alcohol would extract harsher tannins.

cards.title: Extraction methods
cards.body:
- **Punch down** (pigeage) and **pump over** (remontage) control extraction.
- **Whole-bunch** fermentation adds fragrance, spice and structure.
- **Carbonic maceration** gives soft, fruity reds with kirsch and banana.
- **Fermentation temperature**: cooler for fruit, warmer for extraction.
- **Vessel**: steel, oak, concrete or clay (amphora, qvevri).

cards.q: Carbonic maceration is most associated with…
cards.explain: Carbonic maceration is most associated with Beaujolais: whole bunches in a CO₂-filled vessel give juicy, low-tannin wine with banana and bubblegum notes. Fermentation starts inside each berry.

cards.q: Pigeage means punching the cap down into the wine.
cards.explain: Pigeage means punching the cap down into the wine. It is traditional in Burgundy, sometimes even done by foot, and it extracts color and tannin gently.

cards.q: Which vessel has been used for winemaking in Georgia for about 8,000 years?
cards.explain: Large egg-shaped clay jars buried underground. Georgian qvevri winemaking is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

cards.q: Fermenting with stems attached is called whole-___ fermentation.
cards.explain: Fermenting with stems attached is called whole-bunch fermentation. It is popular for Pinot Noir and Syrah, adding aromatic lift and tannin. The stems must be ripe, or they give a green taste.

cards.title: Finishing the wine
cards.body:
- **Maturation**: in steel (fresh), old oak (gentle oxygen) or new oak (flavor).
- **Blending**: varieties, vineyards, barrels.
- **Clarification**: racking, **fining** (bentonite, egg white) and **filtration**.
- **Stabilization**: cold stabilization prevents harmless tartrate crystals.
- **Closure**: natural cork, screwcap, synthetic or glass.

cards.q: What does fining do?
cards.explain: Agents like bentonite clay or egg white bind to particles, which settle out. Note: egg white and milk proteins mean some wines are not vegan.

cards.q: Tartrate crystals in a bottle are a serious fault.
cards.explain: Tartrates, also called wine diamonds, are harmless crystals of tartaric acid. Cold stabilization prevents them for cosmetic reasons, so they are not a fault.

cards.q: Which closure best eliminates the risk of cork taint?
cards.explain: Screwcaps eliminate the risk of cork taint, and they keep aromatic whites fresh. They are standard in New Zealand and Australia, and increasingly used for Riesling in Europe.

cards.q: Match the vessel to its effect
cards.explain: The vessel is one of the winemaker's biggest stylistic choices: stainless steel keeps freshness, oak adds flavor and gentle oxygen, concrete gives texture without flavor, and amphora gives earthy character.

cards.title: Yeast: wild or cultured
cards.body:
**Ambient** (wild) yeasts from the vineyard and cellar give complexity but can stall or make off-flavors. **Cultured** yeasts are reliable and can be chosen for aroma, speed or tolerance to alcohol.

Many top estates start with wild yeast and keep a cultured strain in reserve.

cards.title: Temperature and time
cards.body:
- **Cool** (12–16 °C) whites keep fruity esters: think Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling.
- **Warm** (25–32 °C) reds extract color and tannin quickly.
- **Extended maceration** after fermentation polymerizes tannins so they feel softer.
- **Cold soak** before fermentation extracts color and fruit without harsh tannin.

cards.title: Oxygen: friend and foe
cards.body:
**Reductive** winemaking keeps oxygen out (inert gas, sealed steel tanks, screw caps) for pure, fresh fruit.

**Oxidative** winemaking lets air in on purpose: barrels, racking, open vats, or the extreme cases of oloroso sherry and tawny port. A little oxygen softens tannin and builds complexity; too much makes wine flat and bruised-apple brown.

cards.title: Barrels in detail
cards.body:
- **Size**: a 225 L *barrique* gives more oak per liter than a 500 L *puncheon* or a 2,000 L *foudre*.
- **Age**: new oak gives the most flavor; after three or four fills it is almost neutral.
- **Origin**: French oak (tight grain: spice, toast, silkier) vs American oak (vanilla, coconut, dill).
- **Toast**: light (fresh wood, coconut) to heavy (coffee, smoke).

cards.title: Alternatives
cards.body:
**Concrete eggs**, **clay amphorae** and Georgia's buried **qvevri** let wine breathe without oak flavor. Georgia has made wine in qvevri for about 8,000 years; it is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

Cheaper wines may use **oak chips or staves** in steel tanks for a fast oak note.

cards.q: Which barrel gives the strongest oak flavor?
cards.explain: Small and new means the most wood contact per liter and the most fresh oak compounds.

cards.q: What does reductive winemaking aim to do?
options: Keep oxygen away for pure, fresh fruit
cards.explain: Steel, inert gas and screw caps are the reductive toolkit.

cards.q: Match the vessel to its effect
pairs: Gentle oxygen with little oak flavor
cards.explain: The vessel shapes texture as much as flavor.

cards.q: American oak tends to show more coconut and vanilla than French oak.
cards.explain: It contains more of the lactones behind coconut aromas.

cards.title: Whole bunch and carbonic
cards.body: **Carbonic maceration** ferments whole, uncrushed grapes inside a CO₂-filled tank. The result is soft, very fruity, low-tannin red with notes of banana, bubblegum and kirsch: classic Beaujolais Nouveau.

cards.title: Fining, filtering, sulfur
cards.body:
Before bottling, wines are often **fined** (agents bind haze-causing particles) and **filtered**. A little **sulfur dioxide** protects against oxidation and microbes.

Some producers skip these steps for "natural" wines, accepting more risk and variation.

cards.q: Banana and bubblegum notes in a light red suggest…
cards.explain: Whole-berry fermentation creates fruity esters, typical of Beaujolais Nouveau: banana and bubblegum in a light red are a sign of carbonic maceration.

cards.q: Sulfur dioxide protects wine from oxidation.
cards.explain: SO₂ is an antioxidant and antimicrobial used in nearly all wines in small amounts. It protects color and freshness, and it is also used to clean barrels.

cards.q: Match the technique to its result
cards.explain: Each technique targets one part of the finished wine: cold soak for color, malolactic for softness, lees stirring for texture, and fining for clarity.

cards.q: What is 'bâtonnage'?
cards.explain: Bâtonnage is stirring dead yeast (lees) back into the wine. It adds body and a creamy, bready character, and is common in white Burgundy and Champagne base wines.

cards.q: Adding sugar to the must to raise alcohol is called ___.
cards.explain: Chaptalization, adding sugar to the must to raise alcohol, is allowed in some cool regions, such as Burgundy and Germany, where grapes struggle to ripen. It increases alcohol, not sweetness, and is banned in warm regions.

units.title: Tasting in depth
units.summary: Structured assessment, quality, readiness and faults: thinking like a sommelier.

cards.title: Measuring precisely
cards.body:
At an advanced level, each structural element gets a precise scale:

- Acidity, tannin, body and finish: **low, medium−, medium, medium+, high**.
- Alcohol: low (under 11%), medium, high (14%+).
- Tannin also has a **nature**: ripe or unripe, fine-grained or coarse.

Precise structure narrows down grape and origin much faster than aromas alone.

cards.title: Development
cards.body:
- **Youthful**: only primary (and secondary) aromas.
- **Developing**: tertiary notes appear alongside fresh fruit.
- **Fully developed**: mostly tertiary aromas.
- **Tired**: fruit fading, drying out.

cards.q: A wine showing fresh fruit with some leather and earth is…
cards.explain: Tertiary notes (leather, earth, mushroom) alongside primary fruit mean the wine is on its way to maturity. Primary aromas come from the grape, secondary from winemaking, and tertiary from age.

cards.q: High acidity, high tannin, pale garnet, tar and roses suggests…
cards.explain: High acidity, high tannin, pale garnet and tar and roses suggest Nebbiolo. Its unusual mix of pale color and fierce structure is a giveaway, so look for it in Barolo and Barbaresco.

cards.q: Unripe tannins tend to feel green, coarse and astringent.
cards.explain: Unripe tannins tend to feel green, coarse and astringent. Ripe tannins feel fine-grained and silky, so tannin texture is a clue to grape ripeness and winemaking.

cards.q: Alcohol above about ___% is described as high.
cards.explain: Alcohol above about 14% is described as high. Below 11% is low, and 11–13.9% is medium. High alcohol shows as warmth and weight on the finish.

cards.title: BLIC in practice
cards.body:
- **Balance**: fruit vs acid vs tannin vs alcohol vs sweetness.
- **Length**: medium+ or long for good wine.
- **Intensity**: pronounced aromas and flavors.
- **Complexity**: many layers: primary, secondary, tertiary.

Then decide readiness: **too young**, **can drink now but has potential**, **drink now**, or **too old**.

cards.q: A wine with intense fruit, high tannin and high acidity that is still very primary is probably…
cards.explain: Concentrated fruit plus structure is what allows a wine to improve with age: a wine with intense fruit, high tannin and high acidity, still very primary, is probably young and needs time. Fruit will fade slowly, while tannin and acid preserve it.

cards.q: A short finish is a sign of outstanding quality.
cards.explain: Great wines have long, complex finishes, so a short finish is a sign of a simple wine. Length is one of the four BLIC markers.

cards.q: Match each BLIC element to its question
cards.explain: Four simple questions behind every professional quality call: Is it balanced? How long is the finish? How intense are the aromas and flavors? Is it complex? A wine that answers well to all four is high quality.

cards.q: Which wine is most likely to improve with bottle age?
cards.explain: Concentration, acidity and structure let a wine evolve for decades; the others are made to drink young. A tannic, high-acid, concentrated red like Barolo or Bordeaux has more to give with time.

cards.title: When wine goes wrong
cards.body:
- **TCA (cork taint)**: musty, damp cardboard, muted fruit.
- **Oxidation**: brownish, flat, bruised apple.
- **Reduction**: struck match, rotten egg, rubber; sometimes fixed by aeration.
- **Brettanomyces**: barnyard, sticking plaster, sweaty saddle.
- **Volatile acidity (VA)**: vinegar, nail-varnish remover.
- **Heat damage**: cooked, stewed fruit.

cards.q: A wine smelling of nail-varnish remover and vinegar has…
cards.explain: Nail-varnish remover and vinegar smells come from acetic acid and ethyl acetate, usually from bacteria and oxygen exposure. The wine is spoiled, and it will not improve.

cards.q: Struck-match or rotten-egg aromas indicate…
cards.explain: Sulfur compounds form when wine lacks oxygen during winemaking. Mild cases blow off with swirling or decanting.

cards.q: Brettanomyces can give barnyard and sticking-plaster aromas.
cards.explain: Brettanomyces can give barnyard and sticking-plaster aromas. A little can add complexity for some drinkers, but a lot strips the fruit, and the smell can be considered a fault.

cards.q: Match the fault to its smell
cards.explain: Recognizing faults is part of every sommelier's training: cork taint smells of damp cardboard, oxidation of bruised apple and sherry, volatile acidity of vinegar, and Brett of barnyard.

cards.title: Assessing readiness
cards.body:
Ask: is the wine **too young** (tight, primary fruit, firm tannin), **ready** (fruit and developing notes in balance), or **past its best** (fading fruit, drying tannin)?

Long-lived wines need the structure to age: acidity, tannin or sugar, plus concentrated fruit.

cards.title: Deductive tasting
cards.body: Blind tasters reason from clues. High acid and light color suggest a cool climate. Deep color, ripe black fruit and high alcohol suggest warmth. Vanilla and toast suggest new oak; leather and earth suggest age.

cards.q: Which wine is most likely from a cool climate?
cards.explain: Cool climates keep acidity and give leaner, fresher fruit with lower alcohol. A tart, light-bodied wine with green apple or red cherry points to a cool place like Chablis, Mosel or the Loire.

cards.q: Match the clue to what it suggests
cards.explain: Each clue narrows down the grape, place and winemaking: pale color suggests thin skins, pepper suggests Syrah, buttery notes suggest malolactic fermentation. Collect clues and then decide.

cards.q: Wines with high acidity or tannin often age well.
cards.explain: Structure protects a wine while its fruit slowly evolves. Acidity and tannin act like preservatives, which is why the Mosel Riesling and Barolo can last for decades.

cards.q: A red tastes of dried fruit, leather and has drying tannin. It is probably…
cards.explain: Fading fruit and drying tannin are signs a wine has passed its peak. When the fruit has faded, the tannin and acidity are left behind, and the wine tastes thin and hard.

cards.q: Concentration of flavor, balance, length and complexity together judge a wine's ___.
cards.explain: Balance, length, intensity and complexity (BLIC) together judge a wine's quality. Using the same four factors for every wine lets you compare them objectively.

units.title: Bordeaux
units.summary: Left Bank, Right Bank, the 1855 Classification and Sauternes.

cards.title: Gravel and Cabernet
cards.body:
West of the Gironde estuary and the Garonne river lie the **Médoc** and **Graves**. Deep **gravel** banks drain well and store heat, ideal for late-ripening **Cabernet Sauvignon**, which leads the blends.

The Haut-Médoc holds four famous communes, north to south: **Saint-Estèphe**, **Pauillac**, **Saint-Julien** and **Margaux**. In the Graves, the top area, **Pessac-Léognan**, makes both great reds (Haut-Brion) and fine oaked dry whites.

cards.title: The communes
cards.body:
- **Saint-Estèphe**: more clay, firmer, more rustic.
- **Pauillac**: powerful; three First Growths.
- **Saint-Julien**: balanced and consistent.
- **Margaux**: perfumed and silky.

cards.q: Which commune is home to three First Growths: Lafite, Latour and Mouton?
cards.explain: Pauillac is the heart of the Médoc's greatest Cabernet. The other First Growths are Château Margaux and Haut-Brion (Pessac-Léognan).

cards.q: Which is the northernmost of the four famous Haut-Médoc communes?
cards.explain: From north to south the four famous Haut-Médoc communes are Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux. Pauillac, in the middle, holds three of the five First Growths (Lafite, Latour and Mouton), so it is the most powerful, long-lived Cabernet.

cards.q: Merlot is the dominant grape in most top Left Bank blends.
cards.explain: On the Left Bank, Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads the blend, thanks to the gravel soils. Merlot dominates on the Right Bank (Pomerol and Saint-Émilion), where clay and limestone suit it better.

cards.q: Which Left Bank area makes both top reds and fine oaked dry whites?
cards.explain: Pessac-Léognan, on the southern edge of Bordeaux city, makes both top reds and fine oaked dry whites from Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. Haut-Brion and Domaine de Chevalier are the benchmarks, and it is the only place where reds and whites are both classified.

cards.title: Clay, limestone and Merlot
cards.body:
East of the Dordogne, cooler **clay and limestone** soils suit early-ripening **Merlot**, blended with **Cabernet Franc**.

- **Saint-Émilion**: a limestone plateau and slopes around a medieval town.
- **Pomerol**: a small clay-and-gravel plateau; Pétrus and Le Pin.
- Satellites: Fronsac, Castillon, Bourg, Blaye.

cards.title: Entre-Deux-Mers
cards.body: Between the Garonne and Dordogne lies **Entre-Deux-Mers** ("between two seas": the two tidal rivers), best known for fresh, dry whites from Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. Much of the region's generic Bordeaux AOC red comes from here too.

cards.q: Which grape partners Merlot on the Right Bank?
cards.explain: Cabernet Franc adds fragrance and structure to Merlot on the Right Bank. Château Cheval Blanc in Saint-Émilion is famously rich in Cabernet Franc, which ripens well on its gravelly soils.

cards.q: Pomerol has an official classification of its châteaux.
cards.explain: Pomerol has no official classification, yet Pétrus and Le Pin are among the most expensive wines in the world. Tiny estates and a proven track record of clay-grown Merlot let reputation, not a ranking, set the price.

cards.q: 'Entre-Deux-Mers' means between two ___.
cards.explain: Entre-Deux-Mers means between two seas, though the seas are really the tidal Garonne and Dordogne rivers. The area makes fresh, dry whites mainly from Sauvignon Blanc, and good-value reds sold as Bordeaux.

cards.q: Match the soil to the grape it favors
cards.explain: Warm, free-draining gravel helps late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon, while cool, water-retentive clay suits early-ripening Merlot. In a wet year clay keeps Merlot hydrated, and in a hot year gravel protects Cabernet, so many châteaux plant both.

cards.title: 1855 and after
cards.body:
For the Paris Exposition of **1855**, Médoc châteaux (plus Haut-Brion) were ranked from **First** to **Fifth Growth**, based on price. Only one change has ever been made: **Mouton Rothschild** was promoted to First Growth in **1973**.

Sauternes was classified too, with **Château d'Yquem** alone as *Premier Cru Supérieur*. Saint-Émilion's classification is revised roughly every ten years.

cards.title: Sauternes
cards.body: Cool morning mists from the little **Ciron** river meet the warmer Garonne, encouraging **noble rot** on Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc. Pickers make several passes, choosing only botrytized berries.

cards.q: Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
cards.explain: Château Mouton Rothschild was promoted from Second to First Growth in 1973, the only change ever made to the 1855 red classification. Baron Philippe de Rothschild campaigned for it for decades, and his motto changed from 'First I cannot be, second I deign not to be' to 'First I am, second I was'.

cards.q: What was the 1855 Classification based on?
cards.explain: In 1855, for the Paris Exposition, brokers ranked the châteaux by the prices their wines fetched at the time. Price then stood for quality and reputation, and the ranking has hardly changed since, though it is a ranking of estates, not of today's wine quality.

cards.q: Château d'Yquem holds the unique rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in Sauternes.
cards.explain: Château d'Yquem holds the unique rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in Sauternes, placed above all other Sauternes in 1855. Its wine is picked berry by berry in several passes, and in poor years nothing is released.

cards.q: Mists from the cool ___ river help noble rot develop in Sauternes.
cards.explain: The cool Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne, and that contrast creates the autumn morning fog that botrytis needs. The sunny afternoons then dry the grapes so the rot concentrates them instead of spoiling them.

lessons.title: Deep dive: inside a Bordeaux château

cards.title: The blend
cards.body:
Bordeaux is a **blend** country. Five black grapes are allowed: **Cabernet Sauvignon** (structure, blackcurrant, age-worthiness), **Merlot** (plush plum, ripens early), **Cabernet Franc** (perfume, freshness), **Petit Verdot** (color, spice, a splash only) and **Malbec**. **Carmenère** is permitted but rare.

Blending is insurance: if one grape suffers from spring frost or autumn rain, the others carry the vintage.

cards.title: Grand vin and second wine
cards.body:
Each château makes its **grand vin** from the best plots and barrels. Lots that don't make the cut go into a **second wine**: Carruades de Lafite, Pavillon Rouge de Château Margaux, Les Forts de Latour.

Top grands vins spend **18–24 months** in barrels, often **mostly new French oak**, and are racked every few months to clear the sediment.

cards.title: En primeur
cards.body:
Every spring, merchants and critics taste the new vintage from barrel. Châteaux then release a part of the wine **en primeur**: buyers pay now and receive bottles about two years later.

Wine goes from château to *courtier* (broker) to *négociant* (merchant) to the world: the system known as **la Place de Bordeaux**.

cards.title: The Bordeaux bottle
cards.body:
The straight-sided bottle with **high shoulders** is the Bordeaux shape, copied worldwide for Cabernet and Merlot. The shoulders are said to catch sediment when pouring.

Large formats age more slowly; Bordeaux names them differently from Champagne: a **Double Magnum** holds 3 L and an **Impériale** 6 L.

cards.title: Dry whites and clairet
cards.body:
White Bordeaux blends **Sauvignon Blanc** (zest, grass) and **Sémillon** (wax, body, ageing), sometimes with Muscadelle. Simple Entre-Deux-Mers is fresh and unoaked; Pessac-Léognan whites are barrel-fermented and age for decades.

**Bordeaux clairet** is a deep rosé from a short maceration: the ancestor of the English word *claret*.

cards.q: What is a 'second wine' in Bordeaux?
options: Wine made from lots not chosen for the grand vin
A wine from the second harvest
A cheaper wine from another region
A wine aged a second year
cards.explain: A second wine is made from younger vines or lesser barrels of a top château, for example Pavillon Rouge de Château Margaux. It gives a taste of the house style at a lower price and is ready to drink earlier.

cards.q: Which grape gives Bordeaux blends their backbone and long ageing?
cards.explain: Cabernet Sauvignon gives Bordeaux blends their backbone and long aging: its thick skins give firm tannin and blackcurrant fruit, especially on Left Bank gravel. Merlot adds softness, and Cabernet Franc adds perfume.

cards.q: En primeur means buying wine before it is bottled.
cards.explain: En primeur means buying wine before it is bottled: buyers pay while the wine is still in barrel and receive it two years later. It can offer savings in good vintages, but prices can fall, so it is a gamble.

cards.q: Match the Bordeaux grape to its role
cards.explain: Each grape plays a part: Cabernet Sauvignon gives structure, Merlot gives plush fruit, Cabernet Franc adds perfume and Petit Verdot adds color and spice. The blend changes every vintage with the weather.

cards.q: The English call red Bordeaux ___.
cards.explain: The English call red Bordeaux claret, from the French clairet, the pale reds once shipped to England. Bordeaux was English for three centuries, so claret is one of the oldest wine words in the language.

cards.title: Why vintages matter here
cards.body:
Bordeaux sits on the Atlantic: some years are warm and dry, others wet and cool. A great **vintage** needs a warm summer, a dry September and no rain at harvest.

Recent stars include **2005, 2009, 2010, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2020** and **2022**. In cooler years, Merlot on the Right Bank often does better than late-ripening Cabernet.

cards.title: How claret ages
cards.body:
Young top Bordeaux is **dark, tannic and oaky**: blackcurrant, cedar and vanilla.

After 10–20 years, tannins soften and **tertiary** notes appear: **cedar, cigar box, leather, forest floor, dried fruit**. The color fades from purple to **garnet** with a brick rim.

cards.title: Decanting
cards.body: Young claret benefits from **decanting** for air; old claret is decanted gently to leave its **sediment** behind. Stand the bottle upright a day before, then pour slowly over a light until the sediment reaches the neck.

cards.q: What does an aged Bordeaux typically smell of?
cards.explain: An aged Bordeaux smells of cedar, tobacco, leather, forest floor and dried fruit. These tertiary notes come from years in bottle, and are the reason old Bordeaux is so prized.

cards.q: In a cool, rainy Bordeaux vintage, which grape often fares better?
cards.explain: Merlot ripens earlier than Cabernet, so in a cool, rainy vintage it can be picked before the autumn rain. That is why Right Bank wines often do better in wet years, and Left Bank in hot, dry ones.

cards.q: Old red wine is decanted partly to separate it from its sediment.
cards.explain: Tannins and pigments drop out as a fine deposit over the years, so old red wine throws sediment. Decanting separates the clear wine from it, so you don't pour a gritty glass.

cards.title: Roman port, English market
cards.body:
The Romans planted vines at **Burdigala** in the 1st century AD. But Bordeaux's fortune came from **trade**: after **1152**, when Eleanor of Aquitaine married the future Henry II of England, Bordeaux shipped its light red **clairet** to London for three hundred years. The English still call red Bordeaux **claret**.

When the English left in **1453**, Bordeaux kept its sea trade with Britain, the Netherlands and northern Europe.

cards.title: Draining the Médoc
cards.body:
Until the 1600s, the Médoc was marsh. **Dutch** engineers dug drainage channels and revealed **gravel ridges** along the Gironde. On that warm, free-draining gravel, Cabernet Sauvignon could finally ripen.

Rich families of Bordeaux's Parliament built estates there. **Haut-Brion** was sold by name in London by **1663**; Lafite, Latour and Margaux soon followed: the birth of the **château** as a brand.

cards.title: Merchants, 1855 and beyond
cards.body:
Bordeaux's **négociants** (merchants), many of them British, Irish, Dutch and German families, bought wine young, aged and sold it. Their price lists became the **1855 classification**.

Phylloxera, two world wars and the 1930s depression hit hard. The modern boom began with **Émile Peynaud**'s scientific winemaking in the 1950s–60s and Robert Parker's praise of the **1982** vintage, which turned the Grands Crus into global luxury goods.

cards.q: Why do the British call red Bordeaux 'claret'?
options: From the light red 'clairet' shipped to England after 1152
Because it is always clear in color
From the Latin word for wine
cards.explain: Bordeaux belonged to the English crown for three centuries, and its pale red clairet was London's everyday wine.

cards.q: What did the Dutch do for Bordeaux in the 1600s?
options: Planted Merlot on the Right Bank
cards.explain: Drainage exposed the gravel ridges where Cabernet Sauvignon ripens; the Médoc's great estates followed.

cards.q: Château Haut-Brion was already sold by name in London in the 1660s.
cards.explain: The diarist Samuel Pepys wrote of drinking 'Ho Bryan' in 1663: one of the first wines sold under its estate's name.

cards.title: The 1855 Classification
cards.body:
In 1855, Médoc châteaux (plus Haut-Brion in Graves) were ranked into five growths by price. **First Growths**: Lafite, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion, and since 1973, Mouton Rothschild.

Sauternes was classified at the same time, with Yquem alone at the top.

cards.title: Bordeaux's dry whites and sweet wines
cards.body: Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon make crisp whites in Entre-Deux-Mers and serious oaked whites in Pessac-Léognan. In **Sauternes** and **Barsac**, autumn mists from the Ciron river bring noble rot for rich, honeyed sweet wines.

cards.q: Which château became a First Growth in 1973?
cards.explain: Château Mouton Rothschild became a First Growth in 1973: the only change ever made to the 1855 red classification. The other four First Growths are Lafite, Latour, Margaux and Haut-Brion.

cards.q: Pomerol has an official classification like the Médoc.
cards.explain: Pomerol has no classification, unlike the Médoc and Sauternes, though Pétrus and Le Pin are among the world's most expensive wines. Its tiny estates, nearly all Merlot on clay, rely on reputation.

cards.q: Match the appellation to its main grape
cards.explain: Left Bank appellations lean Cabernet Sauvignon, Right Bank ones lean Merlot, and the sweet wines of Sauternes lean on Sémillon. The grape tells you the blend and, roughly, the style.

cards.q: What brings noble rot to Sauternes?
options: Autumn mists from the Ciron river
cards.explain: Misty mornings and sunny afternoons are perfect for botrytis: the damp spreads the fungus, and the sun then dries the grapes so it concentrates, not rots. Not every year works, which is one reason Sauternes is expensive.

cards.q: Château ___ is the only Graves estate in the 1855 classification.
cards.explain: Château Haut-Brion, the only Graves estate in the 1855 classification, was so famous that it was included alongside the Médoc. It is also the oldest of the First Growths, with a fame going back to the 17th century, even in London.

units.title: Burgundy & Beaujolais
units.summary: The Côte d'Or hierarchy, Chablis, the Mâconnais and the Beaujolais crus.

cards.title: The golden slope
cards.body:
A narrow, east-facing escarpment of limestone and marl south of Dijon.

- **Côte de Nuits** (north): almost all red. Gevrey-Chambertin, Chambolle-Musigny, Vougeot, Vosne-Romanée, Nuits-Saint-Georges.
- **Côte de Beaune** (south): great whites (Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet) and reds (Pommard, Volnay, Corton).

cards.title: The quality pyramid
cards.body:
- **Grand Cru** (33 vineyards; names like Le Chambertin or Le Montrachet appear alone on the label)
- **Premier Cru** (village + vineyard, e.g. Meursault 1er Cru Perrières)
- **Village** (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin)
- **Regional** (Bourgogne)

The best sites sit mid-slope, with ideal drainage and sun.

cards.q: Which half of the Côte d'Or is most famous for white wine?
cards.explain: Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet, Chassagne-Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne make the world's most revered Chardonnay.

cards.q: Approximately how many Grand Cru vineyards does Burgundy have?
cards.explain: Burgundy has about 33 Grand Cru vineyards, which together make only about 1–2% of the region's wine. That rarity, together with its fame, explains why prices are so high.

cards.q: In the Côte d'Or, the finest vineyards are usually at the bottom of the slope.
cards.explain: Mid-slope sites usually have the best balance of drainage, soil depth and sun. The top of the slope is thin and cold, and the bottom is fertile and damp, so most Grand Crus sit in a band halfway up the Côte d'Or.

cards.q: Match the wine to its part of Burgundy
cards.explain: The Côte de Nuits is red country; the great whites shine in the southern Côte de Beaune; the Mâconnais and Chalonnaise offer value.

cards.title: Chablis
cards.body:
Far to the north-west, on **Kimmeridgian** limestone rich in fossilized oyster shells. Chardonnay here is **steely**, with green apple, lemon and wet stones. Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and **seven Grand Cru** climats on one slope.

Frost is the big risk, fought with heaters and sprinklers.

cards.title: Chalonnaise & Mâconnais
cards.body:
- **Côte Chalonnaise**: Mercurey, Givry, Rully, Montagny. Value Burgundy.
- **Mâconnais**: warmer and riper Chardonnay: Mâcon-Villages, **Pouilly-Fuissé**, **Saint-Véran**.

cards.q: The soil of Chablis is famous for…
options: Kimmeridgian limestone with fossil oyster shells
cards.explain: Chablis is built on Kimmeridgian soils, full of fossilized oyster shells from the Jurassic sea about 150 million years ago. Many link its minerality to these soils, which are also found in Sancerre and the Côte des Bar.

cards.q: Pouilly-Fuissé is a Chardonnay from the Mâconnais.
cards.explain: Pouilly-Fuissé is Chardonnay from the Mâconnais in southern Burgundy. Do not confuse it with Pouilly-Fumé, a Sauvignon Blanc from the Loire, a classic exam trap.

cards.q: What is the main climatic threat in Chablis?
cards.explain: Being far north, Chablis often loses buds to spring frost. Growers light heaters or burn straw among the vines, or spray them with water to freeze a protective coat of ice around the buds.

cards.q: Chablis has ___ Grand Cru climats, all on a single slope.
cards.explain: Chablis has seven Grand Cru climats, all on a single south-west-facing slope above the town, including Les Clos, Vaudésir and Valmur. The slope catches the afternoon sun, so the grapes ripen better than elsewhere in Chablis.

cards.title: Gamay on granite
cards.body:
Granite hills in the north, clay and limestone in the south.

- **Beaujolais** and **Nouveau**: light, fruity, often carbonic.
- **Beaujolais-Villages**: a step up.
- **The ten crus** (Fleurie, Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent and more): more structure; some age for a decade.

cards.q: How many Beaujolais crus are there?
cards.explain: From north to south: Saint-Amour, Juliénas, Chénas, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie, Chiroubles, Morgon, Régnié, Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly.

cards.q: Beaujolais crus usually show the word 'Beaujolais' prominently on the label.
cards.explain: Crus usually show just the village name, such as Morgon or Fleurie, not Beaujolais. The ten crus are above the village-level Beaujolais-Villages and basic Beaujolais, so the label gives the quality away.

cards.q: Which cru is known for the most powerful, age-worthy Beaujolais?
cards.explain: Moulin-à-Vent, named after its windmill, is known for the most powerful, age-worthy Beaujolais. Its granite is rich in manganese, which gives structured wines that can resemble Pinot Noir after 10 years.

cards.q: Most Beaujolais lies on ___ soils in the northern hills.
cards.explain: Most Beaujolais lies on granite soils in the northern hills. Granite gives the crus their structure and floral perfume, while the limestone-clay in the south gives lighter, simpler wines.

cards.title: Four levels
cards.body:
Burgundy ranks **land**, not producers:

1. **Grand Cru** (about 1% of wine): named vineyards only, such as *Chambertin*, *Montrachet*, *Corton*.
2. **Premier Cru** (about 10%): village + vineyard, *Gevrey-Chambertin 1er Cru Clos Saint-Jacques*.
3. **Village** (about 37%): *Meursault*, *Vosne-Romanée*.
4. **Regional** (about half): *Bourgogne*, *Mâcon-Villages*.

cards.title: Climats and clos
cards.body:
A named vineyard plot is a **climat**; there are over 1,200, listed by UNESCO since 2015. A **clos** is a vineyard enclosed by a stone wall, often built by medieval monks.

Because of Napoleonic inheritance laws, one vineyard is usually split between **many owners**: Clos de Vougeot's 50 hectares have around 80.

cards.title: Domaine or négociant
cards.body:
A **domaine** grows and bottles its own grapes. A **négociant** (merchant house such as Louis Jadot, Joseph Drouhin, Bouchard) buys grapes or wine and bottles under its name.

So the same vineyard name can appear on dozens of different labels: the producer matters as much as the plot.

cards.title: How red Burgundy is made
cards.body:
Pinot Noir is thin-skinned and delicate. Winemakers often do a **cold soak** before fermentation for color, use gentle **punch-downs**, and may keep some **whole bunches** for perfume.

It ages 12–18 months in French oak *pièces* (228 L barrels); the share of new oak rises with the quality level.

cards.title: The Burgundy bottle
cards.body: The Burgundy bottle has **sloping shoulders** and a wider body, the shape used worldwide for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay (and in the Rhône for Syrah).

cards.q: Which is the top level of the Burgundy hierarchy?
cards.explain: Grand Cru is the top level of the Burgundy hierarchy: the wines carry only the vineyard name, like Romanée-Conti or Le Montrachet. Below it come Premier Cru, village and regional wines, a pyramid based on place.

cards.q: What is a 'clos'?
cards.explain: A clos is a vineyard enclosed by a wall, usually built by monks centuries ago. Clos de Vougeot and Clos de Tart are famous examples, and some walls are still standing.

cards.q: In Burgundy, one vineyard is often shared by many owners.
cards.explain: Inheritance laws split plots over generations, so one famous vineyard can have dozens of owners, some with just a few rows. The producer therefore matters as much as the vineyard.

cards.q: Match the label to its level
cards.explain: More specific place means higher level: Bourgogne is regional, a village name is next, then a Premier Cru vineyard, then a Grand Cru. Reading the label from the bottom of the pyramid up tells you the quality tier.

cards.title: Chablis on Kimmeridgian clay
cards.body:
Chablis is cool and isolated, nearer to Champagne than to Beaune. Its best slopes sit on **Kimmeridgian** marl full of tiny fossilized oyster shells.

Levels: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru, and **seven Grands Crus** on one south-west-facing hill above the town (Les Clos, Vaudésir, Blanchot…). Most is unoaked; some Grands Crus use old oak.

cards.title: Beaujolais and carbonic maceration
cards.body:
**Gamay** on granite hills south of Mâcon. For juicy, fruity styles, whole bunches are sealed in tanks full of carbon dioxide: fermentation starts **inside each berry** (**carbonic maceration**), giving banana, bubblegum and kirsch notes and low tannin.

**Beaujolais Nouveau** is released on the third Thursday of November. The **ten crus** (Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie…) are deeper and can age.

cards.q: What makes Chablis' best soils special?
options: Kimmeridgian marl with fossil oyster shells
cards.explain: Chablis' best soils are Kimmeridgian limestone, packed with fossilized oyster shells from a Jurassic sea. The soil is linked with Chablis' steely, saline character and its affinity with oysters.

cards.q: What is carbonic maceration?
cards.explain: In carbonic maceration, whole bunches sit in a CO₂-filled tank and enzymes start fermenting each berry from the inside. The result is a soft, fruity, low-tannin wine with banana and bubblegum notes, typical of Beaujolais.

cards.q: Chablis has seven Grand Cru vineyards, all on one hillside.
cards.explain: Chablis has seven Grand Cru vineyards, all on one hillside that faces south-west across the Serein river from the town. The slope catches afternoon sun, so the grapes ripen better than elsewhere in Chablis.

cards.title: A thousand years of plots
cards.body:
Burgundy's vineyards were shaped by the Church. From the 10th century, the **Benedictines of Cluny** and then the **Cistercians of Cîteaux** (founded 1098) were given vineyards by nobles hoping for salvation.

The monks noticed that wines from neighboring plots tasted different, and named and walled them: the **Clos de Vougeot**, **Clos de Tart**, **Romanée**. These named plots, the **climats**, were listed by UNESCO in 2015.

cards.title: The dukes and their Pinot
cards.body: The **Valois Dukes of Burgundy** were among Europe's richest rulers in the 1300s–1400s and used wine as diplomacy. In **1395**, Duke **Philip the Bold** banned the "disloyal" **Gamay** grape from the Côte d'Or, keeping it for Pinot Noir, which is why Gamay moved south to Beaujolais.

cards.title: Revolution and the tiny plots
cards.body:
In **1789** the Revolution seized Church land and sold it in lots. Then **Napoleon's inheritance law** required land to be shared equally among all children. Over generations, vineyards were split again and again.

That is why **Clos de Vougeot** (50 ha) has more than **80 owners**, why one grower may own just a few rows of a Grand Cru, and why **négociants** who buy and blend grapes from many owners became so important. From the 1920s, growers such as the Marquis d'Angerville pushed for **domaine bottling**: the grower's own wine under their own name.

cards.q: Who banned Gamay from the Côte d'Or in 1395?
cards.explain: The Duke of Burgundy called Gamay 'disloyal' and kept the Côte d'Or for Pinot Noir; Gamay found its home in Beaujolais.

cards.q: Why are Burgundy's vineyards split among so many owners?
options: The Revolution sold Church land and inheritance law divided it among heirs
The monks sold small plots to raise money
The AOC rules require small plots
cards.explain: Napoleonic inheritance law split each estate equally among the children, generation after generation, so vineyards got cut into tiny parcels. That is how Clos de Vougeot ended up with more than 80 owners.

cards.q: Burgundy's climats are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
cards.explain: In 2015 UNESCO listed the climats of Burgundy, the named vineyard plots mapped by monks and growers over a thousand years.

cards.title: The Côte d'Or
cards.body: The **Côte de Nuits** (north) is mostly red Pinot Noir: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée, Chambolle-Musigny. The **Côte de Beaune** (south) is famous for whites: Meursault, Puligny- and Chassagne-Montrachet, plus reds from Pommard and Volnay.

cards.title: Climats
cards.body: Burgundy is divided into hundreds of named plots called **climats**, recognized by UNESCO. Many are split between several owners, so the producer matters as much as the vineyard.

cards.q: Which village is in the Côte de Beaune?
cards.explain: Meursault is a great white-wine village of the Côte de Beaune, famous for rich, nutty Chardonnay. The Côte de Beaune lies south of the Côte de Nuits, and includes Pommard and Volnay for red.

cards.q: The Côte de Nuits is best known for red wines.
cards.explain: The Côte de Nuits is best known for red wines: nearly all its Grand Crus are Pinot Noir, with Musigny having a tiny white exception. The villages include Gevrey-Chambertin and Vosne-Romanée.

cards.q: Match the Grand Cru to its color
cards.explain: Côte de Beaune Grand Crus are mostly white (Montrachet, Corton-Charlemagne), while Côte de Nuits ones are mostly red (Chambertin, Romanée-Conti). The exception is Corton, which is a red Grand Cru in the Côte de Beaune.

cards.q: Why does the producer matter so much in Burgundy?
options: Many vineyards are split between owners
cards.explain: The producer matters so much because plots are split among many owners: Clos de Vougeot alone has more than 80 owners, each making different wine from the same vineyard. Two bottles with the same label can differ widely in price and quality.

cards.q: Burgundy's named vineyard plots are called ___.
cards.explain: Burgundy's named vineyard plots are called climats. The climats of Burgundy became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015, recognizing centuries of monks mapping every slope.
