units.title: Grape files
units.summary: Every Level 4 grape on one card: aromas, structure, origin and where it grows.

cards.title: Torrontés
cards.body:
Argentina's aromatic white: exuberantly floral like Muscat, but dry, with a bitter-citrus finish.

- **Aromas:** rose, orange blossom, peach, lemon zest, lychee.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Argentina (a cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica).
- **Where it grows:** Salta, Argentina.
- **Food:** empanadas, spicy asian dishes, ceviche.

cards.title: Furmint
cards.body:
The great grape of Tokaj: searing acidity, smoky minerality and a strong affinity for noble rot.

- **Aromas:** lime, pear, quince, smoke, apricot, marmalade.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Hungary.
- **Where it grows:** Tokaj, Hungary, Somló.
- **Food:** foie gras, blue cheese, roast pork.

cards.title: Assyrtiko
cards.body:
Bone-dry, mineral and saline, keeping high acidity even in hot sun. Grown on Santorini in basket-shaped vines (kouloura).

- **Aromas:** lemon, grapefruit, saline, flint, wet stones, smoke.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity.
- **Origin:** Santorini, Greece.
- **Where it grows:** Santorini, Greece, Crete.
- **Food:** grilled fish, octopus, feta, fava dip.

cards.title: Melon de Bourgogne
cards.body:
The neutral grape behind Muscadet: light, lemony and briny, often given texture by ageing on its lees (sur lie).

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, saline, bread dough, wet stones.
- **Structure:** low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France.
- **Also called:** Muscadet.
- **Where it grows:** Muscadet, Loire Valley.
- **Food:** oysters, moules marinière, fish and chips.

cards.title: Garganega
cards.body:
The grape of Soave: almond, lemon and white flowers, with a gentle, textured finish.

- **Aromas:** lemon, pear, almond, blossom, peach.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Veneto, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Veneto.
- **Food:** risotto, seafood pasta, mild cheeses.

cards.q: Which grape shows **rose, orange blossom, peach**?
cards.explain: Argentina's aromatic white: exuberantly floral like Muscat, but dry, with a bitter-citrus finish.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lime, pear, quince**?
cards.explain: The great grape of Tokaj: searing acidity, smoky minerality and a strong affinity for noble rot.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, grapefruit, saline**?
cards.explain: Bone-dry, mineral and saline, keeping high acidity even in hot sun. Grown on Santorini in basket-shaped vines (kouloura).

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Glera
cards.body:
The grape of Prosecco: light, fresh, with pear, apple and white flowers.

- **Aromas:** pear, green apple, melon, blossom, acacia.
- **Structure:** low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Veneto & Friuli, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Veneto, Friuli.
- **Food:** aperitivo, prosciutto e melone, fried snacks.

cards.title: Verdejo
cards.body:
Rueda's grape: herbaceous and citrusy with a slightly bitter almond finish.

- **Aromas:** lime, grapefruit, fennel, grass, almond, peach.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Rueda, Spain.
- **Where it grows:** Rueda.
- **Food:** tapas, salads, white fish.

cards.title: Cortese
cards.body:
The grape of Gavi: delicate, crisp and lemony with a hint of almond.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, almond, blossom.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Gavi, Piedmont.
- **Food:** pesto, seafood, vitello tonnato.

cards.title: Verdicchio
cards.body:
Central Italy's finest white: high acidity, lemon, green almond and a gently bitter finish; ages surprisingly well.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, almond, fennel, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Marche, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Marche.
- **Food:** fish soup, fried seafood, pasta with clams.

cards.title: Fiano
cards.body:
Waxy, nutty and honeyed southern Italian white with good acidity. Best from Fiano di Avellino.

- **Aromas:** pear, peach, hazelnut, honey, acacia, smoke.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Campania, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Campania, Sicily.
- **Food:** seafood risotto, buffalo mozzarella, roast chicken.

cards.q: Which grape shows **pear, green apple, melon**?
cards.explain: The grape of Prosecco: light, fresh, with pear, apple and white flowers.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lime, grapefruit, fennel**?
cards.explain: Rueda's grape: herbaceous and citrusy with a slightly bitter almond finish.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, green apple, almond**?
cards.explain: The grape of Gavi: delicate, crisp and lemony with a hint of almond.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Greco
cards.body:
Greco di Tufo: firm, mineral and peachy with bright acidity and a light phenolic grip.

- **Aromas:** peach, lemon, almond, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Campania, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Campania.
- **Food:** grilled fish, pizza bianca, seafood.

cards.title: Palomino
cards.body:
A neutral, low-acid grape that is the perfect base for Sherry, where flor and oxygen create the flavors.

- **Aromas:** almond, bread dough, saline, walnut.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Andalucía, Spain.
- **Also called:** Palomino Fino, Listán.
- **Where it grows:** Jerez (Sherry).
- **Food:** jamón, olives, almonds, fried fish.

cards.title: Pedro Ximénez
cards.body:
Sun-dried in Jerez and Montilla to make PX: black, syrupy and intensely raisined.

- **Aromas:** raisin, fig, prune, coffee, toffee, chocolate.
- **Structure:** high body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Andalucía, Spain.
- **Also called:** PX.
- **Where it grows:** Jerez (Sherry).
- **Food:** vanilla ice cream, blue cheese, chocolate desserts.

cards.title: Marsanne & Roussanne
cards.body:
Rhône partners: Marsanne brings body and nutty richness, Roussanne aroma and acidity. White Hermitage is their peak.

- **Aromas:** pear, peach, almond, honey, acacia, sweet spice.
- **Structure:** medium-high body, medium-low acidity.
- **Origin:** Northern Rhône, France.
- **Where it grows:** Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Rhône Valley.
- **Food:** roast poultry, lobster, rich fish dishes.

cards.title: Trebbiano
cards.body:
High-yielding and neutral with high acidity. Across Italy it makes simple whites; in France, as Ugni Blanc, it is distilled into Cognac and Armagnac.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, pear, almond.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium-high acidity.
- **Origin:** Italy.
- **Also called:** Ugni Blanc.
- **Where it grows:** Abruzzo, Tuscany, Emilia-Romagna.
- **Food:** light pasta, salads.

cards.q: Which grape shows **peach, lemon, almond**?
cards.explain: Greco di Tufo: firm, mineral and peachy with bright acidity and a light phenolic grip.

cards.q: Which grape shows **almond, bread dough, saline**?
cards.explain: A neutral, low-acid grape that is the perfect base for Sherry, where flor and oxygen create the flavors.

cards.q: Which grape shows **raisin, fig, prune**?
cards.explain: Sun-dried in Jerez and Montilla to make PX: black, syrupy and intensely raisined.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

cards.title: Vermentino
cards.body:
Herbal, citrusy and saline: the Mediterranean seaside white of Sardinia, Liguria, coastal Tuscany and Provence (as Rolle).

- **Aromas:** lime, grapefruit, green apple, fennel, saline, almond.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Mediterranean coast.
- **Also called:** Rolle.
- **Where it grows:** Sardinia, Tuscany, Provence.
- **Food:** grilled fish, pesto, bouillabaisse.

cards.title: Pinot Blanc
cards.body:
Gentle, round and apple-scented, a softer cousin of Chardonnay. Widely used for Crémant d'Alsace.

- **Aromas:** red apple, pear, almond, blossom.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Burgundy, France (a mutation of Pinot Noir).
- **Also called:** Pinot Bianco, Weissburgunder.
- **Where it grows:** Alsace, Trentino-Alto Adige, Baden, Pfalz.
- **Food:** quiche, light fish, tarte flambée.

cards.title: Macabeo
cards.body:
The main white grape of Rioja (as Viura) and a key Cava grape. Neutral and fresh, or nutty when aged in old oak.

- **Aromas:** lemon, green apple, blossom, almond, hazelnut.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Spain.
- **Also called:** Viura.
- **Where it grows:** Rioja, Penedès.
- **Food:** tapas, seafood paella, croquetas.

cards.title: Silvaner
cards.body:
Earthy, herbal and quietly mineral; at its best in Franken, bottled in the squat Bocksbeutel flask.

- **Aromas:** green apple, pear, grass, wet stones.
- **Structure:** medium-low body, medium acidity.
- **Origin:** Central Europe.
- **Where it grows:** Franken, Rheinhessen.
- **Food:** asparagus, freshwater fish, salads.

cards.title: Barbera
cards.body:
Deep in color but low in tannin, with mouthwatering acidity and juicy black cherry: Piedmont's everyday red.

- **Aromas:** black cherry, red plum, blackberry, dried herbs, vanilla.
- **Structure:** medium body, high acidity, medium-low tannin.
- **Origin:** Piedmont, Italy.
- **Where it grows:** Barbera d'Asti, Piedmont.
- **Food:** pizza, pasta with ragù, salami.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lime, grapefruit, green apple**?
cards.explain: Herbal, citrusy and saline: the Mediterranean seaside white of Sardinia, Liguria, coastal Tuscany and Provence (as Rolle).

cards.q: Which grape shows **red apple, pear, almond**?
cards.explain: Gentle, round and apple-scented, a softer cousin of Chardonnay. Widely used for Crémant d'Alsace.

cards.q: Which grape shows **lemon, green apple, blossom**?
cards.explain: The main white grape of Rioja (as Viura) and a key Cava grape. Neutral and fresh, or nutty when aged in old oak.

cards.q: Match each grape to a place where it grows
cards.explain: Each grape is matched with one of its key regions from the cards above.

units.title: Appellations to know
units.summary: Every Level 4 region on a card, with its map, grapes and climate.

cards.title: Jura
cards.body:
Quirky mountain region known for Vin Jaune, a Savagnin wine aged under a flor-like yeast for over six years, plus Vin de Paille and Crémant du Jura.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Savoie
cards.body:
Alpine vineyards making crisp, light whites (Jacquère, Altesse) and reds (Mondeuse) perfect with fondue.

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Gamay, Chardonnay.

cards.title: South West France
cards.body:
A patchwork of local grapes and styles: Cahors (Malbec), Madiran (Tannat), Bergerac (Bordeaux varieties) and Jurançon (sweet and dry whites).

- **Where:** France.
- **Grapes:** Malbec, Tannat, Merlot, Sémillon.

cards.title: Médoc
cards.body:
The northern, lower-lying part of the Left Bank peninsula. More clay and Merlot than the Haut-Médoc; good-value reds and many Crus Bourgeois.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Haut-Médoc
cards.body:
The heart of the Left Bank, home to four famous communes and most of the 1855 classified growths.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot.
- **Climate:** Gravel ridges near the estuary drain well and store heat, helping late-ripening Cabernet.

cards.title: Saint-Estèphe
cards.body:
The northernmost famous commune: more clay, firmer and more rustic wines with high acidity and tannin. Cos d'Estournel and Montrose are leaders.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Pauillac
cards.body:
Home of three First Growths (Lafite, Latour, Mouton). Powerful, long-lived Cabernet with blackcurrant, cedar and pencil shavings.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Saint-Julien
cards.body:
Small and consistent: balanced, elegant, classic claret between Pauillac and Margaux. Léoville Las Cases, Ducru-Beaucaillou.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Jura**?
cards.explain: Jura: Quirky mountain region known for Vin Jaune, a Savagnin wine aged under a flor-like yeast for over six years, plus Vin de Paille and Crémant du Jura.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Savoie**?
cards.explain: Savoie: Alpine vineyards making crisp, light whites (Jacquère, Altesse) and reds (Mondeuse) perfect with fondue.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Margaux
cards.body:
Thin gravel soils give the most perfumed, silky wines of the Médoc. Château Margaux is its First Growth.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot.

cards.title: Pessac-Léognan
cards.body:
The northern Graves, on Bordeaux's doorstep. Smoky, earthy reds and the best oaked dry whites. Home of First Growth Haut-Brion.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon.

cards.title: Graves
cards.body:
Named after its gravel soils, south of the city along the Garonne. Red and dry white wines.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon.

cards.title: Entre-Deux-Mers
cards.body:
'Between two seas': the land between the Garonne and Dordogne rivers. Fresh dry whites and plenty of Bordeaux AOC red.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Merlot.

cards.title: Fronsac
cards.body:
Hilly Right Bank appellation west of Libourne: sturdy, value Merlot.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Franc.

cards.title: Castillon
cards.body:
Castillon Côtes de Bordeaux: limestone slopes east of Saint-Émilion, a source of value Merlot.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Cabernet Franc.

cards.title: Côtes de Bourg
cards.body:
Right bank of the Gironde opposite Margaux: robust, good-value Merlot-based reds.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot.

cards.title: Blaye
cards.body:
Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux: rolling hills north of Bourg, fruity reds and some whites.

- **Where:** Bordeaux, France.
- **Grapes:** Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Margaux**?
cards.explain: Margaux: Thin gravel soils give the most perfumed, silky wines of the Médoc. Château Margaux is its First Growth.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Pessac-Léognan**?
cards.explain: Pessac-Léognan: The northern Graves, on Bordeaux's doorstep. Smoky, earthy reds and the best oaked dry whites. Home of First Growth Haut-Brion.

cards.q: Match each region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Each region is matched with a grape it is known for, as in the cards above.

cards.title: Côte Chalonnaise
cards.body:
Value Burgundy from villages such as Mercurey, Givry, Rully and Montagny; also Bouzeron (Aligoté).

- **Where:** Burgundy, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Marsannay
cards.body:
The northern gateway to the Côte d'Or, just south of Dijon. The only Burgundy village appellation allowed to make rosé, alongside fresh Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Fixin
cards.body:
A small village making firm, sturdy, rustic Pinot Noir, often good value compared with its famous neighbors. Clos de la Perrière is the best-known Premier Cru.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Gevrey-Chambertin
cards.body:
The largest village of the Côte de Nuits and home of nine Grand Crus. Powerful, dark, structured reds with black cherry and spice, said to be Napoleon's favorite.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Morey-Saint-Denis
cards.body:
A small village between Gevrey and Chambolle with four Grand Crus (Clos de Tart, Clos des Lambrays, Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis). Its reds sit between Gevrey's power and Chambolle's silk.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Chambolle-Musigny
cards.body:
The most delicate and perfumed reds of the Côte de Nuits, grown on chalky, limestone-rich soils. Home of the Grand Crus Musigny and Bonnes-Mares.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Vougeot
cards.body:
The smallest village appellation of the Côte de Nuits, dominated by the walled Clos de Vougeot, built by Cistercian monks. A rare white Premier Cru, Clos Blanc de Vougeot, also exists.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Vosne-Romanée
cards.body:
Arguably the greatest red wine village on earth: Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, La Romanée, La Grande Rue, Échezeaux and Grands-Échezeaux. Silky, spicy, long-lived Pinot Noir.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Côte Chalonnaise**?
cards.explain: Côte Chalonnaise: Value Burgundy from villages such as Mercurey, Givry, Rully and Montagny; also Bouzeron (Aligoté).

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Marsannay**?
cards.explain: Marsannay: The northern gateway to the Côte d'Or, just south of Dijon. The only Burgundy village appellation allowed to make rosé, alongside fresh Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

cards.title: Nuits-Saint-Georges
cards.body:
The wine capital of the Côte de Nuits and its biggest town. Robust, earthy, age-worthy reds. It has no Grand Cru, but many fine Premiers Crus such as Les Saint-Georges and Les Vaucrains.

- **Where:** Côte de Nuits, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Ladoix
cards.body:
The first village of the Côte de Beaune, sharing the slope of Corton. Fresh reds and whites, with parts of the Grand Crus Corton and Corton-Charlemagne.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Aloxe-Corton
cards.body:
A village beneath the hill of Corton, which carries Burgundy's only red Grand Cru on the Côte de Beaune and the white Corton-Charlemagne.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Pernand-Vergelesses
cards.body:
A quiet village behind the hill of Corton. Good-value whites and reds, plus a share of Corton-Charlemagne on its western slope.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Savigny-lès-Beaune
cards.body:
Light, red-fruited, early-drinking Pinot Noir from a village on both sides of a small valley north of Beaune.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Chorey-lès-Beaune
cards.body:
Soft, fruity reds from flat land beside the road, mostly village-level wine and often excellent value.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Beaune
cards.body:
The wine capital of Burgundy, with its famous Hospices de Beaune auction each November. Elegant, perfumed reds from many Premiers Crus (no Grand Cru) and some whites.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Pommard
cards.body:
Powerful, structured reds with dark fruit and firm tannins that age well. Les Rugiens and Les Épenots are the best-known Premiers Crus.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Nuits-Saint-Georges**?
cards.explain: Nuits-Saint-Georges: The wine capital of the Côte de Nuits and its biggest town. Robust, earthy, age-worthy reds. It has no Grand Cru, but many fine Premiers Crus such as Les Saint-Georges and Les Vaucrains.

cards.q: Which grape is most associated with **Ladoix**?
cards.explain: Ladoix: The first village of the Côte de Beaune, sharing the slope of Corton. Fresh reds and whites, with parts of the Grand Crus Corton and Corton-Charlemagne.

cards.title: Volnay
cards.body:
Among the most elegant red Burgundies: pale, perfumed, silky, with red cherry and violets. Clos des Chênes and Caillerets are top Premiers Crus.

- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Monthélie

A small village next to Volnay and Meursault, making good-value, Volnay-like reds and a little white.

- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Auxey-Duresses

A hillside village at the end of a valley behind Meursault: affordable reds and nutty whites.

- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir, Chardonnay.

cards.title: Saint-Romain

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Meursault
cards.body:

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay.

- **Grapes:** Chardonnay.

cards.title: Chassagne-Montrachet
cards.body:

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Saint-Aubin
cards.body:
A high valley next to Puligny and Chassagne: crisp, mineral Chardonnay at a fraction of the price of its famous neighbors.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Santenay

The southern end of the Côte de Beaune: sturdy, earthy reds, and a spa town.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Maranges
cards.body:
The last appellation of the Côte d'Or, covering three villages: rustic, good-value Pinot Noir.

- **Where:** Côte de Beaune, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Bouzeron

- **Grapes:** Chardonnay.

cards.title: Rully

- **Where:** Côte Chalonnaise, France.
- **Grapes:** Chardonnay, Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Mercurey
cards.body:
The biggest and best-known red village of the Côte Chalonnaise: sturdy, fruity Pinot Noir at friendly prices.

- **Where:** Côte Chalonnaise, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Givry
cards.body:
Soft, red-fruited Pinot Noir, once the favorite wine of King Henri IV.

- **Where:** Côte Chalonnaise, France.
- **Grapes:** Pinot Noir.

cards.title: Montagny
cards.body:
The Côte Chalonnaise's white-only appellation: crisp, unoaked-leaning Chardonnay, and everything is classed Premier Cru.

cards.title: Saint-Joseph

units.title: Rhône, Loire, Alsace & Champagne
units.summary: France beyond Bordeaux and Burgundy, in depth.

cards.title: Two different worlds
cards.body:
- **Northern Rhône**: moderate continental climate, steep **granite** terraces, **Syrah** alone (sometimes with a little white grape co-fermented). Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage, Cornas, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage, plus Viognier in Condrieu.
- **Southern Rhône**: Mediterranean heat, the **Mistral** wind, **Grenache**-led blends. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Vacqueyras, Côtes du Rhône, Tavel rosé.

cards.q: What is the Mistral?
options: A cold, dry wind in the Southern Rhône
cards.explain: The Mistral is a cold, strong wind that blows down the Rhône Valley. It reduces disease pressure and can damage vines, so many old vines are trained as low bush vines, which resist it.

cards.q: Which Northern Rhône appellation may include Viognier co-fermented with Syrah?
cards.explain: Côte-Rôtie may include up to 20% Viognier co-fermented with Syrah, adding perfume and stabilizing color, though most producers use far less. The effect is a floral lift to the Syrah's dark fruit.

cards.q: Châteauneuf-du-Pape's galets roulés are large stones that store and radiate heat.
cards.explain: Châteauneuf-du-Pape's galets roulés, rounded quartzite pebbles, cover many vineyards. They store heat by day and release it at night, helping Grenache ripen.

cards.q: Match the appellation to its style
cards.explain: North for single varietals, south for blends and rosé: Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie are Syrah, Condrieu is Viognier, Châteauneuf is a blend, and Tavel is rosé. Place tells you the style.

cards.title: Four sections
cards.body:
- **Pays Nantais**: Muscadet (Melon de Bourgogne), maritime.
- **Anjou-Saumur**: Chenin (dry Savennières, sweet Coteaux du Layon), Cabernet Franc, sparkling Saumur.
- **Touraine**: Vouvray, Montlouis, Chinon, Bourgueil.
- **Central Vineyards**: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé (Sauvignon Blanc).

cards.q: Which Loire sub-region is closest to the Atlantic?
cards.explain: The Pays Nantais, around Nantes, is closest to the Atlantic. Its maritime climate suits Muscadet, made from Melon de Bourgogne, a crisp wine that is perfect with oysters.

cards.q: Coteaux du Layon is known for…
cards.explain: Coteaux du Layon is known for sweet Chenin Blanc. Autumn mists along the Layon river encourage noble rot, and Quarts de Chaume and Bonnezeaux are the top crus.

cards.q: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé face each other across the Loire.
cards.explain: Sancerre is on the west bank and Pouilly-sur-Loire on the east, facing each other across the river. Both are Sauvignon Blanc, but Sancerre is on limestone and flint (silex) soils and tends to be crisper.

cards.q: Pouilly-___ is a Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is a Burgundy Chardonnay.
cards.explain: Pouilly-Fumé is a Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is a Burgundy Chardonnay. The name Fumé refers to the smoky, flinty note from the soil, and it is a classic exam trap.

cards.title: Sheltered and dry
cards.body:
The **Vosges mountains** cast a rain shadow, making Alsace one of France's driest, sunniest regions. Wines are labeled by grape: **Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat** (the four 'noble' grapes for Grand Cru), plus Pinot Blanc and Pinot Noir.

Special sweet styles: **Vendanges Tardives** (late harvest) and **Sélection de Grains Nobles** (botrytis).

cards.q: Why is Alsace so dry and sunny for its latitude?
options: The Vosges mountains create a rain shadow
cards.explain: Alsace is dry and sunny for its latitude because the Vosges mountains block westerly rain, leaving the eastern foothills dry. It is one of the driest regions in France, which suits grapes like Riesling.

cards.q: Alsace wines are usually labeled by grape variety.
cards.explain: Unusually for France, the grape name is front and center in Alsace, and the wine comes in tall flûte bottles. This reflects the region's German history, and a Grand Cru label then adds the vineyard.

cards.q: Sélection de Grains Nobles means…
cards.explain: Sélection de Grains Nobles is made from individually selected noble-rot berries, rich and luscious. It is rarer and sweeter than Vendange Tardive, which is simply a late harvest.

cards.q: Match the Alsace grape to its style
cards.explain: Muscat in Alsace is usually dry and grapey, Gewurztraminer is rich and lychee-scented, Riesling is dry and mineral, and Pinot Gris is full and smoky. Alsace is where all four noble grapes shine.

cards.title: Assemblage and house style
cards.body:
Champagne is about **blending** (assemblage): grapes, villages and **reserve wines** from older vintages create a consistent non-vintage house style.

Villages are rated: **17 Grand Cru** and **42 Premier Cru**. Growers' own Champagnes ('grower Champagne') bear **RM** on the label; big houses use **NM**.

cards.title: Sweetness ladder
cards.body: From driest: **Brut Nature** (0–3 g/L), **Extra Brut**, **Brut** (under 12), **Extra Dry**, **Sec**, **Demi-Sec**, **Doux** (over 50).

cards.q: What do reserve wines give non-vintage Champagne?
cards.explain: Reserve wines, older wines from previous years, are blended in to smooth out vintage variation and add depth. It lets a house keep a consistent style each year, which is the art of non-vintage Champagne.

cards.q: Which is the driest sweetness term?
cards.explain: Brut Nature is the driest: no sugar added at dosage, 0–3 g/L. Extra Brut has up to 6 g/L, and Brut up to 12.

cards.q: 'RM' on a Champagne label means the grower made the wine from their own grapes.
cards.explain: RM means Récoltant-Manipulant: a grower who makes Champagne from their own grapes. NM (Négociant-Manipulant) is a house that buys grapes, so RM wines can show more of a single place.

cards.q: Champagne has ___ Grand Cru villages.
cards.explain: Champagne has 17 Grand Cru villages, including Aÿ, Bouzy, Cramant, Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger. The Grand Cru rating applies to the village, not to individual vineyards.

lessons.title: Deep dive: the Rhône, north and south

cards.title: Northern Rhône: Syrah on granite
cards.body:
A narrow valley of steep **granite** terraces. **Syrah** is the only black grape, giving black pepper, blackberry, olive and violet.

- **Côte-Rôtie**: may co-ferment up to 20% **Viognier** for perfume.
- **Hermitage**: one south-facing hill, the most powerful and long-lived.
- **Cornas**: 100% Syrah, wild and tannic. **Crozes-Hermitage** and **Saint-Joseph**: larger, more affordable.
- **Condrieu**: 100% Viognier white, apricot and blossom.

cards.title: Southern Rhône: the GSM blend
cards.body:
A wide, sunny plain swept by the cold **mistral** wind. Reds are blends led by **Grenache**, with **Syrah** (color, pepper) and **Mourvèdre** (structure, meaty depth): **GSM**.

**Châteauneuf-du-Pape** allows 13 varieties; its vineyards are covered in big rounded stones, the **galets roulés**. The papal coat of arms is embossed on many bottles. Neighbors: **Gigondas**, **Vacqueyras**, **Tavel** (rosé only), and great-value **Côtes du Rhône**.

cards.q: What is the only black grape of the northern Rhône?
cards.explain: Syrah is the only black grape of the northern Rhône (Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Cornas), while the south is dominated by Grenache-led blends. Know the north and south split.

cards.q: What does GSM stand for?
cards.explain: GSM is Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre: the classic southern Rhône blend, copied in Australia's McLaren Vale and Barossa. Grenache provides fruit, Syrah spice and color, Mourvèdre structure.

cards.q: Côte-Rôtie may include some white Viognier in its red wine.
cards.explain: Co-fermenting a little Viognier with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie lifts the aroma and stabilizes color. Up to 20% is allowed, though most producers use far less.

cards.q: Match the appellation to its wine
cards.explain: Rhône appellations each have a signature: Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie are Syrah, Condrieu is Viognier, Châteauneuf-du-Pape is a blend and Tavel is rosé.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Loire, Alsace and Champagne houses

cards.title: The Loire: four grapes, one river
cards.body:
From the Atlantic inland: **Muscadet** (Melon, sur lie), **Anjou-Saumur** (Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc, sweet Coteaux du Layon), **Touraine** (Vouvray Chenin, Chinon Cabernet Franc), and the **Centre** (**Sancerre** and **Pouilly-Fumé**, Sauvignon Blanc).

Chenin Blanc can be bone dry, sparkling, or lusciously sweet, sometimes from the same village.

cards.title: Alsace: French wines, German grapes
cards.body:
Sheltered by the Vosges mountains, Alsace is one of France's **driest** regions. Wines are labeled by **grape**, unusual for France: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat are the four "noble" ones, with 51 **Grands Crus**.

Wines come in the tall, slender **flûte** bottle. *Vendanges Tardives* (late harvest) and *Sélection de Grains Nobles* (botrytis) are the sweet styles. Most wines skip new oak and many skip malolactic conversion to keep acidity.

cards.title: Champagne's great houses
cards.body:
Big houses (*grandes marques*) aim for a consistent **non-vintage** style year after year by blending many villages and **reserve wines** from older years.

Prestige *cuvées* are their flagships: Dom Pérignon (Moët), Cristal (Roederer), La Grande Dame (Veuve Clicquot). Krug and Bollinger ferment in oak; Ruinart is known for Chardonnay.

cards.q: How are Alsace wines usually labeled?
cards.explain: Alsace is the main French region that puts the grape front and center on the label. That reflects its German heritage, and the wines come in tall flûte bottles.

cards.q: Which Loire grape makes Vouvray?
cards.explain: Vouvray is made from Chenin Blanc and can be sec, demi-sec, moelleux or sparkling. Chenin's high acidity balances any sweetness, so the wines age very well.

cards.q: Reserve wines help Champagne houses keep a consistent non-vintage style.
cards.explain: Reserve wines, older wines kept from earlier years, are blended in to smooth out differences between years. That is how a house keeps a consistent non-vintage style.

cards.title: The Rhône and the popes
cards.body:
The **northern Rhône**'s terraces at **Hermitage** and **Côte-Rôtie** were planted under the Romans; in the 1700s–1800s Hermitage was so prized that Bordeaux merchants added it to their best wines ("hermitagé").

In the south, the **popes** moved to **Avignon** in **1309**. Pope John XXII built a summer castle nearby: **Châteauneuf-du-Pape**, "the pope's new castle". In the 1920s its growers, led by **Baron Le Roy**, wrote the rules that became the model for France's **AOC** system (1935).

cards.title: The Loire, garden of kings
cards.body:
The Loire was the playground of French kings, whose **châteaux** line the river. Its wines traveled easily by boat to Paris and to the Dutch, who loved the sweet Chenin Blanc of **Anjou** and **Vouvray**.

**Sancerre** was mostly a red-wine and goat-cheese village until phylloxera; it was replanted with **Sauvignon Blanc**, which became world-famous only in the 1960s–70s through Paris bistros.

cards.title: Champagne's inventors
cards.body:
Kings of France were crowned at **Reims** cathedral, and the region's still wines were served at court. Cold winters stopped fermentation, which restarted in spring: early Champagne was fizzy by **accident**. The monk **Dom Pérignon** (1638–1715) worked to make better, clearer wine, but he did not invent the bubbles.

Stronger English glass bottles let the fizz survive. In **1816** the widow **Barbe-Nicole Clicquot** invented **riddling**, removing the yeast to make clear sparkling wine. In **1911**, growers rioted against merchants buying grapes from outside the region, which led to Champagne's strict boundaries.

cards.title: Alsace, between two countries
cards.body:
**Alsace** changed hands between France and Germany four times between 1871 and 1945. Under German rule (1871–1918) its vineyards were pushed toward cheap bulk wine; afterwards growers rebuilt on quality.

That history explains the **German-sounding** names, the tall **flûte** bottles, and why Alsace labels its wines by **grape**, unlike the rest of France.

cards.q: What does 'Châteauneuf-du-Pape' mean?
cards.explain: The popes lived in Avignon from 1309, and John XXII built a summer castle at Châteauneuf, the new castle of the Pope. The papal crest is embossed on the bottles.

cards.q: Who invented riddling, making clear sparkling wine possible?
cards.explain: The widow Clicquot's riddling table (around 1816) slowly moved the yeast into the neck so it could be removed.

cards.q: Dom Pérignon invented Champagne's bubbles.
cards.explain: Bubbles came from fermentation restarting in spring. Dom Pérignon improved the wine, its blending and its clarity.

cards.q: Why do Alsace wines have German-sounding names?
options: Alsace changed hands between France and Germany several times
The grapes all come from Austria
cards.explain: Between 1871 and 1945 Alsace switched between Germany and France four times, so many family names and wine words are German. That is also why Alsace labels by grape, like Germany.

cards.title: Champagne houses and growers
cards.body: Big **houses** (négociants) buy grapes from many villages and blend for a consistent house style. **Grower Champagnes** come from a single estate's own vines, showing their village's character. Look for "RM" (récoltant-manipulant) on the label.

cards.title: The Loire's many faces
cards.body: From the Atlantic inland: **Muscadet** (Melon), **Anjou-Saumur** (Chenin Blanc, Cabernet Franc), **Touraine** (Vouvray Chenin, Chinon Cabernet Franc) and the **Centre** (Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé Sauvignon Blanc).

cards.q: What does 'RM' on a Champagne label mean?
options: A grower making wine from their own grapes
cards.explain: Récoltant-Manipulant: the same family grows, makes and bottles the wine. These grower Champagnes are often more distinct and cheaper than the big houses.

cards.q: Match the Loire wine to its grape
cards.explain: The Loire grows mostly single varieties, each in its own district: Sauvignon Blanc in Sancerre, Chenin Blanc in Vouvray, Cabernet Franc in Chinon, and Melon de Bourgogne in Muscadet.

cards.q: Alsace wines are usually labeled with the grape variety.
cards.explain: Unusually for France, Alsace names the grape: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris. Most other French regions name the place, so Alsace is a bridge between Old and New World labeling.

cards.title: The south and the mountains
cards.body:
- **Languedoc-Roussillon**: France's biggest vineyard, sun and garrigue: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre and old Carignan. **Roussillon**, by the Pyrenees, also makes sweet fortified Grenache: **Banyuls** and **Maury**.
- **Provence**: the home of pale, dry **rosé**; **Bandol** makes long-lived red from Mourvèdre.
- **South West**: **Cahors** (Malbec, the "black wine"), **Madiran** (tannic Tannat) and sweet **Jurançon**.
- **Jura**: in the mountains near Switzerland. **Vin jaune** from Savagnin ages over six years under a veil of yeast, like Fino, and is bottled in a 62 cl **clavelin**; Château-Chalon is the most famous.

cards.q: Which southern French region is known for Grenache-based Banyuls and Côtes du Roussillon?
cards.explain: Roussillon, next to the Pyrenees, makes powerful Grenache-based reds and sweet fortified wines such as Banyuls and Maury. The fortified wines are made like Port, but with Grenache.

cards.q: Jura's oxidative 'yellow wine' is called vin ___.
cards.explain: Vin jaune ages under a veil of yeast for over six years in barrel, like a French cousin of Fino sherry. It is bottled in a special 62 cl bottle called a clavelin, and the best known is Château-Chalon.

units.title: Italy
units.summary: Piedmont, Tuscany, the North East and the South.

cards.title: The Langhe
cards.body:
Fog-wrapped hills around **Alba**. Continental climate; best sites face south.

- **Barolo**: Nebbiolo, minimum 38 months' ageing (18 in wood). Powerful, structured.
- **Barbaresco**: Nebbiolo, 26 months. Often more elegant.
- **Barbera d'Asti** and **Dolcetto d'Alba**: everyday reds.
- **Moscato d'Asti**: gently sparkling and sweet. **Gavi**: crisp Cortese.

cards.title: Barolo's communes
cards.body:
Barolo is five main villages, and each speaks differently:

- **La Morra** and **Barolo**: softer Tortonian marl, perfumed, elegant, earlier-drinking wines.
- **Serralunga d'Alba**: older, compact Helvetian soils, the most powerful and structured Barolo, needing 15 years or more.
- **Castiglione Falletto** and **Monforte d'Alba**: in between, with firm structure and depth.

cards.q: What is the minimum ageing for Barolo?
cards.explain: Barolo must age at least 38 months, including 18 months in wood. Riserva requires 62 months. Barolo is released later than almost any other red, since Nebbiolo's tannins need time.

cards.q: Which Piedmont grape is deeply colored with high acidity but low tannin?
cards.explain: Barbera has deep color, high acidity and low tannin: its juicy acidity and soft tannin make it a perfect food wine. Piedmont's Barbera d'Alba and d'Asti are everyday favorites.

cards.q: Barbaresco is made from Sangiovese.
cards.explain: Barbaresco, like Barolo, is 100% Nebbiolo, not Sangiovese. It is grown in a smaller, warmer zone near Alba, so it tends to be a little more elegant and earlier-maturing.

cards.q: Gavi is a crisp white wine from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: Gavi is a crisp white made from the Cortese grape: lemon, green apple and almond, a classic with pesto from nearby Liguria. The best Gavi di Gavi is a DOCG.

cards.title: Sangiovese country
cards.body:
- **Chianti Classico**: the historic heart (black rooster symbol), ≥80% Sangiovese. Annata → Riserva → **Gran Selezione**.
- **Brunello di Montalcino**: 100% Sangiovese, released five years after harvest.
- **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano**: Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile).
- **Bolgheri**: coastal Super Tuscans from Bordeaux varieties.

cards.q: Brunello di Montalcino is made from…
cards.explain: Brunello is the local name for a Sangiovese clone (Sangiovese Grosso). Warm, dry Montalcino gives power and longevity, and the wine has to age five years before release.

cards.q: What is a Super Tuscan?
options: A Tuscan wine made outside traditional rules
cards.explain: Starting with Sassicaia and Tignanello in the 1970s, often with Cabernet or Merlot, first released as table wine.

cards.q: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is made from the Montepulciano grape.
cards.explain: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from the town of Montepulciano in Tuscany. The Montepulciano grape is grown in Abruzzo, which is a classic exam trap.

cards.q: Match the Tuscan wine to its place
cards.explain: Three of Tuscany's great names: Chianti Classico between Florence and Siena, Brunello di Montalcino in the south and Bolgheri on the coast. Each is a different expression of Sangiovese or Bordeaux grapes.

cards.title: Veneto and beyond
cards.body:
- **Valpolicella** (Corvina): light Valpolicella, **Ripasso**, dry **Amarone** and sweet **Recioto** from dried grapes (appassimento).
- **Soave** (Garganega). **Prosecco** (Glera).
- **Friuli**: fine whites and orange wines. **Alto Adige**: Alpine aromatic whites.

cards.q: How is Amarone made?
options: From grapes dried for months before fermentation
cards.explain: Amarone is made by appassimento: grapes are dried for months, which concentrates sugar. Fermenting to dryness gives a powerful wine of about 15–16% abv with raisin and cherry flavors.

cards.q: Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on leftover Amarone skins.
cards.explain: Ripasso is Valpolicella refermented on leftover Amarone skins. It adds body, alcohol and dried-fruit flavor, which is why it is called baby Amarone.

cards.q: Soave is made mainly from the ___ grape.
cards.explain: Soave is made mainly from Garganega, grown on volcanic and limestone hills east of Verona. Good Soave Classico is crisp, with almond and white peach notes.

cards.q: Which Italian region is known for skin-contact orange wines?
cards.explain: Pioneers near the Slovenian border revived long skin maceration for white grapes such as Ribolla Gialla.

cards.title: Volcanoes and sunshine
cards.body:
- **Campania**: Taurasi (Aglianico), Fiano di Avellino, Greco di Tufo.
- **Basilicata**: Aglianico del Vulture.
- **Puglia**: Primitivo and Negroamaro.
- **Sicily**: Nero d'Avola, and elegant Etna wines (Nerello Mascalese, Carricante) from volcanic slopes.
- **Sardinia**: Cannonau (Grenache) and Vermentino.

cards.q: Taurasi is made from…
cards.explain: Taurasi, from Campania, is made from Aglianico and is often called the Barolo of the South, high in tannin and acidity. It needs years to soften and can age for decades.

cards.q: Cannonau, from Sardinia, is the same grape as Grenache.
cards.explain: Cannonau, from Sardinia, is the same grape as Grenache. Sardinia has a long tradition of the grape, possibly as old as Spain's, and the island has one of the highest numbers of centenarians in the world.

cards.q: Why are Mount Etna's wines fresher than much of Sicily's?
cards.explain: Mount Etna's vineyards climb above 1,000 m, giving cool nights and elegant wines. The black volcanic soils and old vines of Nerello Mascalese make reds compared to Burgundy.

cards.q: Match the southern grape to its region
cards.explain: Three of southern Italy's most important grapes: Aglianico in Campania and Basilicata, Nero d'Avola in Sicily and Primitivo in Puglia. Each gives a bold, sunny red.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Piedmont and Tuscany up close

cards.title: Barolo and Barbaresco
cards.body:
In the **Langhe** hills near Alba, **Nebbiolo** ripens late, often picked in October fog (*nebbia*). It is pale in color but high in **tannin and acidity**, smelling of **roses, tar, cherry and licorice**.

**Barolo**: at least 38 months of ageing (18 in wood), 62 months for Riserva. **Barbaresco**: at least 26 months. Single vineyards are labeled as **MGA** (*menzioni geografiche aggiuntive*), like Cannubi or Rabajà.

cards.title: Traditionalists vs modernists
cards.body:
In the 1980s–90s the "Barolo wars" split producers: **traditionalists** used long macerations and big old casks (*botti*); **modernists** used short macerations and new French *barriques* for softer, oakier wines.

Today most producers sit in between.

cards.title: Chianti Classico and Brunello
cards.body:
**Sangiovese** loves Tuscany's hills: sour cherry, tomato leaf, dried herbs, high acidity.

- **Chianti Classico**: the historic zone, black rooster on the neck; Annata, Riserva and **Gran Selezione** (top tier).
- **Brunello di Montalcino**: 100% Sangiovese, released five years after harvest.
- **Vino Nobile di Montepulciano**: the town, not the grape.
- **Super Tuscans**: Bordeaux varieties on the coast at **Bolgheri** (Sassicaia, Ornellaia), first sold as humble *vino da tavola*.

cards.title: The Italian pyramid
cards.body:
- **DOCG**: the top, with a numbered neck strip (Barolo, Brunello, Chianti Classico…).
- **DOC**: controlled origin.
- **IGT**: regional wine with freer rules: where many Super Tuscans began.
- **Vino**: table wine.

cards.q: Which grape makes Barolo and Barbaresco?
cards.explain: Nebbiolo makes Barolo and Barbaresco. The name probably comes from nebbia, the fog of harvest time, and the grape ripens very late.

cards.q: What symbol marks Chianti Classico?
cards.explain: The gallo nero, the black rooster, has been the emblem of the Chianti Classico consortium for nearly a century. Look for it on the neck of the bottle.

cards.q: Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is made from the Montepulciano grape.
cards.explain: Vino Nobile is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano, not the Montepulciano grape, which grows in Abruzzo. It is a classic exam trap.

cards.q: Match the Italian wine to its grape
cards.explain: Italy's great wines rest on native grapes: Barolo on Nebbiolo, Chianti on Sangiovese, Amarone on Corvina, Taurasi on Aglianico. Italy has hundreds of native varieties.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Veneto, the South and the islands

cards.title: Amarone and appassimento
cards.body:
In Valpolicella, **Corvina** grapes are dried for about **100 days** in lofts (*fruttai*), losing a third or more of their weight. Fermented dry, they make **Amarone**: 15–16% alcohol, raisin, cherry and chocolate. Fermentation stopped early gives sweet **Recioto**.

**Ripasso** re-passes young Valpolicella over Amarone skins for extra body.

cards.title: The South awakens
cards.body:
- **Campania**: **Aglianico** in Taurasi (the "Barolo of the South"), whites **Fiano di Avellino** and **Greco di Tufo**.
- **Puglia**: rich **Primitivo** (Zinfandel) and **Negroamaro**.
- **Sicily**: **Nero d'Avola**, and on volcanic **Etna**, elegant Nerello Mascalese reds and Carricante whites at up to 1,000 m.
- **Sardinia**: **Vermentino** and **Cannonau** (Grenache).

cards.q: How long are grapes typically dried for Amarone?
cards.explain: Grapes for Amarone are dried for about three to four months, which concentrates sugar and flavor. The wine is then fermented to dryness, giving a powerful 15–16% wine.

cards.q: Primitivo from Puglia is genetically the same as…
cards.explain: Primitivo from Puglia is genetically the same as Zinfandel. Both trace back to the Croatian grape Crljenak Kaštelanski (Tribidrag).

cards.q: Cannonau, Sardinia's main red grape, is Grenache.
cards.explain: Cannonau, Sardinia's main red grape, is Grenache (Garnacha). Sardinians claim it as their own, and DNA shows it is the same variety.

cards.title: The land of vines
cards.body:
The **Etruscans** made wine in central Italy before Rome, and **Greek** settlers called the south **Oenotria**, "land of vines". Rome turned wine into an industry: amphorae from Campania traveled across the empire.

After Rome, wine survived in monasteries and noble families. Some Tuscan families, the **Antinori** and **Frescobaldi**, have made wine for more than **600 years**.

cards.title: Chianti's rules
cards.body:
In **1716**, **Cosimo III de' Medici** drew the borders of Chianti, one of the world's first legal wine zones. In **1872** **Baron Bettino Ricasoli** wrote a recipe: mostly **Sangiovese**, softened with Canaiolo and a little white Malvasia.

Twentieth-century rules forced in too much white grape and too-high yields. Quality fell, until rebels broke away.

cards.title: The Super Tuscan revolt
cards.body:
In **1968** the Marchese Incisa della Rocchetta released **Sassicaia**, a Cabernet from the coast at **Bolgheri**, as a humble *vino da tavola*: the rules had no place for it. **Tignanello** (Antinori, 1971) and others followed, blending Sangiovese with Cabernet and aging in French barrels.

These "**Super Tuscans**" sold for more than any Chianti. The law caught up: the **IGT** category (1992) and the **Bolgheri DOC** (Sassicaia got its own DOC in 2013).

cards.title: Barolo, king of wines
cards.body:
Until the mid-1800s **Nebbiolo** in Piedmont was often made sweet and fizzy. The **Marchesa Giulia Falletti** of Barolo and **Count Cavour** (later Italy's first prime minister) hired the French winemaker **Louis Oudart**, who made it dry and age-worthy.

Barolo became "the wine of kings and the king of wines", favored by the House of Savoy, Italy's royal family.

cards.q: Who drew Chianti's borders in 1716?
cards.explain: His decree defined Chianti, Carmignano, Pomino and Valdarno: one of the first legally defined wine regions.

cards.q: Why was Sassicaia first sold as a simple 'vino da tavola'?
options: Its Cabernet blend didn't fit any DOC rules
cards.explain: Tuscany's rules had no place for Cabernet from the coast; the law later created IGT and the Bolgheri DOC.

cards.q: Barolo used to be made sweet and slightly fizzy before the mid-1800s.
cards.explain: Cold autumns stopped fermentation; the Marchesa Falletti and Count Cavour brought in a French winemaker to make it dry.

cards.title: Super Tuscans
cards.body: In the 1970s, producers like Sassicaia and Tignanello broke DOC rules, using Cabernet Sauvignon and French oak. Sold as simple table wine, they became famous as **Super Tuscans**, and Bolgheri later got its own DOC.

cards.title: The Veneto
cards.body: **Valpolicella** blends Corvina with other local grapes. **Amarone** is made from grapes dried for months (appassimento), giving rich, high-alcohol, dry reds. **Ripasso** passes young Valpolicella over Amarone skins for extra body.

cards.q: What is 'appassimento'?
cards.explain: Appassimento is drying grapes: it concentrates sugar and flavor, and it is how Amarone and Recioto are made. Grapes are dried for months on racks or in lofts.

cards.q: Match the wine to its region
cards.explain: Italy's twenty regions each have their own grapes and wines: Piedmont for Nebbiolo, Tuscany for Sangiovese, Veneto for Corvina, Campania for Aglianico. Matching them is a core Italian skill.

cards.q: Super Tuscans often include Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot.
cards.explain: International grapes are what made Super Tuscans break the old rules: from the 1970s Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot were blended outside the DOC rules. The wines were labeled humble vino da tavola, but became icons.

cards.q: Which grape is the backbone of Valpolicella and Amarone?
cards.explain: Corvina is the backbone of Valpolicella and Amarone, giving sour cherry and almond notes. Its thick skins let it dry well without rotting, so it suits appassimento.

cards.q: Sassicaia comes from the coastal Tuscan zone of ___.
cards.explain: Sassicaia comes from Bolgheri, on the Tuscan coast, which became famous for Bordeaux-style blends. Sassicaia, first made in 1968, was the first Super Tuscan, and got its own DOC in 1994.

units.title: Spain & Portugal
units.summary: Rioja and Ribera, Spain's diverse regions, and Portugal from Vinho Verde to the Douro.

cards.title: Rioja
cards.body:
Along the **Ebro**, sheltered by mountains. Three zones: cooler **Rioja Alta** and **Rioja Alavesa**, warmer **Rioja Oriental**.

**Tempranillo** leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo (Carignan). Traditional producers age long in American oak; modern ones use French oak, riper fruit and single vineyards.

cards.title: Ribera del Duero
cards.body: A high plateau (about 750–850 m) along the Duero. Hot days and very cold nights produce deep, powerful **Tinto Fino** (Tempranillo). Vega Sicilia and Pingus are icons.

cards.q: Which Rioja zone is the warmest?
cards.explain: Rioja Baja is the warmest zone, lower and more Mediterranean, so it suits Garnacha. Rioja Alta and Alavesa are cooler and higher and make the finer, more acidic Tempranillo.

cards.q: Ribera del Duero's vineyards are at high altitude, giving cold nights.
cards.explain: Ribera del Duero's vineyards are at high altitude (about 800 m), giving cold nights. Frost is a risk, but the big difference between day and night keeps acidity and color in the Tempranillo (Tinto Fino).

cards.q: Mazuelo, used in Rioja, is better known as…
cards.explain: Mazuelo is Cariñena (Carignan) in other places. It adds acidity, color and tannin to Rioja blends, and is the same grape that makes old-vine wines in Priorat.

cards.q: A red Rioja Reserva must age at least ___ years, one in oak.
cards.explain: A red Rioja Reserva must age at least three years, one in oak. Crianza needs two years (one in oak); Gran Reserva needs five (two in oak). The label tells you how long it spent in cask and bottle.

cards.title: From Galicia to Andalucía
cards.body:
- **Rías Baixas**: Albariño. **Rueda**: Verdejo. **Bierzo**: Mencía.
- **Priorat**: old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena on llicorella slate.
- **Penedès**: Cava (Macabeo, Xarel·lo, Parellada).
- **La Mancha**: the huge central plain. **Jumilla**: Monastrell.
- **Jerez**: Sherry.

cards.q: Priorat's famous slate soil is called…
cards.explain: Dark, crumbly slate that forces roots deep and gives low yields of intense wine. Albariza is the white chalk of Jerez.

cards.q: Match the Spanish region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Spain is far more than Tempranillo: Albariño in Rías Baixas, Verdejo in Rueda, Garnacha in Priorat, Mencía in Bierzo. Each region leans on a local hero grape.

cards.q: Albariza is the chalky white soil of the Sherry region.
cards.explain: Albariza, the chalky white soil of the Sherry region around Jerez, holds winter rain like a sponge and bakes into a hard crust in summer. That water keeps Palomino vines alive through the dry summers.

cards.q: Which grapes make Cava?
cards.explain: Cava is made from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada, with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir also permitted. The local trio gives a lemony, earthy, rounder style than Champagne.

cards.title: The Douro and beyond
cards.body:
- **Vinho Verde**: rainy north-west; fresh, light whites, Alvarinho at its best.
- **Douro**: hot schist terraces; Port and powerful dry reds from Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz.
- **Dão**: granite plateau, elegant reds. **Bairrada**: Baga.
- **Alentejo**: hot plains; ripe reds; cork forests.

cards.q: The Douro's vineyards grow on…
cards.explain: The Douro's vineyards grow on schist, which breaks into layers that let vine roots dig deep for water in the hot, dry summers. Steep terraces were cut by hand, and they are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.q: Portugal is the world's largest producer of cork.
cards.explain: Portugal is the world's largest producer of cork, mostly from cork oak forests in the Alentejo. The bark is harvested every nine years without felling the tree.

cards.q: Which grape is considered Portugal's finest black variety?
cards.explain: Touriga Nacional is considered Portugal's finest black grape: deep, floral and structured. It is key to both Port and Douro reds, and also grows well in Dão.

cards.q: LBV Port stands for Late Bottled ___.
cards.explain: LBV Port stands for Late Bottled Vintage: a single-vintage Port aged 4–6 years in wood, ready to drink sooner than Vintage Port. It is a better-value alternative that doesn't need decanting in many cases.

cards.title: Rioja's ageing ladder
cards.body:
Rioja splits into **Rioja Alta**, **Rioja Alavesa** (cooler, higher) and **Rioja Oriental** (warmer, more Garnacha). **Tempranillo** leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo (Carignan).

Labels show **time in oak and bottle** (red minimums):
- **Joven**: little or no oak.
- **Crianza**: 2 years, at least 1 in oak.
- **Reserva**: 3 years, at least 1 in oak.
- **Gran Reserva**: 5 years, at least 2 in oak.

Traditional bodegas use **American oak**: vanilla, coconut, dill.

cards.title: The new Spain
cards.body:
- **Ribera del Duero**: Tempranillo (Tinto Fino) on a high plateau; Vega Sicilia, Pingus.
- **Priorat**: old Garnacha and Cariñena on black slate (*llicorella*); one of only two **DOCa** with Rioja.
- **Rías Baixas**: Albariño by the Atlantic.
- **Bierzo**: Mencía, fresh and floral.
- **Toro** and **Jumilla** (Monastrell): power and sun.

cards.q: Which Rioja label means at least 5 years of ageing?
cards.explain: Gran Reserva reds age at least five years, two of them in oak. It is made only in the best vintages and usually released after a decade.

cards.q: What is llicorella?
cards.explain: Llicorella is the broken black slate of Priorat. It forces roots deep and gives very low yields, so the wines are dense and mineral.

cards.q: Match the Spanish region to its grape
cards.explain: Spain is far more than Tempranillo: Albariño in Rías Baixas, Garnacha in Priorat, Mencía in Bierzo and Verdejo in Rueda. Each region has a local hero.

cards.q: Traditional Rioja is often aged in American oak.
cards.explain: Traditional Rioja is aged in American oak, which gives the classic vanilla and coconut notes. Modern producers use more French oak for a more subtle style.

cards.title: Over 250 native grapes
cards.body:
Portugal kept its own grapes when much of the world planted French ones.

- **Touriga Nacional**: violet, black fruit, the star of Port and Douro reds.
- **Touriga Franca**, **Tinta Roriz** (Tempranillo), **Baga** (Bairrada's tannic red).
- **Alvarinho** and **Loureiro** in Vinho Verde; **Encruzado** in Dão; **Arinto** everywhere for acidity.

cards.title: Regions to know
cards.body:
- **Vinho Verde**: light, fresh, sometimes spritzy whites.
- **Douro**: Port, and now great dry reds from the same terraces.
- **Dão**: granite hills, elegant reds.
- **Bairrada**: Baga reds and traditional-method sparkling.
- **Alentejo**: hot plains, ripe reds; some still fermented in clay **talhas**.
- **Setúbal**: sweet fortified Moscatel.

cards.q: Which grape is considered Portugal's finest red?
cards.explain: Touriga Nacional is considered Portugal's finest red, with deep color, violet perfume and structure. It is used in Port and in dry Douro and Dão reds.

cards.q: What are talhas?
cards.explain: Talhas are large clay amphorae used to ferment wine in the Alentejo, a Roman-era tradition revived under the Vinho de Talha DOC. The wine is made like ancient wine, with the skins in the pot.

cards.q: Tinta Roriz is Portugal's name for Tempranillo.
cards.explain: Tinta Roriz is Portugal's name for Tempranillo; it is also called Aragonez in the Alentejo. It is one of the main grapes of Port.

cards.title: Sack and the sea
cards.body:
**Jerez** traded wine with England for centuries. In **1587**, **Sir Francis Drake** raided Cádiz and carried home nearly **3,000 barrels** of "sack", as the English called sherry. Shakespeare's Falstaff praised it.

Fortifying with spirit protected the wine on long voyages, and Spanish ships took it to the New World.

cards.title: Port, made for England
cards.body:
At war with France, England bought Portuguese wine instead. The **Methuen Treaty** of **1703** gave Portuguese wine low taxes in England. To survive the sea journey, Douro wine was fortified with brandy: the birth of **Port**, and of British houses such as **Taylor's**, **Croft** and **Graham's**.

In **1756** the **Marquis of Pombal** demarcated the **Douro**, one of the world's first protected wine regions, to stop fraud.

cards.title: Rioja and the French
cards.body:
When **phylloxera** and mildew struck Bordeaux in the **1860s–70s**, French merchants crossed the Pyrenees to **Rioja** for wine. They brought **oak barrels** and Bordeaux methods. The railway from **Haro** to Bordeaux (opened 1880) carried the wine north.

Bodegas founded then, such as **López de Heredia** (1877) and **CVNE** (1879), still make classic, long-aged Rioja. Phylloxera reached Rioja itself around **1899**.

cards.q: Which treaty gave Portuguese wine low taxes in England in 1703?
cards.explain: The Methuen Treaty of 1703 gave Portuguese wine low taxes in England. England, at war with France, turned to Portugal, and fortified Douro wine became Port.

cards.q: Why did French merchants come to Rioja in the 1870s?
options: Phylloxera and mildew had ruined their own vineyards
cards.explain: In the 1870s phylloxera struck Bordeaux, and French merchants moved to Rioja, bringing barrels and Bordeaux methods. That shaped the oak-aged Rioja style.

cards.q: The Douro was demarcated in 1756, one of the first protected wine regions.
cards.explain: The Marquis of Pombal mapped the best vineyards and created a company to control quality and stop fraud.

cards.title: Rioja's subregions
cards.body: Rioja has three parts: **Rioja Alta** (cooler, elegant), **Rioja Alavesa** (limestone, finesse) and **Rioja Oriental** (warmer, Garnacha-rich). Traditional producers age in American oak; modern ones favor French oak and riper fruit.

cards.title: Port styles
cards.body: **Ruby** and **Vintage** Port age mostly in bottle and stay deep red with black fruit. **Tawny** ages in small casks, turning amber with nutty, caramel notes; 10, 20, 30 and 40 Year Old labels give an average age.

cards.q: Which Port style ages in small casks and turns amber?
cards.explain: Tawny Port ages in small casks, where oxygen through the wood turns it amber and gives nutty, caramel flavors. Ruby Port is kept in tanks and bottle, so it remains red and fruity.

cards.q: Match the Spanish region to its signature grape
cards.explain: Spain's regions each lean on a local hero grape: Tempranillo in Rioja, Garnacha in Priorat, Albariño in Rías Baixas, Palomino in Jerez. Learning the pairs is key to blind tasting Spain.

cards.q: American oak gives stronger coconut and vanilla notes than French oak.
cards.explain: American oak gives stronger coconut and vanilla notes than French oak, because it has more lactones. That is why traditional Rioja often smells of vanilla and coconut, while modern Riojas use more French oak.

cards.q: What does '20 Year Old' on a Tawny Port mean?
options: A blend with an average age of about 20 years
Every drop is exactly 20 years old
It must be drunk within 20 years
cards.explain: A 20 Year Old Tawny is a blend of casks that tastes like the stated age, not a wine that spent exactly 20 years in wood. The stated ages are 10, 20, 30 and 40.

cards.q: Priorat's dark slate and quartz soil is called ___.
cards.explain: Llicorella, Priorat's dark slate and quartz soil, forces vine roots deep and gives the wines their mineral intensity. The steep terraces and old Garnacha and Cariñena vines yield tiny crops.

units.title: Germany, Austria, Hungary & Greece
units.summary: Prädikat levels, Austrian classics, Tokaji and Greece's revival.

cards.title: Ripeness levels
cards.body:
German **Prädikatswein** is classified by grape sugar at harvest:

- **Kabinett**: light, often off-dry.
- **Spätlese**: late harvest, riper.
- **Auslese**: selected bunches.
- **Beerenauslese (BA)**: selected berries, often botrytized.
- **Eiswein**: frozen grapes.
- **Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA)**: shriveled botrytized berries.

A ripeness level is not a sweetness level: a Spätlese can be **trocken** (dry).

cards.q: Which Prädikat is made from individually picked shriveled, botrytized berries?
cards.explain: Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) is made from individually picked, shriveled, botrytized berries. It is one of the world's rarest and sweetest wines, sometimes with under 6% alcohol, and can age for a century.

cards.q: A Spätlese is always sweet.
cards.explain: Spätlese means late harvest: a ripeness level, not a sweetness level. It can be fermented dry (Spätlese trocken), which gives a ripe, full-bodied dry wine.

cards.q: Which region is famous for delicate, low-alcohol Riesling on steep slate?
cards.explain: The Mosel is famous for delicate, low-alcohol Riesling on steep slate slopes. The blue and red slate slopes are among the steepest in the world, and the river reflects light and holds heat.

cards.q: Match the German region to its specialty
cards.explain: Germany's regions have specialties: Mosel for delicate Riesling, Rheingau for richer Riesling, Pfalz for full-bodied wines, and Baden, Germany's warmest region, for the Pinot family (Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder).

cards.title: Precision and purity
cards.body:
- **Niederösterreich**: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal: Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.
- **Wachau** ripeness categories: **Steinfeder** (light), **Federspiel**, **Smaragd** (richest).
- **Burgenland**: Blaufränkisch, Zweigelt and sweet wines around Lake Neusiedl.
- **Steiermark**: Sauvignon Blanc.

**DAC** (*Districtus Austriae Controllatus*) labels show typical regional styles.

cards.q: In the Wachau, the ripest dry style is called…
cards.explain: Smaragd, named after an emerald-green lizard that basks on the warm terraces, is the Wachau's ripest dry style. It is full-bodied and often 13% alcohol or more, above Steinfeder and Federspiel.

cards.q: Lake Neusiedl's humidity helps produce botrytized sweet wines.
cards.explain: Lake Neusiedl is shallow and warm, and the morning mists from it encourage noble rot. The Burgenland region makes top sweet wines such as Ausbruch and Trockenbeerenauslese.

cards.q: Austria's most planted red grape is…
cards.explain: Austria's most planted red grape is Zweigelt, a 1922 cross of St. Laurent and Blaufränkisch. It makes juicy, cherry-fruited reds, while Blaufränkisch makes the more serious ones.

cards.q: DAC stands for Districtus Austriae ___.
cards.explain: DAC stands for Districtus Austriae Controllatus. It marks wines typical of their region, such as Weinviertel DAC for peppery Grüner Veltliner, and is Austria's equivalent of the French AOC.

cards.title: Tokaji
cards.body:
In north-east **Hungary**, volcanic hills and river mists favor noble rot on **Furmint** and Hárslevelű.

- **Tokaji Aszú**: aszú berries macerated in base wine; at least 120 g/L sugar.
- **Eszencia**: the free-run syrup of aszú berries; can be 500+ g/L sugar and as low as 3% alcohol.
- Increasingly fine **dry Furmint**.

cards.title: Greece
cards.body:
- **Assyrtiko** (Santorini): mineral, high-acid white from basket-trained, ungrafted vines.
- **Xinomavro** (Naoussa): tannic, high-acid red.
- **Agiorgitiko** (Nemea): soft, plummy red.

cards.q: Tokaji's main grape is…
cards.explain: Tokaji's main grape is Furmint: high acidity, smoky minerality and a strong affinity for botrytis. That acidity keeps the sweet Aszú wines lively and lets them age for generations.

cards.q: Santorini's vines are grafted onto American rootstock.
cards.explain: Phylloxera cannot survive in Santorini's volcanic sand, so vines grow on their own roots, some very old.

cards.q: Which Greek grape is often compared to Nebbiolo?
cards.explain: Xinomavro, from northern Greece, is often compared to Nebbiolo: pale, high in tannin and acidity, with tomato, olive and red fruit. Naoussa is its most famous appellation.

cards.q: Tokaji ___ is the rare syrup of aszú berries, one of the sweetest wines on earth.
cards.explain: Tokaji Eszencia is the rare syrup of aszú berries that drips by its own weight, one of the sweetest wines on earth. It ferments for years and reaches only a few percent alcohol, and is traditionally used as a medicine.

cards.title: Prädikat levels
cards.body:
German quality wine is graded by **grape ripeness at harvest**, not by sweetness in the glass:

**Kabinett** → **Spätlese** (late harvest) → **Auslese** (selected bunches) → **Beerenauslese** (selected berries, usually botrytized) → **Trockenbeerenauslese** (dried botrytized berries) and **Eiswein**.

Kabinett and Spätlese are often off-dry; **Trocken** on a label means dry.

cards.title: VDP and Grosses Gewächs
cards.body: The VDP growers' association uses a Burgundy-style pyramid: **Gutswein**, **Ortswein** (village), **Erste Lage** (premier cru) and **Grosse Lage** (grand cru). A dry wine from a Grosse Lage is a **Grosses Gewächs** (GG), shown by "GG" on the bottle.

cards.title: Regions and bottles
cards.body:
- **Mosel**: steep slate, light, racy, low alcohol.
- **Rheingau**: south-facing slopes on the Rhine, fuller and drier.
- **Pfalz**: warmest, rich dry Riesling and Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir).
- **Nahe**, **Rheinhessen**, **Franken** (Silvaner in the flat *Bocksbeutel* bottle).

Most German wine comes in the tall **flûte** bottle: brown glass traditionally for the Rhine, green for the Mosel.

cards.q: What do German Prädikat levels measure?
cards.explain: German Prädikat levels measure grape ripeness at harvest, from Kabinett up to Trockenbeerenauslese. A Spätlese can be dry or sweet, so check the label for the word trocken.

cards.q: What does 'GG' on a German bottle mean?
options: A dry wine from a top vineyard
cards.explain: GG stands for Grosses Gewächs: a dry wine from a VDP Grosse Lage, a top vineyard. It is Germany's equivalent of a Grand Cru dry wine.

cards.q: Put the Prädikat levels in order with their meaning
cards.explain: Each step up means riper, rarer grapes: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese. The higher levels are often sweet, and only the sweetest need botrytis.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Austria, Hungary and Greece

cards.title: Austria
cards.body:
**Grüner Veltliner** (white pepper, citrus) and **Riesling** shine on the Danube terraces of the **Wachau**, **Kremstal** and **Kamptal**. The Wachau grades dry wines as **Steinfeder**, **Federspiel** and **Smaragd** (richest).

**Blaufränkisch** and **Zweigelt** make spicy reds in Burgenland; around Lake **Neusiedl**, mists bring noble-rot sweet wines.

cards.title: Hungary
cards.body: Beyond Tokaji: dry **Furmint** is now a serious white; **Eger** makes the red blend *Egri Bikavér* ("Bull's Blood"); **Villány** in the warm south grows Cabernet Franc and Bordeaux blends.

cards.title: Greece
cards.body:
- **Santorini**: **Assyrtiko** on volcanic ash; vines trained into low baskets (*kouloura*) to shelter grapes from wind. Sweet **Vinsanto** from sun-dried grapes.
- **Naoussa**: **Xinomavro**, tannic and tomato-scented, Greece's "Barolo".
- **Nemea**: soft, fruity **Agiorgitiko**.

cards.q: What is the richest dry wine category in the Wachau?
cards.explain: Smaragd, named after the emerald lizard sunning itself on the terraces, is the Wachau's richest dry category. It is full-bodied and often 13% alcohol or more.

cards.q: Why are Santorini vines trained into baskets?
options: To protect grapes from strong winds and sun
cards.explain: Santorini's strong winds would shred the vines, so they are trained into low baskets called kouloura that shelter the bunches inside the coiled vine. Volcanic ash soil also spared the island from phylloxera.

cards.q: Egri Bikavér is a sweet white wine.
cards.explain: Egri Bikavér, Bull's Blood of Eger, is a red blend, not a sweet white. Legend says the defenders of Eger castle drank the wine in 1552 and fought like bulls.

cards.title: Tokaji, wine of kings
cards.body:
In **Tokaj**, Hungary, noble rot was understood by the **1600s**; by legend a harvest delayed by Turkish raids led to the first Aszú. In **1730** the vineyards were classified, more than a century before Bordeaux's 1855 list.

Louis XIV called it "**the wine of kings, the king of wines**". Communism (1949–1989) turned Tokaj into a state farm; investment from France and Spain after 1990 revived it.

cards.title: Germany's late harvest
cards.body:
The Romans planted the **Mosel**, and monasteries such as **Kloster Eberbach** made the Rheingau famous. In **1775**, at **Schloss Johannisberg**, the messenger carrying permission to start the harvest was late; the grapes rotted, the wine was wonderful, and **Spätlese** ("late harvest") was born.

In the 1800s, top Rieslings cost more than First Growth Bordeaux. Wars, then cheap sweet exports such as Liebfraumilch, hurt its name; today's dry **Grosses Gewächs** wines have rebuilt it.

cards.title: Austria's clean start
cards.body:
In **1985** a few Austrian brokers were caught sweetening wine with **diethylene glycol**. Exports collapsed overnight. Austria responded with some of the strictest wine laws in the world.

A new generation focused on dry **Grüner Veltliner** and **Riesling** from the **Wachau** and Kamptal, and Austrian wine is now admired for its purity.

cards.q: What happened at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775?
options: A late messenger delayed the harvest and Spätlese was born
cards.explain: The overripe, partly botrytized grapes made exceptional wine: the start of Germany's late-harvest tradition.

cards.q: Tokaj's vineyards were classified in 1730, before Bordeaux's 1855 classification.
cards.explain: Tokaj's vineyards were classified in 1730, well before Bordeaux's 1855 classification. That makes it one of the oldest classifications in the world, and shows how highly its sweet wines were prized.

cards.q: What did the 1985 scandal lead to in Austria?
options: Very strict wine laws and a focus on quality
The end of Austrian wine exports forever
cards.explain: After the 1985 glycol scandal, when some producers added antifreeze to make wine seem sweeter, Austria rebuilt its reputation on dry, pure, carefully controlled wines with strict quality laws.

cards.title: German Riesling styles
cards.body: German Riesling ranges from bone-dry **Grosses Gewächs** to sweet **Beerenauslese** and **Trockenbeerenauslese**. The **Mosel** gives light, delicate, often off-dry wines on steep slate; the **Pfalz** and **Rheingau** give fuller, drier styles.

cards.title: Tokaji Aszú
cards.body: In Hungary's **Tokaj**, botrytized aszú berries are soaked in base wine or must. The result is one of the world's great sweet wines, with apricot, orange peel and honey, kept fresh by Furmint's acidity.

cards.q: Which German region is famous for steep slate slopes along a winding river?
cards.explain: The Mosel's slate slopes along its winding river are among the steepest vineyards in the world. The slate stores heat, which helps ripen Riesling in a cool climate.

cards.q: Match the wine to its main grape
cards.explain: Central Europe's classics rely on local stars: Riesling in the Mosel, Grüner Veltliner in the Wachau, Furmint in Tokaj and Blaufränkisch in Burgenland. Learning the grape for each place helps a lot.

cards.q: Trockenbeerenauslese is a dry wine.
cards.explain: Despite trocken in the name, TBA is made from shriveled botrytized berries and is intensely sweet. Trockenbeeren means dried berries, not dry wine, which is a classic trap.

cards.q: In the Wachau, what is 'Smaragd'?
cards.explain: Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd rank the Wachau's dry whites by ripeness: Smaragd is the ripest and richest. The names come from a grass, a falconry term and a lizard.

cards.q: Hungary's most famous sweet wine comes from ___.
cards.explain: Hungary's most famous sweet wine comes from Tokaj, the world's first classified wine region, in 1730. Its Aszú wines are measured in puttonyos, the baskets of botrytized berries added to the base wine.

units.title: The New World
units.summary: USA, Chile and Argentina, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.

cards.title: The West Coast
cards.body:
- **California**: Mediterranean climate cooled by Pacific fog. Napa (Cabernet), Sonoma (Pinot, Chardonnay, Zinfandel), the Central Coast (Pinot in the Santa Rita Hills, Rhône varieties in Paso Robles), Lodi (old-vine Zinfandel).
- **Oregon**: cool, wet Willamette Valley; Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris.
- **Washington**: dry, irrigated Columbia Valley east of the Cascades; Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah, Riesling.

cards.title: Napa up close
cards.body: Napa is cooler in the south (Carneros, near San Pablo Bay) and hotter up-valley toward Calistoga. Famous AVAs include Oakville, Rutherford and Stags Leap District, plus mountain AVAs like Howell Mountain.

cards.q: Why does Washington's Columbia Valley need irrigation?
options: It lies in the rain shadow of the Cascades
The soils hold too much water
cards.explain: Eastern Washington is semi-desert, receiving less than 200 mm of rain a year, so vineyards need irrigation. The Columbia river and its tributaries supply water, and the dry climate means little rot or disease.

cards.q: Which Oregon region is famous for Pinot Noir?
cards.explain: The Willamette Valley is famous for Pinot Noir. Its cool, cloudy climate echoes Burgundy, and it is the same latitude as Burgundy, about 45° north.

cards.q: Carneros, in the south of Napa and Sonoma, is cooled by San Pablo Bay.
cards.explain: Carneros, in the south of Napa and Sonoma, is cooled by San Pablo Bay. Wind and fog from the bay make it ideal for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine, not Cabernet.

cards.q: The 1976 Judgment of ___ put Napa Valley on the world map.
cards.explain: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet and Chateau Montelena Chardonnay beat top French wines in a blind tasting.

cards.title: Chile: between ocean and Andes
cards.body: A narrow strip cooled by the **Humboldt Current** and Andean air. **Maipo** for Cabernet, **Colchagua** for Carmenère, **Casablanca** and Leyda for cool whites and Pinot Noir. Chile is phylloxera-free.

cards.title: Argentina: wine in the high desert
cards.body: High-altitude desert at the foot of the Andes. **Mendoza** and the **Uco Valley** for Malbec; **Salta** (Cafayate) for Torrontés at up to 3,000 m.

cards.q: Why can Argentina make fresh wines despite intense sun?
options: Very high altitude and cold nights
cards.explain: Altitude gives a big difference between day and night, preserving acidity, and the thin air means strong UV, which builds thick skins and deep color. That is why high-altitude Malbec is so dark and fresh.

cards.q: Which Chilean valley is known for cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc?
cards.explain: Casablanca Valley is known for cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. Morning fog from the Pacific keeps it cool, so the wines are fresh and aromatic.

cards.q: Argentina's vineyards are irrigated with Andean snowmelt.
cards.explain: Argentina's vineyards are irrigated with Andean snowmelt, since rainfall in Mendoza is only about 200 mm a year. Channels built by the Huarpe people centuries ago still feed the vines.

cards.q: Match the region to its signature
cards.explain: Four classic South American pairings: Malbec in Mendoza, Torrontés in Salta, Carmenère in Colchagua, and Sauvignon Blanc in Casablanca. Each place is matched to its grape.

cards.title: Australia
cards.body:
- **Barossa** & **McLaren Vale**: rich Shiraz, Grenache.
